0.title: Faith That Works: The Letter of James
0.overview:
James is the most practical book in the New Testament — and one of the most misunderstood. Martin Luther famously called it “an epistle of straw,” contrasting its apparent emphasis on works with Paul’s gospel of grace. He was wrong — his polemical situation against Roman Catholic merit theology made him over-read James as a rival to Paul rather than as his complement. Read on its own terms, James is not a rival to the gospel of grace but its most searching ethical application: what does genuine, living, gospel-produced faith actually look like? The answer is not passive and invisible. It looks like patience in trials, generosity to the poor, a bridled tongue, peaceful wisdom, and prayer that moves heaven.

The author identifies himself as “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). The most natural identification is James the brother of Jesus, the leader of the Jerusalem church, the man who had not believed in Jesus during his earthly ministry (John 7:5) but was transformed by a resurrection appearance (1 Cor 15:7) into the pillar of the first church (Gal 2:9) and its martyred leader (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9). The letter was probably written before the Jerusalem Council of AD 49, making it possibly the earliest New Testament letter — which means James was wrestling with the application of the gospel to practical life before Paul had written most of his letters.

The letter draws deeply on the Sermon on the Mount, which James had presumably heard from Jesus himself, and on the Old Testament wisdom tradition — Proverbs, Job, the Psalms of lament. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” — Jewish Christians scattered beyond Palestine, probably after the persecution that followed Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1). These were people under pressure: economic hardship, social marginalization, the temptation to compromise, the fracturing of community under stress.

James’s relationship to Paul is complementary, not contradictory. Paul says Abraham was justified by faith (Rom 4); James says Abraham was justified by works (Jas 2:21). The difference is not in the content of justification but in its reference point: Paul speaks of justification before God in the court of heaven (the forensic verdict of “righteous” that comes through faith alone); James speaks of justification before men in the arena of visible life (the demonstration that faith is genuine, which appears in its works). Both agree that dead faith saves no one; both agree that living faith produces fruit. Paul says faith alone justifies; James says the faith that justifies is never alone.

Read James as the letter that will not let you be comfortable with a merely intellectual Christianity. It asks the hardest questions: Does your faith survive under pressure? Does it make you generous? Does it control your tongue? Does it make you humble? Does it make you pray? These are not questions about earning salvation but about whether what you call faith is the real thing. James is not offering a second route to justification; he is describing what justification produces in the life of the one who has genuinely received it. It produces the kind of faith that works — which is the only kind that is faith at all.

1.title: Tested and Proven: Trials, Wisdom, and the Word
1.overview:
Chapter 1 sets out the letter’s concern: real faith under pressure. James starts with circumstance, not doctrine. His readers are in trials, and in God’s hands trials produce what nothing else can: tested faith, steadfastness and maturity.

Three threads run through the chapter: trials and the faith they prove (vv. 2–12); temptation, which comes from our own desires, not from God, the unchanging giver of every good gift (vv. 13–18); and the word of God, which gives new birth, must be done and not only heard, and produces pure religion (vv. 19–27). The key word is “perfect” or “complete” (vv. 4, 17, 25): not flawless, but whole. Its opposite is the double-minded man (v. 8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Trials, Wisdom, and the God Who Does Not Change
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James, a servant of Christ, writes to scattered believers. Count trials joy, because tested faith produces steadfastness and maturity. If you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously, but ask without being double-minded. Poor and rich alike should boast in what God has made them. The one who endures will receive the crown of life. God never tempts anyone; temptation comes from our own desire and ends in death. But every good gift comes from the unchanging Father of lights, who gave us new birth by the word of truth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing and Tempting

God tests to prove and strengthen; he never tempts. Temptation comes from our own desire, while every good gift comes from the Father of lights, who does not change.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were scattered believers under real pressure and real poverty.

Now: Counting trials joy is a judgment about what they produce, and it can be made while we are still in pain.

verseByVerse.quote: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: Greetings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: Greetings.

Meaning first. James 1 introduces the letter’s great theme: genuine faith shows itself in a whole, consistent life. It begins with trials (vv. 2–4): meet them with joy, because the testing of faith produces endurance, and endurance leads to maturity. If anyone lacks the wisdom to handle trials, he should ask God, who gives generously, but ask in faith, not with a divided mind (vv. 5–8). Both poor and rich should see their situation in God’s light: the poor are exalted, the rich will fade like grass (vv. 9–11). Those who endure trial will receive the crown of life (v. 12). But no one should blame God for temptation; temptation arises from our own desires, which conceive sin and give birth to death, while God gives only good gifts and has brought us to new birth by his word (vv. 13–18). So be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to anger, get rid of filth, and humbly receive the implanted word that can save (vv. 19–21). And do not merely hear the word; do it. A hearer who does not act is like someone who looks in a mirror and forgets his face; the one who looks into the perfect law of liberty and acts will be blessed (vv. 22–25). True religion is not just talk but bridling the tongue, caring for orphans and widows, and keeping oneself unstained by the world (vv. 26–27). And behind every command in the chapter stands one unchanging Father, the giver of every good gift, who brought us to birth by his own will.

The setting. James was most likely the brother of Jesus, who came to faith after the resurrection (Mark 6:3; John 7:5; 1 Corinthians 15:7) and became the leading elder of the Jerusalem church (Acts 12:17; 15:13–21; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). He was known as James the Just for his righteousness and prayerfulness; an early tradition preserved by Eusebius says his knees grew hard like a camel’s from kneeling in prayer for his people. He was martyred around AD 62: the Jewish historian Josephus records that the high priest Ananus had him stoned during a gap between Roman governors. The letter was probably written in the 40s, which would make it one of the earliest New Testament writings. It is intensely practical, full of echoes of Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount, and close in feel to Old Testament wisdom literature like Proverbs: short, vivid, memorable sayings, each one aimed at the conscience.

James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. The word is doulos: slave, bondservant, a man who belongs to someone else. And the restraint in it is remarkable once you know who is almost certainly writing. Not one of the Twelve. The James who leads the Jerusalem church in Acts 15, whose ruling settles the Gentile question for the whole movement, and whom Paul lists among the pillars (Galatians 2:9). He is also, the New Testament tells us plainly, the Lord’s brother (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19).

The brother who says slave. Weigh that against the single word he chooses. He grew up in the same house. He watched Jesus learn the carpenter’s trade, ate at the same table, slept under the same roof for perhaps thirty years. Any claim he wished to make was available to him, and in a church that prized connection with Jesus it would have opened every door. He writes slave, and never mentions the relationship at all. The one man in the early church who could have said I knew him before any of you did chose instead to say that he belongs to him like a purchased servant.

The Lord Jesus Christ. And there is a further thing behind it. During the ministry his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5); they came once to take him home, because people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). What changed is recorded in a single line: then he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). We are told nothing about that meeting. We are only shown the result: a man who once thought his brother was mad now calls him Lord, gives him the title Christ, the promised Messiah, and names him in the same breath as God. A brother does not come to worship the boy he grew up with unless something has happened that cannot be explained any other way. The resurrection is the only explanation the New Testament offers, and it is the only one that fits.

To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion. The Dispersion (diaspora, scattering) was the name for Jews living outside the land of Israel. Here it most likely means Jewish Christians driven out by the persecution that followed Stephen’s death (Acts 8:1; 11:19). These are refugees. It matters for everything that follows: the trials in verse 2 are not hypothetical, the poverty in chapter 2 is not a theological example, and the exploited labourers in chapter 5 had names. And twelve tribes is the name of the whole people of God. James addresses a scattered, frightened, poor collection of believers by the most dignified name in Israel’s history. The church, made up of Jewish and later Gentile believers, is God’s people scattered as pilgrims in the world (1 Peter 1:1), and nobody in it is a stray.

Greetings. The ordinary salutation of a Greek letter, chairein, the word on any business note of the period, and literally rejoice. As a letter greeting it appears in only two other places in the New Testament: a Roman officer’s letter (Acts 23:26), and the letter from the Jerusalem council in Acts 15:23, drafted under this man’s presidency. It is a small fingerprint, and it points the same way. And it is a wordplay. The very next word in Greek is joy (charan): greetings, rejoice; count it all joy. James has barely said hello before he is talking about joy, and he is talking to refugees.

Where Christians differ: was James a full brother of Jesus? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin all her life, so that the brothers of Jesus were cousins or children of Joseph by an earlier marriage; many Orthodox Christians hold the second view. Verdict: the most natural reading of the New Testament is that James was a younger half-brother of Jesus, a son of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus. Matthew 1:25 says Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son, and Jesus is called her firstborn (Luke 2:7). The Gospels name his brothers and mention sisters alongside Mary (Mark 6:3), and the Greek has perfectly good words for cousin which are never used of them. The doctrine of perpetual virginity is not taught in Scripture. This does not lessen Mary’s honour as the mother of our Lord. All generations call her blessed (Luke 1:48), and the best honour we can give her is to do what she said at Cana: whatever he tells you, do it (John 2:5).

What it does not mean. Servant does not mean James was a lesser follower. It expresses his complete devotion, and in the Old Testament servant of the LORD is the title of Moses, David and the prophets. Nor does addressing the twelve tribes mean the letter is only for ethnic Jews; it is Scripture for the whole church, and it has fed Gentile believers for two thousand years.

Which James is this? The New Testament has several. James the son of Zebedee, John’s brother, was one of the Twelve, but Herod had him killed very early, around AD 44 (Acts 12:2), probably too early to have written this letter. James the son of Alphaeus was also one of the Twelve, but nothing else is known of him. The James who could simply sign himself James, with no further description, and expect every church to know who he meant, was the leader of the Jerusalem church, the Lord’s brother. That is why most scholars, and the church from early on, have taken him to be the author.

Should James be in the Bible at all? Luther did call it an epistle of straw, in 1522, comparing it with Romans, Galatians and John, because he found it said too little about Christ and grace and feared it taught justification by works. But Luther kept it in his Bible, preached from it, and his own later followers and the whole Reformed tradition have received it gladly as Scripture. James does not deny justification by faith; he denies that a faith which produces nothing is the faith that justifies, which is exactly what Paul teaches too (Galatians 5:6). Read James as the Spirit’s word to comfortable believers, and the straw turns out to be iron.

In a sentence. From James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to God’s people scattered among the nations: greetings.

On a Tuesday. Notice how you introduce yourself, and what you reach for when you want to be taken seriously: the job title, the connection, the qualification, the person you know. James had the best connection in the history of the world and did not use it. Ask what it would look like this week to let belonging to Christ be the first and sufficient thing about you. And if you feel scattered, displaced or overlooked, remember that God addresses his scattered people by their royal name.

For worship. The man who knew Jesus longest from the outside came to know him last from the inside, and when he did, he bowed. The carpenter’s son who shared his brother’s bed and table rose from the dead, met the brother who had doubted him, and made him a pillar of his church. That is what the risen Christ does with unbelief: he does not argue it away, he appears to it. And the Lord who would not leave his own family in their unbelief is Lord of the scattered still, gathering them by name into one people, twelve tribes, not one lost.
verseByVerse.note: James was most likely the brother of Jesus, who came to faith after the resurrection and led the Jerusalem church. He was put to death about AD 62. “The Dispersion” means Jewish believers scattered outside the land of Israel. The letter echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

Count it all joy, my brothers. It is one of the hardest sentences in the New Testament, and it is the first thing James says after hello. Notice first what he does not say. Not feel joy. The verb is hēgēsasthe: reckon, consider, evaluate. It is an accounting word, the same family Paul uses in Philippians 3:7 when he counts his credentials as loss. James is not commanding an emotion, which nobody can produce on demand. He is commanding a judgment about what trials are, and a judgment can be made while you are still miserable. All joy (pasan charan) means nothing but joy, pure joy: not joy in the pain itself, but joy in what God is doing through it. And my brothers, which he says fifteen times in this short letter, is not a formula. He is a pastor writing to people he loves, and he does not tell them hard things from a distance.

When you meet trials. When, not if. And the verb behind meet (peripesēte) means to fall into, to encounter unexpectedly. It is the word used of the man who fell among robbers on the Jericho road (Luke 10:30). Trials are not scheduled. You come round a corner into them: the phone call, the diagnosis, the letter, the conversation that goes wrong. And the word for trials (peirasmois) can mean either outward hardships or inner temptations to sin. Here it is hardships; by verse 13 James will be using the same root for temptation, and the double meaning is part of his teaching.

Of various kinds. The word is poikilois: many-coloured, variegated, like a woven cloth. Poverty, persecution, illness, bereavement, conflict, disappointment, the slow ache of a prayer not yet answered. Trials come in every colour. And there is a beautiful echo in Peter. He uses the same word for trials of many kinds (1 Peter 1:6), and then three chapters later uses it again of God’s grace: good stewards of God’s varied grace (1 Peter 4:10). Many-coloured trials, many-coloured grace. There is no shade of suffering for which God does not have a matching shade of grace.

For you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. Then the reason, and the whole command depends on it. The joy is not irrational; it is informed. James gives a fact and expects the reckoning to follow from it. The word for testing (dokimion) is the assayer’s term: the process that proves metal genuine and refines it in the same fire (1 Peter 1:7). And what it produces (katergazetai, works out, achieves) is hypomonē, which is not passive resignation. It is the capacity to remain under a weight without collapsing, and it is the one virtue that cannot be acquired any other way. There is no shortcut to it, no book that confers it, no prayer that installs it. It is only ever made in the place where it is needed. Paul says the same: suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope (Romans 5:3–4). Trials are God’s gymnasium for faith.

And let steadfastness have its full effect. There is a warning folded into that. The process can be cut short: by escaping at any cost, by numbing it, by getting bitter, all of which end the discomfort and end the work with it. The full effect (ergon teleion) is the finished work, the completed result. James is asking his readers not to walk out of the refiner’s shop while the metal is still in the fire.

That you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing. Perfect here is teleioi, meaning finished, having reached its end, not sinless. It is what you say of a full-grown animal or a completed building. Complete (holoklēroi) means whole in every part, with nothing missing, the word used of a sacrifice without blemish. James is describing maturity: a Christian character fully formed, more and more like Christ. And he says the road to it runs through the thing you would most like to avoid.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should pretend trials do not hurt, or enjoy pain itself, or seek out suffering. Jesus wept at a friend’s tomb and agonised in the garden (John 11:35; Luke 22:44). Christian joy is not the absence of tears but something underneath them. It means we can rejoice, even through tears, because God is using the trial for our good (Romans 8:28; Hebrews 12:11). Nor does it mean every hardship should simply be accepted. If you can lawfully escape danger, or get treatment, or leave an abusive situation, you should. Endurance is for what God does not remove, not a reason to stay where he has given you a way out.

Does this mean God sent my suffering? Scripture says God rules over all things, including our trials, and that nothing reaches his children except by his permission and for his purpose (Romans 8:28; Lamentations 3:37–38). But he does not delight in our pain, and many trials come through other people’s sin, which he hates. The comfort is not that every hard thing is good in itself. It is that no hard thing is wasted. The same God who allowed Joseph to be sold by his brothers used it to save many lives (Genesis 50:20). You may not see the purpose this side of heaven, and you are not required to. You are invited to trust the one who does.

How can I count it joy when I am crushed or grieving or depressed? Remember the verb: it is reckoning, not feeling. You may weep every day this month and still be counting it joy, if in the middle of the tears you say: Lord, I do not understand this, but I believe you are working, and I will not let go. That is what the Psalms do; many of them begin in darkness. If you are depressed, seek help from your doctor and your pastor; that is not a failure of faith. The joy James means is often a quiet thing: a stubborn confidence that God is not finished, held with a trembling hand.

In a sentence. My brothers and sisters, whenever you run into trials of many kinds, treat it as an occasion for pure joy, because you know that the testing of your faith produces endurance. Let endurance finish its work, so that you may be mature and whole, not lacking anything.

On a Tuesday. Name the trial you are actually in right now, not the general sense that life is hard, but the specific thing. Then ask two questions of it. What would it look like for me to cut this short, to escape it, numb it or turn bitter? And what might God be building in me that could not be built any other way? Then say thank you, aloud if you can, not for the pain but for the God who is at work in it. You may not feel joyful afterwards. You will have done what James asked.

For worship. James can ask this because he has seen it done. His brother endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). He counted it all joy in the only trial that was ever unmixed suffering, and he did it with nothing in him to refine, for our sake, so that our trials could become a refiner’s fire rather than a judge’s. The furnace you are in has been entered before you by the Son of God, and he walks in it with you, as he walked with three young men in Babylon. The fire burns only the ropes.

verseByVerse.quote: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind.

If any of you lacks wisdom. The connection to what precedes is easy to miss and it is the point. James has just said trials produce maturity, lacking in nothing (v. 4). The immediate practical problem is that when you are in one you cannot see what it is doing, and you do not know what to do next. Hence: if any of you lacks. It is the same word (leipetai). If you are lacking anything in the trial, it is probably wisdom. And this is not a general offer of intelligence. It is wisdom for the trial: how to act in the middle of something you did not choose and cannot understand. Biblical wisdom (sophia) is never abstract. It is skill in living, seeing life from God’s point of view, the knowledge of what to do on Tuesday (Proverbs 1:7; 2:6; James 3:13–18).

Let him ask God. That is the whole method. Not work it out, not consult the experienced first, not wait for clarity: ask. The verb is a present imperative, and it carries the sense of keep asking. Solomon was offered anything, and asked for an understanding mind to govern God’s people and to discern between good and evil, and God was pleased (1 Kings 3:9–12). The God who answered that prayer has not changed his mind about it.

Who gives generously to all without reproach. Then two things about the God who is asked, and both remove an excuse. He gives generously (haplōs): the word means singly, simply, without calculation, holding nothing back, with an open hand and a whole heart. And without reproach (mē oneidizontos), which is the tender one. He does not sigh. He does not remind you that you asked last month, or that you would not need to ask if you had listened the first time. He is not like a grudging human benefactor who gives with a lecture. Most of us have been made to feel small by someone we asked for help, and James says: not here.

And it will be given him. A flat promise, without conditions about how clever you are or how well you have done. It is the same promise Jesus made: ask, and it will be given to you; how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him (Matthew 7:7–11).

But let him ask in faith, with no doubting. And this needs care, because it has wounded people. The doubting described is not the ache of a believer who struggles. The New Testament is full of tenderness toward that, and the man who said I believe; help my unbelief got what he asked for (Mark 9:24). The word (diakrinomenos) means to be divided, at odds within oneself, debating with oneself whether to trust God or rely on something else. To ask in faith is to come trusting God’s character and promise, not trusting your own certainty.

Like a wave of the sea. And the image explains it. Not a stone sinking. A wave, something with no fixed position at all, driven and tossed by the wind, moved by whatever is blowing at the time, going wherever it is pushed and returning nowhere (Ephesians 4:14; Isaiah 57:20). That is the picture: a man who wants God’s wisdom on Sunday and the world’s on Monday, who asks and then goes to arrange matters himself. He is not weak in faith. He is in two minds, and the next verses name it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean any flicker of doubt cancels prayer. The father who said I believe; help my unbelief was answered. The doubting here is a settled double-mindedness, not trusting God wholeheartedly. Nor does it mean God will give whatever we ask if we only believe hard enough; the promise here is for wisdom, and in all our asking God answers according to his will (1 John 5:14). Faith is not a force we generate to make things happen. It is trust in a Person.

How does God actually give wisdom? Should I expect a voice or a sign? Ordinarily God gives wisdom through his word, which is able to make you wise (2 Timothy 3:15), through a mind being renewed by it (Romans 12:2), through the counsel of mature believers (Proverbs 15:22), and through his providence opening and closing doors. Scripture is complete and sufficient, so we do not need new revelations; the Spirit’s work is to help us understand and apply what he has already said. In practice, wisdom often comes quietly: a passage that suddenly fits your situation, a friend’s question, a growing clarity over days. Ask, read, seek counsel, then act on the best light you have, trusting God to correct you if you are wrong.

I asked for wisdom and I still do not know what to do. Sometimes wisdom is not a clear answer about the future but the grace to take the next right step. God may not show you the whole road; he promises a lamp to your feet (Psalm 119:105), which lights one step at a time. If two paths are both lawful and both seem wise, you are free to choose, and God is not waiting to punish you for picking the wrong door. And sometimes the wisdom we lack is not what to do but how to bear what we cannot change, patiently, without bitterness. That is wisdom too, and it is often the deepest answer to this prayer.

In a sentence. If any of you is short of wisdom, ask God for it. He gives freely to everyone and does not scold you for asking, and it will be given to you. But when you ask, you must believe and not waver, because a person who wavers is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.

On a Tuesday. Write down the one decision or trial you most need wisdom for right now. Ask God for wisdom about it today, specifically, by name. Then ask yourself honestly: if he shows me something I do not want, will I do it? If the answer is no, that is the place to start praying. And over the next week, read Scripture, talk to one wise believer, and watch for how he answers.

For worship. God does not merely give wisdom; he has given us Wisdom in person. Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30), and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). The Father who gives without reproach did not reproach us when we came to him with nothing; he gave us his Son. He is the God whose hand is always open, who never tires of being asked, who has never once answered a humble prayer with a sigh. Generous, simple, whole-hearted giving is not something God does occasionally. It is what he is.

verseByVerse.quote: For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord; he is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord; he is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.

For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord. It is a blunt sentence and it sounds harsh until you see why. Suppose (oiesthō) means to think, imagine, expect. The person who prays with a divided heart should not expect an answer: not because God is stingy, but because such a person is not truly trusting him.

He is a double-minded man. The reason is in this line. The word is dipsychos, two-souled, and so far as we can tell James coined it. It appears nowhere in Greek before this letter. He needed a new word because he is describing something the old ones did not cover: not a man who disbelieves, and not a man who half-believes, but a man with two centres operating at once. Two sets of loyalties, both genuine, pulling in different directions. He prays sincerely and hedges sincerely. He tries to serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). And notice the contrast with God, who gives simply (haplōs, v. 5), with a single heart. The giver is undivided, and the asker is in two pieces.

The disease of the whole letter. Double-mindedness is the root of everything James will confront. Faith without works (2:14), blessing and cursing from one mouth (3:10), friendship with God and with the world (4:4): every section of James is an application of this one word. He will use it again at 4:8, where he names the remedy: draw near to God, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. The whole letter is a call to be one person before God.

Unstable in all his ways. Not unstable only in his prayer life; in all his ways. The word (akatastatos) means restless, unsettled, disorderly, and James uses it again of the tongue, a restless evil (3:8). A man divided at the centre is divided everywhere, and the instability shows up in his work, his relationships and his commitments, not merely in his religion.

Why does such a man receive nothing? Not because God is withholding out of pique. It is nearer to say he is unable to receive: a man who asks for wisdom while intending to keep his options open has not actually asked for it. He has asked for a second opinion, which he will weigh against the others. The searching question this puts is not whether you doubt. It is whether, before you prayed, you had already decided what you would do if the answer went the wrong way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God ignores weak or struggling believers. He hears the cry of the weak; a bruised reed he will not break (Isaiah 42:3). It means a heart deliberately divided between God and something else cannot expect to receive from him.

How do I know whether I am double-minded or simply weak? The weak believer wants God wholly and finds he cannot do it well; the double-minded man wants God partly and is content to keep it that way. The weak believer grieves over his divided heart and brings it to God; the double-minded man has made his peace with it. So ask: is there an area of my life where I have quietly decided God will not have the final word? Money, a relationship, my reputation, a habit? If you find one and it troubles you, that trouble is the Spirit’s work, and it is the first sign of a heart being made whole.

Can a divided heart be made whole? Yes, and God is the one who does it. David prayed: unite my heart to fear your name (Psalm 86:11). God promised his people one heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 11:19). So start there: pray David’s prayer, and then take the one area you are holding back and give it to God in some concrete act this week. A heart is unified the way a divided kingdom is, by surrendering one province at a time to the rightful King.

In a sentence. That kind of person should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. Such a person is divided in loyalty and unstable in everything they do.

On a Tuesday. Before you pray about anything important this week, stop and ask: what will I do if God’s answer is not the one I want? If you have already made a plan B that leaves God out, confess it. Then pray with your hands open. And look for the hedge: the money kept back, the option kept quietly open, the relationship you will not let him touch.

For worship. There was one man who was never in two minds. Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and nothing turned him: not the crowds, not Peter, not the agony in the garden, where he prayed not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). His heart was single toward the Father from the manger to the cross. And that undivided obedience is counted to us who are so often double, while his Spirit works in us to unite our hearts. We are not saved by our singleness of heart; we are saved by his, and made single by his grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits.

Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation. James turns to money, and he will keep coming back to it; this letter has more to say about rich and poor than any other in the New Testament. Lowly (tapeinos) means humble, poor, of low status. The poor believer, and in that congregation of refugees that meant genuinely poor, is told to boast (kauchasthō, glory, take pride) in his exaltation (hypsei, high position). Not in his poverty, and not merely in a future compensation. In what he already is: a child of God, an heir of the kingdom (2:5), seated with Christ in the heavenly places. His social position is the least true thing about him. Poverty is one of the trials of verse 2; faith sees it from God’s viewpoint.

And the rich in his humiliation. The sentence is built as a crossing, and each half says the opposite of what the world says. The rich believer is told to boast in his humiliation (tapeinōsei, being brought low): in discovering that his money buys him nothing at all where it counts, that he came to God with empty hands like everybody else, a sinner saved by grace standing on the same level as the poorest member of his church. That is a harder boast, and it is the only one available to him. And perhaps also in the trials that bring him low, the losses that teach him what his wealth could never teach. God has always reversed the world’s rankings: he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:52–53; 1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

Because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. Then the reason, and the image is drawn from a landscape James walked in, and from Isaiah 40:6–8, which his readers knew by heart: all flesh is grass, the grass withers, the flower fades. Wealth and the rich person alike are temporary.

For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass. Anyone who has seen a Palestinian spring knows this exactly. The hills turn green and flower after the rains, and then the scorching heat comes (kausōn, which may mean the hot east wind off the desert, the sirocco), and within a day the whole thing is brown. Not months. A day. Its flower falls, and its beauty (euprepeia, the grace of its appearance) perishes. However beautiful, it does not last.

So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits. That last phrase is the sting. Pursuits (poreiais) means journeys, business trips, the ways he goes about. Not after his pursuits, when he has finished and can look back. In the middle of them, with the plans half-made and the diary full. It is exactly the man in the Lord’s parable who had just decided to build bigger barns and was told: this night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:16–21). Wealth does not protect from death. It only gives a man more to leave behind.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all rich people are unbelievers or that wealth is sinful. Abraham and Job were rich and loved God. If brother applies to both halves of the sentence, James is addressing a rich believer. It means wealth is temporary and gives no standing before God, while the poor believer has an eternal inheritance.

Where Christians differ: is the rich man in verse 10 a believer? Some think brother carries over, so James is telling rich Christians to glory in their humbling. Others note that the rich in this letter are always outsiders and oppressors (2:6–7; 5:1–6), and read the line as bitter irony: let the rich man boast in the only thing coming to him, which is his destruction. Both readings are held by careful interpreters. The first fits the grammar a little better and gives a word to wealthy church members; the second fits the rest of the letter. Either way the lesson for us is the same: money is a flower, and anyone who builds his life on it is building on something that will be brown by evening.

Who counts as rich today? Most of us reading this. If you have food for tomorrow, a roof, a choice about what to wear, and some savings or a pension, then by any historical or global measure you are rich. It is easy to read James and think of billionaires. He would read it to us. That is not meant to produce guilt but freedom: to hold what you have loosely, to give generously (1 Timothy 6:17–19), and to find your boast not in what you own but in being a beggar who has been made an heir.

I am poor, and I am ashamed of it. What does this say to me? It says your poverty is real but it is not the truest thing about you. In God’s house there is no second class. You are a son or daughter of the King, and your inheritance cannot be repossessed (1 Peter 1:4). Hold your head up in church. And if you are in real need, it is not shameful to let your brothers and sisters help; the early church shared so that no one among them was needy (Acts 4:34), and that is still how a church is meant to work.

In a sentence. The believer in humble circumstances should take pride in their high position in Christ, and the rich should take pride in being brought low, because the rich will pass away like a wild flower. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and dries up the plant; its blossom falls and its beauty is gone. In the same way, the rich will fade away even while they go about their business.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement for last month as if it were a diary, because it is one. What does it say you love? Then do one thing that loosens money’s grip: give something away quietly, or cancel something you do not need. If you are poor, spend five minutes thanking God for specific riches you have in Christ: forgiveness, a Father, a future, a family. If you are well off, ask: if it all went tomorrow, what would I still have?

For worship. Here is the great crossing behind James’s crossing. Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The Lord of glory was brought lower than any refugee: born in a borrowed place, buried in a borrowed tomb, stripped even of his clothes. He took the humiliation so that the lowly could have the exaltation. And unlike the flower of the grass, the riches he gives do not fade. The word of our God will stand for ever (Isaiah 40:8), and so will everyone who is hidden in him.

parallels.desc: The grass withers, the flower fades

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.

Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial. The word is makarios, the word of the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12): happy, fortunate, approved by God. And this verse rounds off everything since verse 2. There the command was to reckon trials joy; here is the outcome that makes the reckoning reasonable. Remains steadfast (hypomenei) is the verb form of the steadfastness of verse 3.

For when he has stood the test. The assayer’s word again (dokimos genomenos), and this time as a verdict rather than a process. The metal has been through the fire and passed. The trial had a purpose, and the purpose was reached.

He will receive the crown of life. The crown is stephanos, the victor’s wreath at the games, not a royal diadem (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4; Revelation 2:10). And the phrase almost certainly means the crown which is life. The reward is not a decoration to wear on top of eternal life. It is life itself, eternal life as the prize.

Which God has promised to those who love him. Then the two clauses that keep this from being a wage. It is a crown which God has promised, so it rests on a promise, not on the quality of the endurance. And it is promised to those who love him, not to those who endure impressively. That last phrase quietly reorders the whole verse. The person described is not a stoic with unusual reserves of grit. He is somebody who loves God, and the steadfastness is what love looks like when it is put under weight. Endurance without love is merely stubbornness, and James does not promise it anything. Those who love him is simply a description of true believers (2:5; Romans 8:28; 1 Corinthians 2:9), and love for God shows itself in not abandoning him when trials come.

A hinge. And the verse is a hinge. It closes the passage on trials from outside, and its word for trial is the same one that means temptation, which is what James turns to next. The same circumstance that God uses to prove faith is the one our own desire uses to solicit sin, and everything depends on knowing which is which.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eternal life is earned by enduring. It is God’s promised gift to those who love him. Endurance is the evidence of genuine love and faith, which God himself produces (v. 3), and those whom God has called he keeps to the end (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5).

What if I did not endure well? I gave in, or grew bitter, or nearly walked away. Then hear the gospel before you hear anything else: the crown rests on God’s promise, not on your performance. Peter denied Christ three times in one night and was restored by the fire on the beach (John 21:15–19). Endurance in Scripture is not a perfect record but a faith that keeps getting up and coming back. If you are reading this and still want Christ, you have not fallen away; you have stumbled, and the God who began a good work in you will finish it. Confess what went wrong, receive his forgiveness, and take the next step.

Are there different crowns for different Christians? The New Testament speaks of crowns in several places: of life, of righteousness, of glory (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4). These are best read not as separate prizes for an elite but as different ways of describing the one great gift every believer receives: eternal life with Christ, the righteousness he gives, the glory he shares. Scripture does teach that faithful service will be rewarded (1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but no believer will be outside the joy, and the elders in Revelation cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). The crowns end up at his feet.

In a sentence. Happy is the person who keeps going under trial, because when they have passed the test they will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love him.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone in your church who is under a long trial: an illness, a hard marriage, a disabled child, a slow grief. Endurance is often lonely. Send them a message today, or visit, and tell them you see what they are carrying. And if you are the one under the weight, say to God, in your own words, that you love him, and that you are staying. That is what endurance is.

For worship. The crown of life was first given to the one who endured most. Jesus was tested without remainder, stood the test in the wilderness and in Gethsemane and on the cross, and was crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). He wore a crown of thorns so that we could wear a crown of life. And the promise is his own: be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life (Revelation 2:10). The one who promised it rose from the dead to keep the promise, and he will set it on every head that loved him, however bruised.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.

Let no one say when he is tempted, I am being tempted by God. Now the same root (peirazō) shifts its meaning from test to tempt: an inner enticement to sin. Somebody was saying it, or James would not forbid it, and the excuse is perennial. He made me this way. He put the opportunity in front of me. He could have stopped it. Human beings have always blamed God for their sin. The very first man did it, within minutes of the very first sin: the woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate (Genesis 3:12). Notice the clause he put first. Not the woman; the woman you gave.

For God cannot be tempted with evil. The answer comes in two parts, and both are absolute. God cannot be tempted with evil (apeirastos, untemptable): there is nothing in him for evil to appeal to, no foothold, no answering appetite. He is utterly holy, light in whom is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5).

And he himself tempts no one. Never, in any circumstance, in any life. This needs holding alongside the fact that God does test. He tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1), and James has just spent eleven verses saying trials do good work. The same Greek root covers both, which is exactly why the confusion arises. The distinction is in the aim: a test is designed to prove and strengthen; a temptation is designed to destroy. One circumstance can be both at once, and the difference lies in who is using it for what. Joseph’s brothers meant it for evil; God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). Same event, two purposes.

But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then James names the real source, and it is closer to home. Both verbs come from hunting and fishing. Lured (exelkomenos) is to be dragged out of cover, an animal drawn out of its safe place; enticed (deleazomenos) is from the word for bait. The picture is a fish drawn from under the rock by something that looks like food, with the hook hidden inside it. And note the ownership: his own desire (epithymia). Not the devil, who does not appear in this analysis at all, and not the circumstance. The bait works because of what is already in the fish.

Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin. Then the metaphor changes to conception and birth, traced through four stages. Desire conceives: when it is welcomed and embraced by the will, it becomes pregnant (syllabousa). It gives birth to sin, the act. Sin grows to full term (apotelestheisa, brought to completion, matured). And what it delivers (apokyei) is death (Romans 6:23). It is a terrible genealogy: desire, sin, death. Sin is never satisfied; it grows until it kills.

Every stage looks manageable. The sequence is the point, because at every stage it looks manageable. A desire is not yet a sin, and can be entertained. A sin is small and can be handled. Nothing in the process announces where it is going, which is why James lays the whole line out in one sentence: so that you can see the end of it from the beginning, which is the one thing desire never lets you do. The bait never shows you the hook, and the first step never shows you the grave.

Where Christians differ: if God is sovereign over all things, is he the author of sin? Some object that the Reformed view of God’s sovereignty makes God responsible for evil. Verdict: God is sovereign over all things, including the sinful acts of human beings, which he permits and overrules for his good purposes (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Yet he is never the author of sin, never tempts anyone, and never approves of evil (Westminster 5.4). Sin arises from the creature’s own desires. God’s sovereignty and human responsibility are both taught in Scripture and must both be held, even when we cannot fully explain how they fit together. The cross is the proof: the most wicked act in history was planned by God for the salvation of the world, and the men who did it were guilty of it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean temptation itself is sin. Jesus was tempted without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Sin begins when desire is embraced. Nor does it deny that Satan tempts us (Matthew 4:1–11); but he can only work through our own desires, and we remain responsible. The devil can dangle the bait. He cannot make us bite.

Then why does the Lord’s Prayer say lead us not into temptation? God brings his people into trials, but never to make them sin. In that prayer (Matthew 6:13) we ask to be kept from trials that would overwhelm us, and to be delivered from the evil one when they come. It is the prayer of someone who knows his own weakness and does not trust himself, which is exactly the posture James wants.

Is being tempted itself a sin? No. Jesus was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Sin begins when the desire is welcomed and cherished, when it conceives (v. 15). A temptation resisted is a victory, not a failure. Many sensitive Christians are tormented by thoughts they hate. The thought that arrives uninvited is the bait being dangled; it becomes sin when you take it in, turn it over, and want it. The very fact that you hate it shows whose side you are on.

So what do I actually do in the moment of temptation? Name it honestly: this is my desire, not God’s plan. Look past the bait to the hook, and say to yourself where this leads. Then flee if you can (2 Timothy 2:22); Joseph left his cloak and ran. Pray, briefly and immediately, because he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). Fill the empty space with something good, and tell a trusted friend afterwards, since secrecy is the womb where desire conceives. And remember the promise: God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

In a sentence. When tempted, no one should say, God is tempting me. For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he does not tempt anyone. Instead, each person is tempted when they are dragged away and lured by their own desire. Then, once desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is fully grown, gives birth to death.

On a Tuesday. Identify your most frequent temptation and trace its genealogy honestly. When does the desire usually begin: tiredness, loneliness, a particular screen, a particular person, a particular time of night? That is where the battle is won or lost, long before the act. Plan this week to kill the desire before it conceives: remove the bait, change the hour, tell a friend. And stop saying, even silently, that it is not really your fault. Taking the blame is the beginning of freedom.

For worship. The God who cannot be tempted with evil sent his Son into the place of temptation for us. In the wilderness, hungry and alone, Jesus heard every lie that had ever worked on a human being and answered each with the word of God. He felt the full pull of temptation, more than we ever do, because he never gave in and so never felt it slacken. Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). The genealogy of desire, sin and death was reversed in him: he took our death, and gives us his life.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.

Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. The warning attaches to what has just been said. The lie about God, that he is behind your temptation, that he set you up, is not a harmless mistake. It is a deception (mē planasthe, do not be led astray), and James corrects it not by argument but by describing what God is actually like.

Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above. The traffic runs one way. Nothing bad comes down that road. If it is good, it came from there; if it came from there, it is good. In Greek the line has a poetic rhythm, almost a hexameter, and may be a saying James is quoting. Good gift (dosis agathē) is the act of giving that is good; perfect gift (dōrēma teleion) is the gift itself, complete. God gives well, and what he gives is whole. Far from tempting us, he is the source of everything good, from above (anōthen), from heaven.

Coming down from the Father of lights. The maker of sun, moon and stars (Genesis 1:14–18; Psalm 136:7–9), which is a title chosen for the sake of what follows. Because the one thing everybody knows about heavenly lights is that they change. The sun rises and sets and moves through the year; the moon waxes and wanes; the whole sky turns. Shadows shift all day long.

With whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. And there is the point. Variation (parallagē) is alteration; the shadow due to change (tropēs aposkiasma) is the shadow cast by turning, as the shadow moves round a sundial or the moon passes through its phases. The Father who made the changing lights does not himself change (Malachi 3:6; Hebrews 13:8). There is no season in him, no eclipse, no dark side, no angle from which he looks different. He has no moods. This is what theologians call God’s immutability, and here it is not a cold abstraction but a pastoral comfort.

The light does not flicker. That is precisely the comfort a suffering person needs, and it is why the sentence sits here. When you are in a trial, the temptation is not usually to doubt God’s existence. It is to suspect that he has gone cool: that he was favourable last year and is not now. James says the light does not flicker. Your circumstances turn like the sky; the one who loves you does not.

Of his own will he brought us forth. Then verse 18, and it is the supreme instance of the good gift. Of his own will (boulētheis, having willed, having purposed): God’s sovereign choice. Brought forth (apekyēsen) is a birth word, deliberately, because it answers verse 15. There, desire conceived and gave birth to sin, and sin brought forth death; it is the same verb. Here God brings forth life. Two pregnancies, two deliveries, and James sets them three verses apart. Sin gives birth to death; God gives birth to life. This is regeneration, the new birth (John 1:13; 3:3–8; 1 Peter 1:3, 23).

By the word of truth. The word of truth is the gospel (Ephesians 1:13; Colossians 1:5). The new birth begins with God’s will, and he uses his word to do it (1 Peter 1:23). No one is born again without hearing of Christ, and no one who is born again can take the credit, because no one has ever caused his own birth.

That we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures. Firstfruits (aparchē) is harvest language: the first sheaf brought in and offered to God, which is both a real portion and a pledge that the whole harvest belongs to him (Leviticus 23:10). These scattered believers are the opening instalment of a renewed creation; the whole groaning creation will follow (Romans 8:19–23). Early Jewish Christians were literally among the first, and every believer since is a sign of what God will do with everything he has made.

What it does not mean. Of his own will he brought us forth does not mean our response is unreal. We truly believe and truly repent. But our new birth originates in God’s sovereign will, not in our decision (John 1:13). Regeneration precedes and produces faith. This is effectual calling: God does not merely invite the dead to live; he speaks life into them, and they rise and come.

If God never changes, why does the Bible say he relented? When Scripture says God relented or changed his mind (Jonah 3:10), it is describing God’s dealings from our side: his settled character is to punish the unrepentant and spare the repentant, so when people turn, his response turns with them. His purposes and character do not change; that is exactly why his responses are so reliable. And it is why prayer is worth praying. We do not pray to a God who might be in a different mood today, but to one who has promised to hear and whose promises do not shift.

Does every good gift include good things unbelievers enjoy? Yes. Every sunrise, harvest, friendship, piece of music, act of healing and moment of laughter, whoever enjoys it, comes down from the Father of lights. Theologians call this common grace: he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good (Matthew 5:45). The tragedy of the unbeliever is not that he receives no gifts but that he never thanks the Giver (Romans 1:21). The joy of the believer is to trace every good thing back up the road it came down.

In a sentence. Don’t be fooled, my dear brothers and sisters. Every good and perfect gift comes down from above, from the Father who made the lights in the sky, who does not change like their shifting shadows. He chose to give us new birth through the message of truth, so that we might be the first part of the harvest of everything he created.

On a Tuesday. Make a list tonight of ten good things from today, small and large, and trace each one up to the Father of lights. Then notice where you have been suspecting God of going cool on you, and answer that suspicion with this verse. And if you are a believer, remember that you did not author your new birth; that means you cannot un-author it on a bad day either.

For worship. Every good thing you have ever tasted came down one road from one Father. The sun on your face this morning, the bread on your table, the friend who stayed, the forgiveness that met you at the cross: all of it came down from above, and none of it was earned. And the greatest gift was not a thing but a birth. Before you wanted him, he willed you; before you could speak, he spoke his word of truth into your death, and you lived. He does not change. His mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness (Lamentations 3:22–23). The light that shone on the first day will shine on the last, and it has never once flickered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger, because human anger does not produce God’s righteousness. Put off moral filth and humbly receive the word planted in you, which can save you. Do not only hear the word but do it. The hearer who does nothing is like a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face; the doer who keeps looking into the law of liberty is blessed. Religion that cannot control the tongue is worthless. Pure religion is caring for orphans and widows and keeping oneself unstained by the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mirror

Hearing without doing is self-deception. The blessed man looks into the perfect law of liberty, stays there, and acts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Orphans and widows were the people with no one to speak for them.

Now: Pure religion still means turning up for the helpless and keeping unstained from the world — both, not one.

verseByVerse.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.

Know this, my beloved brothers. Either you know this, or take note of this; the Greek (iste) can be read both ways. A new section begins: how to respond rightly to the word of truth that gave us birth (v. 18). And then come three of the most quoted phrases in the letter: quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger.

Not conversational tips. Read in isolation it is good general advice, and it has often been reduced to that. But the context is the word of truth in verse 18 and the implanted word in verse 21. James is not chiefly giving conversational tips. He is saying how to receive Scripture, and then, because the same posture governs both, how to treat each other. The man who listens to God properly will begin to listen to people properly, and the man who interrupts God will interrupt everybody.

Let every person be quick to hear. Quick (tachys): eager, leaning in, ready, the first instinct. It is the opposite of the man who already knows. Especially toward God’s word, but also toward others: hearing the whole sentence, the whole story, the thing behind the thing.

Slow to speak. This is not a call to silence; James preaches, and this letter is not short. It is about order and speed (Proverbs 10:19; 17:27–28). The word that comes out too fast has not been through anything, and in a congregation of displaced and frightened people the quick word was doing damage. He will give the tongue a whole chapter shortly.

Slow to anger. Note he does not say never angry. Slow, which allows that some things ought to produce it, and insists that arriving there quickly is the fault. Anger (orgē) is settled indignation, and in trials it is easy to become angry with God, with others, with circumstances. God himself is described as slow to anger (Exodus 34:6), and the phrase is a compliment to him. James is asking his readers to be like their Father.

For the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God. Then the reason, and it is the sentence that lands. Produce (ergazetai) means work out, accomplish. The righteousness of God here is the righteous life God requires and desires. That is a hard word for people who are angry about something genuine. James does not say the anger is unjustified: these readers had been driven from their homes and defrauded by employers, and chapter 5 shows he thinks that scandalous. He says the anger will not produce what it is aiming at. It feels like the engine of righteousness and it is not one. Whatever gets built by human rage, it is not the life God is after. We think our anger will fix things; it usually makes them worse.

One sequence. And it explains the order of the three. A man slow to hear and quick to speak will be quick to anger; they are one sequence, and it begins with how you listen. Most quarrels are lost at the first stage, when one person stopped hearing and started preparing his reply.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all anger. There is righteous anger at sin and injustice: be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26), and Jesus looked around at the Pharisees with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). But human anger is usually mixed with pride and self-interest, and it must not be quick.

Does this mean I should stay quiet when I am being wronged or abused? No. Slow to anger is not a command to accept abuse or to keep quiet about wrongdoing. Scripture commands us to defend the weak and expose deeds of darkness (Psalm 82:3–4; Ephesians 5:11). If you or anyone else is being harmed, speak up, get help, and if a crime is involved, go to the authorities. What James forbids is the hot, quick, self-righteous anger that lashes out and makes things worse. Righteous action is often calm, deliberate and firm. Justice is better served by a clear head than by a burning one.

How do I become slow to anger when it rises so fast? Start with the first command: be quick to hear. Most anger is fed by assuming the worst. Before you answer, ask a question: what did you mean by that? Give yourself time: a walk, a night’s sleep, an unsent email. Ask what your anger is protecting: often it is pride or fear. Bring it to God before you bring it to the person (Psalm 4:4). And remember how slow God has been with you. Nothing cools anger like remembering how patient he is with us.

In a sentence. My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteous life that God desires.

On a Tuesday. In your next difficult conversation, practise the order: listen fully first, ask one question before you answer, speak slowly, and let anger wait. If it happens online, that is where the rule matters most: read it twice, wait an hour, and ask whether your reply will build anything. And notice where your anger comes fastest, with which person or which subject. That is where God is working on you.

For worship. The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (Psalm 103:8). He has had more cause for anger than anyone, and he is the slowest to it. He listened to Israel’s complaints for forty years. He bore with the disciples’ quarrels. And when his anger against sin was finally poured out, it fell on his own Son, so that for those in Christ it would never fall again. The only anger that has ever produced the righteousness of God was the wrath borne at the cross, and it was borne for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

Therefore put away all filthiness. The verb (apothemenoi) is the one used of taking off a garment: stripping off clothes that are filthy (Ephesians 4:22, 25; Colossians 3:8; 1 Peter 2:1; Hebrews 12:1). Filthiness (rhyparia) is moral dirt, defilement, and there is a striking detail in the word: it was also used in medical writing of earwax, which blocks hearing. Whether or not James intended the pun, the point stands: sin blocks our ears to God’s word. A man cannot be quick to hear with his ears stopped.

And rampant wickedness. Rampant (perisseia) means an overflow, an excess that spills. Wickedness (kakia) is malice, evil. The picture is of something that has grown past its bounds and needs cutting back before anything else can grow: the excess of evil that remains even in believers.

And receive with meekness the implanted word. The two halves are one movement: take off, and take in. You cannot do the second while wearing the first. Receive (dexasthe) means welcome, accept, as you would a guest. With meekness (prautēs), which is not weakness but strength that has stopped fighting back, and is the opposite of the anger of verse 20. Applied to Scripture it means coming without a case to argue: not sitting in judgment on the text, not sifting it for what confirms you, but letting it have the last word.

The implanted word. The striking phrase. Emphytos means innate or engrafted, planted in, rooted. So the word is not merely something they hear from outside; it has been planted in them at their new birth (v. 18), and their job is to let it grow rather than to fetch it. It is Jeremiah’s promise of the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), and the parable of the sower is not far away. They must keep receiving what they have already received.

Which is able to save your souls. A remarkable thing to say about a word. Not able to inform, improve or guide; able (dynamenon, it has power) to save. Save your souls means the final salvation of the whole person (5:20; 1 Peter 1:9). The word that gave new birth continues to work, bringing believers through to final salvation. And note that James, so often accused of moralism, grounds the whole ethical section that follows in something planted by God which does the saving.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are not yet saved at all. They have been born again (v. 18). But salvation has past, present and future aspects: we have been saved from sin’s penalty, are being saved from its power, and will be saved from its presence. The word keeps working until the end.

What does meekness toward Scripture look like when I find a passage hard or I disagree with it? It means assuming that if there is a conflict between you and the Bible, you are the one who needs to move. Read the hard passage carefully, in context; ask what it actually says, not what you fear it says. Seek help from good teachers. Bring your questions to God honestly; the psalmists did. But do not edit Scripture to fit your preferences. Meekness is not pretending to have no questions. It is bringing them to the word as a pupil, not as a judge.

In a sentence. So get rid of all moral filth and the evil that is so widespread, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save you.

On a Tuesday. What is blocking your ears? A sin you are holding onto will make every sermon sound like someone else’s problem. Name it and take it off this week, like a soiled coat. And come to Scripture differently: before you read, pray, speak, Lord, for your servant hears. Read until something cuts against you, and stay there.

For worship. The word that saves is not a dead text but a living seed, and God himself planted it. He did not leave us to climb up to his truth; he sowed it in us, and it took root in hearts that were stony ground. And that word is finally a Person: the Word who became flesh (John 1:14), who was himself planted in the ground like a grain of wheat and rose to bear much fruit (John 12:24). Every word of Scripture that lives in us draws its life from him.

verseByVerse.quote: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.

But be doers of the word. This is the thesis of the letter, and everything from here to chapter 5 is an application of it. The Greek construction is stronger than English shows: literally become doers of the word, keep on being doers (ginesthe). And doer (poiētēs, from which comes our word poet: a maker) is a noun of character, not an action. Not somebody who does things occasionally. Somebody who is a doer. Receiving the word (v. 21) must lead to doing it.

And not hearers only. Notice James does not disparage hearing. He has just commanded it: quick to hear, receive the implanted word. The problem is the word only. Hearers (akroatai) are listeners, an audience, those who attend lectures. In synagogue and church, Scripture was read aloud; it was possible to listen regularly and never act. Hearing is necessary and it is not sufficient, and the man in view is not a man who refuses Scripture. He is a man who attends. Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with the same warning: the wise man hears and does; the foolish man hears and does not, and his house falls (Matthew 7:24–27).

Deceiving yourselves. Then the diagnosis, and it is the sharpest word in the verse. The term (paralogizomenoi) is from accounting: to miscalculate, to reason yourself into a false total. This is not hypocrisy, which is deceiving other people. It is a man doing the sum wrong about himself, and believing the answer. And that is why it is so dangerous. A hypocrite knows. This man does not. He has heard the word, felt the force of it, agreed with it warmly, and has filed the agreeing as though it were the doing. The emotional response registers, in his own books, as obedience.

A peculiarly religious danger. And it grows with exposure. The more sermons a person hears, the more familiar the sensation of being moved becomes, and the easier it is to mistake for change. A man can know the truth very well and think himself spiritual because he knows it. But knowledge without obedience is self-deception. James will now give an illustration to make the self-deception visible, and he chooses a mirror.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is by doing. James will show that genuine faith always works (2:14–26). The doing is the evidence of genuine hearing, the fruit of the implanted word.

Does James contradict Paul here? No. Paul also says it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God (Romans 2:13), and he insists that faith works through love (Galatians 5:6). Both apostles teach that we are saved by grace through faith alone, and that the faith which saves is never alone; it always bears fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10). Paul is fighting people who want to add works to faith as the ground of salvation; James is fighting people who think faith can be real without works. They stand back to back, facing different enemies. See the notes on 2:14–26.

I have been a hearer for years. Where do I even start? Not with a programme but with one thing. Take the clearest thing God has said to you recently, the thing you already know you should do, and do it this week. Most of us are not short of information; we are carrying a backlog of obedience. Start at the front of the queue. And do not despair over the years: the God who planted the word is patient, and a hearer who begins to do is exactly what this verse is for.

In a sentence. Do not merely listen to the word and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says.

On a Tuesday. Take one thing you heard from Scripture last Sunday. Write down the specific action it calls for: not a feeling, an action, with a person or a time attached. Do it before Thursday. And next Sunday, before the sermon begins, ask God: show me one thing to do. Then listen for it.

For worship. There has been one perfect doer of the word. Jesus did not only hear his Father; he said: my food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work (John 4:34). Every word he heard, he did, all the way to the cross. And because he did it for us, our failures to do are covered by his perfect doing, and his Spirit is at work in us to make us doers too. We are not saved by our obedience. We are saved by his, and set free to begin our own.

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like.

For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer. James now gives an illustration, and it is one of the most memorable in the New Testament.

He is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. Get the object right first. Ancient mirrors (esoptron) were polished bronze; they gave a real but imperfect image, which is Paul’s point in 1 Corinthians 13:12. And note the verb (katanoounti): he does not glance. He looks intently, observes, studies himself, gives it proper attention. The hearer in this picture is not careless in the moment. He is engaged. His natural face is literally the face of his birth (to prosōpon tēs geneseōs autou): what he was born with, the thing he did not choose and cannot alter by wishing.

For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like. Then the failure, and it is entirely in the sequel. Three verbs, and the whole tragedy is in their order. He looked, genuinely. He left (apelēlythen, perfect tense: he has gone off). And by the time he was through the door it was gone. Not gradually; the word (eutheōs) means immediately.

What is a mirror for? Not admiration. You look in one to find out what needs attention: the smudge, the collar, the thing you cannot see without help. A mirror is a diagnostic instrument, and its whole value lies in what you do in the ten seconds after you turn away. Scripture is like a mirror: it shows us what we really are. So the man in the illustration has performed the ritual of self-examination and skipped the point of it. He has confused looking with acting.

The walk to the car park. And James has chosen the comparison with care, because nobody would call the mirror useless. The instrument worked perfectly. It told him exactly what was wrong. The information simply did not survive the walk to the door, which is what happens to a sermon between the church and the car park. The hearer sees his sin in Scripture, feels briefly convicted, and walks away unchanged.

What it does not mean. It does not mean looking at ourselves in Scripture is bad. It is essential. The problem is looking and doing nothing.

How do I stop forgetting? Make the response before you leave the mirror. When a passage or a sermon shows you something, act on it while the image is fresh: confess the sin then and there, send the apology that day, write the one sentence of what you will do on a card you will see tomorrow. Tell someone, because things spoken aloud are harder to forget. Reread the passage the next morning. Forgetting is not usually a failure of memory but a failure to act quickly; what we act on, we remember.
