Does the mirror only show my faults? No, and this matters for tender consciences. The same Scripture that shows you your sin shows you your Saviour, and who you are in him: forgiven, adopted, loved. A person who only ever sees condemnation in the mirror is not reading the whole of it. Look until you see both: what needs washing, and the one who washes.

In a sentence. Anyone who listens to the word but does not do what it says is like someone who looks at their face in a mirror and, after looking, goes away and immediately forgets what they look like.

On a Tuesday. When Scripture shows you something about yourself this week, do not walk away. Stop before you close the Bible and respond: confess, decide, act. Ask a friend after church on Sunday: what did God show you today, and what are you going to do about it? Then let them ask you on Wednesday.

For worship. The mirror of the word shows us a face we would rather forget. But it also shows us another face: the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). And as we behold the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The mirror that exposes us is the same mirror in which, gazing at him, we are slowly made like him. God does not merely show us our dirt. He shows us his Son, and remakes us in his likeness.

verseByVerse.quote: But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.

But the one who looks into the perfect law. Now the contrast, and every phrase answers the mirror-man point by point. The verb is different and stronger. Parakypsas means to stoop down and peer in, the word used of Peter and John bending to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5, 11), and of angels longing to look into the salvation the prophets foretold (1 Peter 1:12). Not a glance in passing but a posture: bending over the thing to see it properly. And the perfect law (nomon teleion, complete, mature) is God’s word, including the moral law as fulfilled and interpreted by Christ, the royal law of love (2:8).

The law of liberty. The phrase sounds like a contradiction and is not. James is not describing the law as a system of merit; he has just said the implanted word saves. He means the whole revealed will of God as it now stands in Christ, and it liberates because it is no longer a standard you are trying to reach in order to be accepted. It is written on the heart by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33) and obeyed from love, not compulsion. True freedom is the freedom to do what is right, freed from slavery to sin (John 8:31–36; Romans 8:2). You keep it as a freed man, not as a slave earning his way out. And the law of liberty also judges (2:12).

And perseveres. The word (parameinas) means to remain beside, to stay bent over it. That is the exact opposite of goes away. The difference between the two men is not the quality of the looking. It is that one of them stayed. He keeps looking, keeps applying, does not walk away.

Being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts. Literally not a hearer of forgetfulness but a doer of work, a Hebrew way of speaking. A slightly odd phrase in English, and deliberate: a doer of work, someone whose doing produces something. James will have no category for obedience that leaves no trace.

He will be blessed in his doing. Blessed (makarios), as in verse 12. Not blessed for it, as though the doing purchased a reward. Blessed in it: the blessing is inside the obedience, not attached to it afterwards (John 13:17; Psalm 1:1–3). The man who does what he has seen finds that the doing is itself the good thing, which is precisely what the man walking away from the mirror never discovers.

What it does not mean. Law of liberty does not mean Christians are free to ignore God’s commands. It means God’s commands, written on the heart, set us free to live as we were made to live. Nor does blessing for doing mean salvation by works; it is the blessing of a life in step with God.

Which law is this? Are Christians under the Ten Commandments? Christians are not under the law as a covenant of works, a way of earning acceptance or facing condemnation; Christ has fulfilled it and borne its curse for us (Galatians 3:13). But the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in love for God and neighbour, remains the rule of life for believers, showing us God’s will and our duty (Westminster 19.6). That is what James means: not the ceremonial laws of temple and sacrifice, which Christ fulfilled, but God’s holy will as Jesus taught it. Kept in love, it is not a cage but a road.

Blessed in doing. Does obedience always feel good? Not always in the moment. Forgiving someone who hurt you, telling the truth when it costs, giving when money is tight: these can feel like loss. The blessing James means is deeper than a pleasant feeling. It is the quiet rightness of walking with God, a clear conscience, fruit that grows over time, and the experience of God’s presence and help in the very act. Often the blessing is recognised only looking back. But no one who has obeyed God has ever, in the end, regretted it.

In a sentence. But whoever looks closely into the perfect law that gives freedom, and keeps on doing so, not forgetting what they have heard but putting it into practice, will be blessed in what they do.

On a Tuesday. Choose one passage this week and stoop over it: read it slowly, three times, on three different days. Ask what it commands, what it promises, and what it shows you of Christ. Then do the one thing it asks of you, and notice afterwards whether there was a blessing in the doing that you would have missed by walking away.

For worship. The law that once stood over us as an accuser now lives in us as a friend. The Son has set us free, and if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:36). He kept the perfect law perfectly, bore its curse in our place, and then wrote it on our hearts by his Spirit. Angels stoop to look into this salvation; we are allowed to stoop and look, and to stay. And every act of loving obedience is a small taste of the freedom we will know fully when we see him, and are like him.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.

If anyone thinks he is religious. James now takes the word everyone in that congregation would have used approvingly, religious, and puts it under the test he has just built. Thinks (dokei) means supposes, seems to himself. Religious (thrēskos) refers to religion’s outward exercise: the observances, the worship and ritual, the visible practice. He attends worship, prays, fasts, and considers himself spiritual. And James does not sneer at it. He asks what it is worth, and gives a startling answer in two directions.

And does not bridle his tongue. The bridle (chalinagōgōn, to guide with a bridle, to rein in) is the image James will develop at 3:2–3. An uncontrolled tongue, gossip, slander, harshness, lies, contradicts every religious claim. And note that of all the failures he could have chosen as the disqualifier, he chose speech, a sin which most congregations tolerate entirely.

But deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Self-deception again (v. 22), and thinks he is religious picks it up. Worthless (mataios) means useless, empty, futile, good for nothing, and it is applied not to an unbeliever but to a churchgoer with a loose mouth. All the outward religious activity is empty if the tongue is unrestrained.

Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this. Then the positive, and it is famous. Pure (kathara, clean) and undefiled (amiantos, unstained) are terms of ritual purity. But James redefines purity: not ritual cleanness, but practical love and moral holiness. And before God the Father: what God, not people, counts as genuine. The audience that matters is one person.

To visit orphans and widows in their affliction. Orphans and widows were the standard biblical shorthand for those with no legal standing and no income. In that society a woman without husband or sons had no one to go to court for her. God is their defender: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation (Psalm 68:5; Deuteronomy 10:18). And the verb is visit (episkeptesthai), to look after, care for, see to their needs; it is the root of the word overseer, and the same word used of God visiting his people (Luke 1:68). It does not mean sending money from a distance. It means turning up. True religion cares for those who cannot repay.

And to keep oneself unstained from the world. Two things, and they are usually pulled apart by people who prefer one. Care for the defenceless, and personal holiness. James joins them with an and and gives no permission to choose. Unstained (aspilos) means spotless. The world (kosmos) here is human society organised in rebellion against God, with its values, desires and pressures (4:4; 1 John 2:15–17). True religion is both outward love and inward holiness: compassion for the needy and separation from worldliness.

How does this apply today? In caring for orphans through adoption and fostering, for single mothers, for the lonely elderly and for widows in the church, in personal kindness and in the church’s organised care. And to keep oneself unstained from the world means to refuse the values of a world opposed to God (4:4; 1 John 2:15–17): its greed, its pride, its view of sex, its contempt for the weak.

What it does not mean. It does not mean caring for the needy is the whole of religion, or that worship and doctrine do not matter. James assumes faith in Christ (2:1), and the man who wrote 2:19 knew what he believed. He is showing what genuine faith looks like in practice, as opposed to empty ritual. He is not defining the whole of religion here. He is naming the test. If you want to know whether the word has been implanted, do not look at the intensity of the hearing. Look at whether anyone with nothing to offer you has seen you lately.

Is caring for the needy the same as preaching the gospel? No. The gospel is the announcement of what Christ has done for sinners, and nothing replaces telling people about him (Romans 10:14). But mercy is the fruit and the adornment of the gospel, and a church that preaches grace and ignores the widow down the street is contradicting its own message. Begin with the household of faith (Galatians 6:10), the widows and the struggling in your own church, and then go out to the neighbour. Word and deed belong together, as they did in Jesus’ ministry.

Does unstained from the world mean I should withdraw from society? No. Jesus prayed not that his people be taken out of the world but kept from the evil one (John 17:15). The visiting of orphans and widows takes you right into the world’s mess. Being unstained means not absorbing its values while you serve in it: going into the hospital, the care home, the hard estate, without adopting the greed, cynicism and lust that the world takes for granted. Like a surgeon who works in the wound and scrubs his hands, the Christian goes in close and stays clean, by God’s grace.

In a sentence. Those who consider themselves religious but do not keep a tight rein on their tongues are fooling themselves, and their religion is worthless. The religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.

On a Tuesday. Three questions, one for each clause. What did my tongue do this week that my religion would be embarrassed by? Who in my church or street has no one to go to court for them, the widow, the foster child, the lonely old man, and when did I last turn up at their door? And what worldly habit, a screen, a spending pattern, a way of talking, is quietly staining me? Do one thing about each before Sunday.

For worship. God the Father does not ask of us what he has not done himself. He visited us in our affliction. We were orphans, and he adopted us; we were a widowed people with no one to plead our case, and he became our advocate. The Son came down into the world’s filth and touched lepers and ate with sinners and was never stained by any of it, and then he took our stains onto himself on the cross, so that we could be presented to the Father holy and blameless and above reproach (Colossians 1:22). Pure and undefiled religion is simply the family likeness of a Father who has visited us.
