2.title: No Partiality: Faith That Sees Every Person
2.overview:
Chapter 2 has two movements, closely linked. The first (vv. 1–13) confronts favouritism in the church: welcoming the rich visitor to a good seat and sending the poor man to the floor. The second (vv. 14–26) asks what real faith is: a faith that produces no works is dead. The link is the poor visitor. A faith that produces no love for him is exactly the dead faith of vv. 14–26.

James is not opposing Paul’s gospel. He is opposing a counterfeit of it: the idea that agreeing with correct doctrine is the same as saving faith. Even demons believe that God is one. What saves is living faith in Christ, shown in Abraham offering Isaac and Rahab sheltering the spies. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Gold Ring and the Royal Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not hold faith in the glorious Lord Jesus while showing favouritism. James stages a scene: a man with a gold ring is given a good seat, a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand or sit on the floor. That makes you corrupt judges. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while the rich oppress you. Favouritism breaks the royal law of love, and breaking one command makes you guilty before the one Lawgiver. So speak and act as those who will be judged, for mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Lawgiver

Partiality contradicts faith in the Lord of glory and breaks the royal law. Whoever fails at one point stands guilty before the one who spoke the whole law — and mercy triumphs over judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The congregation seated the man with the gold ring well and the poor man on the floor.

Now: The sin is not only exclusion but ranking people inside a real welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.

Meaning first. James 2 has two linked parts, both showing that genuine faith works itself out in love. First, a warning against favouritism (vv. 1–13). Faith in the glorious Lord Jesus cannot coexist with snobbery. If the church fawns over a rich visitor and humiliates a poor one, it has become a court of corrupt judges (vv. 1–4). God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, while the rich are often those who oppress believers and slander Christ’s name (vv. 5–7). The royal law is to love your neighbour as yourself; favouritism breaks it, and breaking one command makes you guilty of the whole law (vv. 8–11). So speak and act as those who will be judged by the law of liberty, remembering that judgment is merciless to those who show no mercy, and mercy triumphs over judgment (vv. 12–13). Second, the famous passage on faith and works (vv. 14–26). A faith that says the right words but does nothing for a hungry brother is useless and dead (vv. 14–17). Faith is shown by works; even demons believe that God is one, and shudder (vv. 18–19). Abraham’s faith was shown and completed when he offered Isaac, fulfilling the Scripture that he believed God and was counted righteous; so a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (vv. 20–24). Rahab too showed her faith by her actions; faith without works is as dead as a body without breath (vv. 25–26). James is not contradicting Paul: both teach that saving faith is a living faith that produces works, and that a mere profession without works is not saving faith at all. We are justified by faith alone, in Christ alone, and the faith that justifies is never alone.

My brothers, show no partiality. The Greek word (prosōpolēmpsia) is a compound meaning to receive the face: to judge by appearance, to let the look of a person decide how you treat them. It is a Hebrew idiom carried into Greek, and its background is the courtroom. The law forbade a judge to be partial to the poor or defer to the great (Leviticus 19:15), and it grounded that in God himself, who is not partial and takes no bribe (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11). What James is about to describe is a congregation behaving like a corrupt court.

As you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. Note how the command is framed: partiality is set directly against holding (echete, having, possessing) the faith. James clearly assumes faith in Christ as the foundation of the Christian life; the man accused of preaching works opens his great chapter on works with faith in Jesus. And favouritism is not presented as bad manners or poor pastoral practice. It is incompatible with the content of what they believe, and the rest of the verse says why.

The Lord of glory. The Greek is stark, literally our Lord Jesus Christ, of the glory, and it is the highest thing James says about his brother anywhere in the letter. Jesus is the glorious one, the Shekinah, God’s glory dwelling among us (John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 2:8; Hebrews 1:3). And glory belongs to God alone: I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other (Isaiah 42:8). To call Jesus the glory is to call him God.

The placing is the argument. Set beside that glory, the difference between a gold ring and a poor man’s rags is nothing at all. The distinctions we find so legible are invisible from where he stands. When the sun is up, nobody compares candles. A congregation that seats people by their clothes has forgotten who is in the room.

The man who grew up with him. There is also something quiet in the phrase, given who is writing. The man who says the Lord of glory watched him grow up in Nazareth, where there was no glory to see, and where the family had no standing worth having. Can anything good come out of Nazareth? people said (John 1:46). If anyone had learned that appearances mislead, it was James. He had sat at the same table as the Lord of glory for thirty years and seen a carpenter.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all distinctions, such as honouring elders or respecting authorities (Romans 13:7). It forbids treating people differently because of wealth, status, race or appearance, especially in the church.

What does partiality look like in a church today? It rarely involves seats now, but it is the same sin. It is the visitor with a profession and a nice car who is invited to lunch, while the one with a carrier bag gets a handshake. It is noticing the gifted and the articulate for leadership and passing over the faithful and quiet. It is giving celebrities and large donors a platform their character has not earned. It is racial and cultural preference, the sense that some people are more our sort. And it can run the other way too: despising the wealthy or the educated is also face-receiving. The test is simple: am I treating this person according to what Christ has made him, or according to what he can do for me?

Is it wrong to have closer friends at church? No. Jesus himself had Peter, James and John, and John was the disciple whom Jesus loved. Friendship is a gift. The sin James names is not having friends but ranking people’s worth: honouring some and humiliating others because of status. Enjoy your friends, and make sure the circle has an open side, so that the newcomer, the awkward and the poor are welcomed in as brothers and sisters, not tolerated at the edge.

In a sentence. My brothers and sisters, believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favouritism.

On a Tuesday. Notice whom you are naturally drawn to at church and whom you overlook. Ask why: is it shared interests, or is it status, education, age, background, appearance? This Sunday, go out of your way to welcome someone you might normally ignore, and do not leave it at a handshake. Learn their name, sit with them, and find out one thing about their week.

For worship. The Lord of glory did not receive faces. He touched the leper, ate with tax collectors, let a sinful woman weep on his feet, and called a despised little man down from a tree to host him. He looked at the rich young ruler and loved him, and at the widow with two copper coins and praised her. He gave the same welcome to Nicodemus by night and to the woman at the well by day. And when he chose his people, he did not choose by our clothes. He clothed us in his own righteousness, so that the poorest beggar who trusts him stands in garments brighter than any gold ring. Glory belongs to him alone, and he spends it on the lowly.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in, and if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” while you say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit down at my feet,” have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in, and if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” while you say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit down at my feet,” have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?

For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing. James does not argue in the abstract. He puts a scene in front of them, and it is staged with a novelist’s eye. Two men arrive. The first is gold-fingered (chrysodaktylios): perhaps wearing many rings, or the gold ring that in Roman society was not merely jewellery but a mark of rank, the right of the equestrian order. His clothing is literally shining (esthēti lampra), bright, splendid. He has dressed to be read.

Comes into your assembly. The word is synagōgē, synagogue. It is the only place in the New Testament where a Christian meeting is called a synagogue, reflecting the Jewish background of James’s readers. It may refer to a worship service, or perhaps to a church court gathered to settle disputes between members (1 Corinthians 6:1–6), which would make the courtroom language even sharper.

And a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in. The word (rhyparos) means filthy, the same root as the filthiness of 1:21. Not modest, not plain. Dirty, because he has nothing else and nowhere to wash it. Perhaps the only clothes he owned.

And if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing. The verb (epiblepsēte) means to look upon with favour, to gaze at admiringly. Every eye goes to the shining coat, and every face lights up.

You sit here in a good place. Then the treatment, and James gives it in direct speech so that they hear themselves saying it. To the first: here, comfortably, in a place of honour (kalōs).

You stand over there, or, Sit down at my feet. To the second, two options and both an insult. Stand at the back, or sit on the floor, literally under my footstool (hypo to hypopodion mou): down where a servant or a dog would be. A deliberate humiliation.

A genuine welcome. Notice nobody is thrown out. The poor man is welcomed and seated. That is exactly what makes the scene so recognisable: the sin is not exclusion but ranking, and it operates entirely within a genuine welcome. Nobody in that room would have said they were against the poor. They gave him a place. They just made sure he knew which one.

Have you not then made distinctions among yourselves. The verb (diekrithēte) means discriminated, been divided, and it is the same root as the doubting of 1:6. A church that sorts people has divided itself, and it is the double-mindedness of chapter 1 coming out in the seating. The divided heart shows itself in a divided room.

And become judges with evil thoughts? That returns to the courtroom of verse 1. Literally judges whose reasonings are wicked (kritai dialogismōn ponērōn). They have not merely been rude. They have constituted themselves a tribunal, tried both men on the evidence of their clothing, and delivered verdicts, which is precisely the thing the law forbids a judge to do. They have set themselves up as judges of people’s worth, and their standards are corrupt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should never show courtesy to visitors, rich or poor. It means it must not show greater honour on the basis of wealth or appearance.

But what if a wealthy visitor could really help the church? That is exactly the thought James is exposing, and it is why the sin is so tempting: it can be dressed up as good stewardship. The church does not need anyone’s money as much as it needs to be faithful. God provides for his work, and he has never needed a gold ring to do it. Welcome the wealthy visitor warmly, as warmly as anyone else, and no more. If he comes to Christ, he will learn to give gladly. If he is courted for his money, he learns that the church is like every other club, and the poor man learns it too.

What about someone who is dirty, smells, or is disruptive? Love does not pretend; it welcomes. Greet them, sit with them, offer a drink and something to eat, and treat them as you would want to be treated. If someone is genuinely disruptive or unsafe, elders and stewards should deal with it calmly and kindly, because protecting the congregation, especially children, is also love. But the default must be honour. The man in shabby clothes may be the one Christ sends to see how we treat him (Matthew 25:40).

In a sentence. Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in filthy old clothes also comes in. If you show special attention to the man in fine clothes and say, Here is a good seat for you, but say to the poor man, You stand there, or Sit on the floor by my feet, have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with wicked motives?

On a Tuesday. How does your church welcome the poor, the shabby, the awkward? Walk through your Sunday as if you were a stranger with no money and no Christian vocabulary: where would you sit, who would speak to you, would anyone ask your name? Then ask how you could personally help make such people feel honoured. Perhaps it is as simple as choosing to sit next to the person nobody sits next to.

For worship. Christ took the footstool. He who has heaven as his throne and earth as his footstool (Isaiah 66:1) came down and was born where animals ate, and at the end he was stripped of his clothes and dicing soldiers took them. He stood in the place of the poor man in filthy clothes, so that we who were clothed in filthy rags before God could hear him say: take away his filthy garments, and clothe him with pure vestments (Zechariah 3:4). And then he says to the beggar he has dressed: you sit here, in a good place. Sit with me on my throne (Revelation 3:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?

Listen, my beloved brothers. He raises his voice (akousate, hear, pay attention), and then makes three arguments in three verses.

Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world. The first argument is theological. Chosen (exelexato) is the language of election, God’s sovereign choice in salvation (1 Corinthians 1:26–29; Ephesians 1:4). Poor in the world (tous ptōchous tō kosmō) means poor in the world’s eyes, by worldly standards. This is not a claim that poverty is a qualification, and it does not mean every poor person is saved. It is an observation about how God has in fact worked: the early church was mostly made up of the poor (Luke 6:20), and Paul says the same, that not many were wise or powerful or of noble birth (1 Corinthians 1:26). The force of it is this: God has been choosing exactly the people this congregation is seating on the floor. Their ranking runs in the opposite direction to his.

To be rich in faith. Note the reversal: poor in the world, rich in faith. The categories are not abolished; they are inverted. True riches are spiritual, and the man with the filthy coat may be the wealthiest person in the room.

And heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? Heirs (klēronomous) of God’s reign, now and fully in the age to come (Matthew 5:3; 25:34). Those who love him is the phrase of 1:12, a description of true believers. The poor believer is a future king. The congregation is making a prince sit on the floor.

But you have dishonored the poor man. That is the charge, and the word (ētimasate) is strong: to shame, to insult, to treat as worthless the very person God has honoured.

Are not the rich the ones who oppress you. The second and third arguments are brutally practical. Oppress (katadynasteuousin) means exercise power over, exploit, tyrannise. Wealthy landowners and creditors often exploited the poor, and these are not hypothetical rich men; chapter 5 will describe employers withholding wages from the men who mowed their fields (5:1–6).

And the ones who drag you into court? The verb (helkousin) means to haul by force, as Paul and Silas were dragged into the marketplace before the rulers (Acts 16:19). Perhaps over debts, perhaps because of their faith.

Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called? Blaspheme (blasphēmousin) means slander, revile. The honourable name (to kalon onoma, the good, the beautiful name) is the name of Christ. By which you were called is literally which was called over you (to epiklēthen eph’ hymas): an Old Testament phrase for ownership, used of Israel as the people called by God’s name, and probably pointing to baptism, when Christ’s name was pronounced over the believer, marking them as his (Acts 2:38). So the wealthy visitor being ushered to the good seat belongs to the class that exploits this congregation, litigates against it, and insults its Lord. Why fawn over people who mock your Lord?

The irrationality of flattery. James is not saying rich people are beyond salvation, and he is not commanding a reverse partiality; verse 1 forbids that as much as the other. He is exposing the irrationality of the flattery. They are fawning on people who despise them, and they are doing it because of a ring.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every rich person is wicked or every poor person is saved. God saves rich and poor alike by grace. James is speaking generally of the rich unbelievers who oppressed the church. Nor does it mean poverty itself is a virtue; it is a hardship in which God’s grace often shines.

Does God love the poor more than the rich? God shows no partiality (v. 1), and he does not choose anyone because of their bank balance, any more than because of their goodness. Election is of grace alone (Romans 11:5–6). But God has a special care for the poor and the oppressed, and he often chooses the weak to shame the strong, so that no one may boast (1 Corinthians 1:27–29). The rich face a particular danger: it is hard for them to feel their need (Matthew 19:23–26). The poor have often found it easier to come with empty hands, because their hands were already empty.

What does it mean that Christ’s name was called over me? It means you belong to him. In the Old Testament, to have God’s name called over a people, a city or the temple meant that God owned it and would defend it (Deuteronomy 28:10; Jeremiah 14:9). In the church this is marked in baptism, when a believer who has confessed Christ is baptised into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Whatever your church tradition, the point is the same: you carry his name. So treat others, and let yourself be treated, as people whose worth is set by the one whose name they wear.

In a sentence. Listen, my dear brothers and sisters: has God not chosen those who are poor in the world’s eyes to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised those who love him? But you have insulted the poor. Is it not the rich who exploit you? Are they not the ones dragging you into court? Are they not the ones slandering the noble name of him to whom you belong?

On a Tuesday. Think of the people in your church who are poor in the world: the unemployed, the disabled, the refugee family, the elderly widow on a pension. Ask yourself whether you see them as God sees them: rich in faith, heirs of the kingdom, people you could learn from. Then go and learn from one. Ask them how God has kept them. You may hear the richest testimony you have heard in years.

For worship. God’s choice runs downward, and that is the glory of it. He chose a slave nation, a shepherd boy, a peasant girl in Nazareth, fishermen in Galilee. And he chose us when we had nothing to offer him but our sin. The heirs of the kingdom are beggars he has adopted, and the inheritance is not a share of this world’s fading wealth but the kingdom itself, with the King. Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God (Luke 6:20). The beautiful name called over us is the name above every name, and he is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.

If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture. James anticipates the defence. Somebody will say: we were being hospitable. We were loving our neighbour. Really (mentoi) means indeed, if in fact. Fulfil (teleite) means carry out, accomplish. Royal (nomon basilikon) probably means the law of the kingdom, the sovereign law that rules the others. It is royal because it is the supreme law, given by the King, Jesus himself, who called it the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39), and because it belongs to the kingdom just mentioned (v. 5).

You shall love your neighbor as yourself. He grants the principle without hesitation, quoting Leviticus 19:18, and agrees that this is the standard. Love of neighbour sums up the second table of the law (Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14). And notice where James found it: Leviticus 19:18 sits three verses after Leviticus 19:15, the very prohibition of partiality in judgment. He is quoting both halves of one paragraph, and his readers, who knew their Scriptures, would hear it.

You are doing well. Perhaps the favouritists claimed they were loving the rich man as a neighbour. James says: if you truly love your neighbour, all your neighbours, you do well (kalōs poieite).

But if you show partiality, you are committing sin. Then the trap closes. The defence fails because loving your neighbour as yourself has no room for ranking. Whichever man you seated well, you did not treat the other as yourself. Partiality is not a lesser form of love; it is the contradiction of it, because the moment you prefer one neighbour on grounds of appearance you have stopped applying the standard to the other. And it is not a minor social failure. It is sin (hamartia).

And are convicted by the law as transgressors. Back to the courtroom a third time, and now the seating committee is in the dock. They set themselves up as judges (v. 4); the law arraigns them. Convicted (elenchomenoi) means exposed, proved guilty. And transgressor (parabatēs) is a specific word: not a general sinner but one who has stepped over a line that was drawn and marked. The same law they claim to keep convicts them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love of neighbour replaces love of God. The first great commandment remains first. But love of God shows itself in love of neighbour (1 John 4:20).

Does love your neighbour as yourself mean I must learn to love myself first? No. The command assumes that we already love ourselves, in the sense that we naturally care for our own needs, feed ourselves, protect ourselves, and want good things for ourselves (Ephesians 5:29). It does not command self-esteem; it commands that the same care be turned outward. Many people who feel they hate themselves are in fact very focused on themselves. The cure is not more attention to self but the love of God, which frees us to forget ourselves and attend to others.

Who counts as my neighbour? Jesus answered that question with the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37). Your neighbour is whoever God puts in your path who needs your help, including the person of another race, class or religion, including the one you would naturally avoid. The lawyer wanted to limit the list. Jesus turned the question around: not who is my neighbour, but who proved to be a neighbour. In James’s scene the neighbour is the man in the filthy coat.

In a sentence. If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, Love your neighbour as yourself, you are doing right. But if you show favouritism, you sin, and the law convicts you as lawbreakers.

On a Tuesday. Who is the neighbour you find hardest to love as yourself? Picture how you would want to be treated in their place, if you were the one who smelled, or struggled with English, or had a history people whisper about. Then do one practical act of love for them this week, the kind you would want done for you.

For worship. The King who gave the royal law kept it first. He loved his neighbour as himself, and more than himself: he laid down his life for his enemies. He crossed the road to us when we lay half dead, poured in oil and wine, carried us on his own beast and paid for our care. And the law that convicts us as transgressors was fulfilled by him for us, every line of it, so that the law of the kingdom is now written on our hearts by the King’s own Spirit. Love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:10), and he is love.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it. For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it. For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.

For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point. That sounds disproportionate, and everything depends on seeing why it is not. Fails (ptaisē) means stumbles, trips. Even a single failure.

Has become guilty of all of it. Guilty (enochos) means liable, answerable. The law is a unity, like a single sheet of glass: crack it anywhere and the whole is broken. A pane with a single hole in it is a broken window, not a mostly intact one. The law is not a collection of separate rules, where breaking one leaves the others untouched. It is the expression of one will, one God.

For he who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder. The reasoning is in verse 11, and it is about the lawgiver rather than the law. One voice stands behind every command (Exodus 20:13–14; Deuteronomy 5:17–18). So the law is not a list of separate regulations from which you might keep most and fail a few. It is a single expression of one person’s will. Break any of it and you have not damaged one item on a schedule; you have set yourself against the one who spoke.

If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law. And the pairing of the examples is deliberate and pointed. Adultery and murder were the two sins the congregation would have condemned most readily: the obvious, unarguable ones. James sets them beside seating the poor man on the floor and says: same court, same lawgiver, same verdict. You cannot excuse breaking one command by boasting about keeping another.

The grading of sins. That is the argument’s real work. It denies the congregation the move everybody makes, which is to grade sins by how disreputable they look and then to notice that ours never appear near the top of the list. Partiality feels like a lapse of etiquette. James has just put it in a sentence with murder. The favouritists might pride themselves on avoiding adultery and murder, but by favouritism they have broken God’s law and stand guilty before him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all sins are equally serious in every respect. Scripture recognises degrees of sin and punishment (John 19:11; Luke 12:47–48), and plainly weighs consequences differently. The point is narrower and sharper: every sin puts you in the same relation to the same God, and no amount of the law kept compensates for the part broken. Any sin makes us lawbreakers before God, guilty and in need of grace. No one can be justified by law-keeping (Galatians 3:10; Romans 3:19–20). This drives us to Christ, who kept the whole law perfectly for us.

Then what hope does anyone have? None in the law, and that is exactly what the law is meant to teach. If one failure makes us guilty of all, then a lifetime of mostly keeping the rules cannot save anyone. Our only hope is a substitute who kept every point, and then bore the penalty for every point we broke. That is Christ: he was born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5), and he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). James is not preaching despair. He is closing every other door so that we go through the only open one.

If I am already guilty of all, does it matter if I sin a little more? It matters enormously. Every sin offends the God who loves you, damages you and others, and grieves the Spirit (Ephesians 4:30). The point of this verse is not that sins do not matter, but that every sin matters more than we think. A forgiven believer does not reason: since I am covered, I may as well. He reasons: since he paid so much, how can I go on in what he died for (Romans 6:1–2)?

In a sentence. For anyone who keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it. The one who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder. If you do not commit adultery but do commit murder, you have still broken the law.

On a Tuesday. Make an honest list of the sins you consider respectable: the impatience, the snobbery, the gossip, the worry, the lack of prayer, the little dishonesties at work. Put them beside the sins you most condemn in others. Same lawgiver, same voice. Then take them to the cross and confess them by name. And next time you are tempted to feel superior to someone whose sins are louder than yours, remember this verse.

For worship. There is one man who kept the whole law and never failed in one point. Jesus loved God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself every moment of his life: no partiality, no lust, no hatred, no lie. The law could find no fault in him. And this spotless one was counted guilty of all of it, every point broken by every one of his people, and the window we smashed was paid for with his blood. Now his righteousness, whole and unbroken, is counted as ours. The glass is not patched. It is replaced with his.

verseByVerse.quote: So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

So speak and so act. Both verbs (laleite, poieite), present tense: keep on doing so. And the order matters in a letter this concerned with speech; the seating in verse 3 was done with words. James joins speech and action throughout the letter.

As those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. The law of liberty is the phrase from 1:25, and it carries the same paradox. This is not law as a system of merit; James has said the implanted word saves (1:21). It is the whole will of God as it stands in Christ, the law of love written on the heart, and it frees precisely because you keep it as somebody already accepted rather than as somebody trying to be. But notice he does not use it to remove judgment. The freed man is still to be judged (mellontes krinesthai, about to be judged). Believers will stand before God’s judgment, not to determine salvation, but to evaluate their lives (Romans 14:10–12; 2 Corinthians 5:10). That is the note the whole letter keeps striking: those who have been set free are expected to live accordingly.

For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Then verse 13, in two halves that must be held together. Without mercy (aneleos) is merciless. It is the plainest possible statement of the Lord’s own teaching: blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy (Matthew 5:7); the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35); and the petition about forgiving as we are forgiven (Matthew 6:12, 14–15). And it must be read the right way round. A merciless person is not disqualified because he failed to earn mercy by being merciful. He is exposed. Mercy received always produces mercy given, so a life with none flowing out is evidence that none has come in.

Mercy triumphs over judgment. Then the last words, and they are among the most beautiful in the letter. The verb (katakauchatai) means to boast against, to exult over a defeated opponent, to gain the victory. God’s mercy, received and shown, wins over judgment. For those who have received mercy in Christ and show it to others, the judgment holds no terror. Both stand in the same verse. Judgment is real, and mercy is stronger, and the congregation seating men by their clothing is being asked which of the two it has been imitating.

Where mercy and judgment met. How can mercy triumph over judgment without justice being thrown away? Only at the cross. There God did not set aside his judgment against sin; he poured it out in full on his Son, our substitute, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). Mercy did not win by ignoring judgment. It won by bearing it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn God’s mercy by showing mercy. We show mercy because we have received it: be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32). But a merciless life is evidence of an unrenewed heart.

Will Christians really be judged? Yes, but not for condemnation. There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Every believer will stand before the judgment seat of Christ, where our lives are opened and what was done in his name is acknowledged and rewarded (2 Corinthians 5:10; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). It is a Father’s assessment of his children, not a court deciding their fate. The thought should make us serious about our words and deeds, and it should never make a believer fear that Christ will cast him out.

I find it very hard to forgive someone who hurt me. Does that mean I have not received mercy? Not necessarily. Forgiveness of deep wounds is often a long process, and the struggle itself shows that you want to obey. The merciless person James describes does not struggle; he refuses and feels justified. Bring your hurt to God honestly, as the psalmists did, and ask him for the grace to forgive. Remember how much you have been forgiven. Forgiving means giving up your right to revenge and leaving judgment to God (Romans 12:19). It does not mean pretending it did not happen, or trusting the person again immediately.

Does showing mercy mean there should be no consequences? No. Mercy is not the same as excusing evil. Forgiving someone who abused you does not mean staying in danger, keeping silent, or protecting them from the law. The authorities exist to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and churches must report abuse and protect the vulnerable. Mercy refuses personal revenge and longs for the offender’s repentance; justice still holds him accountable. A church that covers up abuse in the name of mercy is not showing mercy to anyone, least of all the victim.

In a sentence. Speak and act as people who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom, because judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

On a Tuesday. To whom do you need to show mercy this week? The colleague who failed you, the family member who keeps disappointing you, the brother whose sin embarrassed the church. Forgive, help, or give, remembering the mercy God has shown you. And listen to your own speech: when you talk about people who have failed, does it sound like someone who has been forgiven much?

For worship. Mercy triumphs over judgment because God is rich in mercy (Ephesians 2:4). He delights in steadfast love (Micah 7:18). He looked at a world under sentence and did not cancel the sentence; he carried it himself, in the person of his Son. At the cross justice and mercy kissed: every demand of judgment met in full, and mercy standing over it in triumph. And the mercy that triumphed there is the mercy that flows out of everyone who has tasted it. Every act of mercy in a Christian’s life is a small echo of Calvary.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What good is it to say you have faith if you have no works? Can that kind of faith save? Words of blessing to a hungry brother with no food given are useless; faith without works is dead. Even demons believe that God is one, and tremble. Abraham was counted righteous when he believed, and his faith was shown and completed when he offered Isaac. Rahab’s faith was shown when she hid the spies. As the body without breath is dead, so faith without works is dead.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith That Works

James asks whether a faith that is only said can save. Abraham was counted righteous by faith, and his obedience showed that faith to be alive. We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Even the demons believe that God is one — and shudder.

Now: Warm words to a hungry brother with nothing given are the picture of dead faith.

verseByVerse.quote: What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?

What good is it, my brothers. Now the most controverted paragraph in the letter, and the first verse repays exact reading, because a great deal of confusion is settled by two small words. What good (ti to ophelos) means what profit, what use, and it is the theme of the whole passage: useful faith versus useless faith.

If someone says he has faith but does not have works? The first key word is says (legē). James is not describing a man who has faith. He is describing a man who claims it, and the whole question is whether the claim is true: a profession with no evidence. And works (erga) here are deeds of love and obedience, like clothing and feeding a poor brother (vv. 15–16), not the works of the law (circumcision, food laws, ritual) that Paul denies can justify.

Can that faith save him? The second key word is the article. The Greek has the faith (hē pistis): can the faith, that faith, the kind just described, save him? James is not asking whether faith saves. He is asking whether this thing does, and the form of the question in Greek expects the answer no. A faith that consists only of words, with no works, cannot save.

Two words settle much. Get those two words right and the supposed clash with Paul largely dissolves before it starts. Paul is answering the question: how is a sinner justified? And the answer is faith, apart from works of law. James is answering a different question: what kind of faith is it that justifies? And the answer is: the living kind, which works.

Where Christians differ: does James contradict Paul? Paul says we are justified by faith, not works (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16); James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (v. 24). Some have thought they contradict each other; Luther once called James an epistle of straw for this reason, though he kept it in his Bible and dropped the phrase from later editions of his preface. Roman Catholic teaching uses James to argue that justification includes good works. Verdict: they do not contradict. They are answering different errors and using key words in different senses. Paul opposes legalism: those who think they can earn God’s acceptance by works of the law. James opposes empty profession: those who think a faith with no fruit can save. For Paul, justify means God’s declaration that a sinner is righteous, received through faith alone. For James, justify here means to show or prove righteous, as Abraham’s faith was vindicated by his deeds. For Paul, works means works of the law done to earn merit; for James, works of love that flow from faith. For Paul, faith means genuine trust in Christ; for James, in verse 14, faith means a mere claim to believe. Both agree: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone; it always produces works (Galatians 5:6; Ephesians 2:8–10).

Back to back. They are answering different errors, and both would have recognised the other’s target as an enemy. Paul writes against people trying to add works to Christ; James writes against people who have subtracted works entirely and are comfortable. Picture two soldiers standing back to back, facing opposite directions, defending the same gospel from attacks on two sides. Above all, note that James never contrasts faith with works. He contrasts living faith with dead faith. Works are not an addition to faith in his argument. They are its vital signs.

What it does not mean. It does not mean works are part of the ground of justification. Christ’s righteousness alone is the ground. It means works are the necessary evidence of genuine faith.

What exactly is saving faith, then? The Reformers described it in three parts. Knowledge (notitia): knowing the truth about who Christ is and what he has done. Agreement (assensus): believing that it is true. And trust (fiducia): resting on Christ personally, relying on him alone for forgiveness and life. The faith James attacks has the first two at most; it never comes to the third. True faith is like a drowning man taking hold of the rope. And a man who has taken hold of the rope does not stay in the water. He is pulled out, and his whole life moves in a new direction.

What about the thief on the cross? He had no time for good works. The thief was saved by faith alone, and his faith was alive. In his last hours it worked: he rebuked the other criminal, confessed his own guilt, defended Jesus’ innocence, and called on him as King (Luke 23:40–43). Works in James’s sense are not a quota to be filled before you qualify; they are the signs of life that appear wherever faith is real, however short the time. A newborn baby has not achieved anything, but it breathes and cries. So did the thief.

In a sentence. My brothers and sisters, what use is it if someone claims to have faith but has no deeds to show for it? Can that kind of faith save them?

On a Tuesday. If someone looked at your life this week, what evidence of faith would they see? Not your church attendance or your views, but how you treated your colleague, your spouse, the person who served you in the shop, the neighbour in need. Ask God to make your faith visible in love. And if you see little, do not try to manufacture evidence; go back to Christ and trust him afresh, because works grow from faith, not the other way round.

For worship. The faith that saves looks entirely away from itself to Christ, and the Christ it looks to is never idle. He is the one who went about doing good (Acts 10:38), who healed, fed, touched and served, and who finished the work the Father gave him on the cross. Faith takes hold of that finished work and is united to that living Lord, and a branch joined to the true vine cannot help bearing fruit. We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10). Even the works that prove our faith are his gift.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says we are justified by faith, not works; James says a faith that produces no works is not saving faith. They answer different errors.

verseByVerse.quote: If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food. James proves the point with a scene rather than an argument, exactly as he did with the gold ring. Note who it is: not a stranger, but someone in the congregation. Brother or sister: James explicitly includes women. Poorly clothed (gymnoi) means naked, inadequately dressed. And lacking in daily food (leipomenoi tēs ephēmerou trophēs) means food for the day itself. This is not want of comfort. The person has nothing to eat today.

And one of you says to them, Go in peace, be warmed and filled. The words are entirely correct. Go in peace (hypagete en eirēnē) is the ordinary Jewish farewell blessing; the two verbs (thermainesthe kai chortazesthe) may even be passives of the sort used in prayer: may you be warmed, may you be filled. This is a man giving a genuine blessing and quite possibly praying.

Without giving them the things needed for the body. And there it is. He has said everything and done nothing, and the words themselves are what make it grotesque. Silence would have been less offensive. Words cannot warm or feed. The words are kind; the absence of help is cruel.

What good is that? The same question as verse 14, and now with a cold answer available: the man is exactly as hungry as before, and has been sent away feeling blessed.

A coat and a meal. The illustration is chosen with precision. James could have picked adultery or theft to expose a hollow faith. He picks a coat and a meal, because the failure he is describing is not scandalous. It is a religion that is fluent, warm, and costs nothing. John says the same: if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? Let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth (1 John 3:17–18).

So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead. By itself (kath’ heautēn) means alone, on its own. Not weak, not immature, not in need of supplement. Dead (nekra), which is a word about what a thing is, not about how much of it there is. A corpse is not a person with reduced vitality. A faith that produces no works is not real, living faith. Just as kind words without help are empty, so a profession of faith without works is empty.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith becomes alive by adding works, as if works give life to faith. Rather, works show that faith is alive. A living tree bears fruit; the fruit does not make it alive.

But if my works are weak and inconsistent, is my faith dead? James is describing a faith with no works at all, words without a life behind them. He himself says we all stumble in many ways (3:2). Living faith may be small and imperfect, but it is real: it trusts Christ, it struggles against sin, and it shows itself, however feebly, in love.

Do I have to give to everyone who asks? James’s example is a brother or sister in the church, in real need, standing in front of you, and you able to help. Start there: your church family comes first (Galatians 6:10), and genuine need you can meet should be met. Beyond that, love uses wisdom. Sometimes giving money feeds an addiction, and a meal, a bag of shopping or a referral to the church’s care is better. Scripture also says that a man able to work but unwilling should not be fed for nothing (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Wisdom shapes how we help. It is never an excuse for not helping at all.

In a sentence. Suppose a brother or sister has no clothes and no food for the day. If one of you says to them, Go in peace; keep warm and eat well, but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith on its own, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have wished well but not helped? The person you said you would pray for, the family going through a hard time, the new parents, the man who lost his job. Move from words to action this week: give food, clothing, money or time. And next time you say I will pray for you, consider whether you could also say: and what can I bring round on Thursday?

For worship. God did not send us away with a blessing. When we were naked and starving, he did not say go in peace, be warmed and filled. He came. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, fed the hungry with his own hands, and gave his body as bread for the life of the world. His love was never words only: in this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). The gospel is not a well-wishing. It is a rescue, and every coat given in his name is a small picture of it.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!

But someone will say, You have faith and I have works. James brings in an objector, and the punctuation of verse 18 has puzzled readers for centuries, since ancient manuscripts carried no quotation marks. The exact boundaries of the quotation are debated. The likeliest sense is someone saying: these are two gifts. You have faith, and I have works. Different people, different strengths, and both are fine. James rejects separating faith and works.

Show me your faith apart from your works. The reply is a challenge that cannot be met. Show (deixon) means demonstrate, prove. It is unanswerable because faith is invisible. There is no way to display it except through what it does. The objector is being asked to produce evidence of something in a medium where no evidence can exist.

And I will show you my faith by my works. While James can simply point. Works are the visible evidence of invisible faith. The only way to show faith is by its fruit; you will recognise them by their fruits (Matthew 7:16–20).

You believe that God is one; you do well. Then verse 19, and it is one of the most chilling sentences in Scripture. That is not a random doctrine. It is the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. Every devout Jew recited it morning and evening; it was the foundation of the whole faith. James picks the most orthodox statement available and grants it fully: you do well. He is not belittling right belief. It is true.

Even the demons believe, and shudder! The demons are perfect monotheists. Their theology is impeccable; in the Gospels they identify Jesus correctly before anybody else does: I know who you are, the Holy One of God (Mark 1:24; 5:7). So orthodoxy cannot be the thing that distinguishes a Christian, because the demons have it and are not saved.

Orthodox and terrified. And the verb is worse than belief. They shudder (phrissousin): the word means to bristle, the hair standing on end. They have an emotional response to God as well. So the creed is right and the feelings are real, and it changes nothing, because they do not trust, love or obey. Which makes this a searching verse for anyone whose Christianity consists of correct convictions and genuine feeling in a service. James has just described that combination and named who else has it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean correct doctrine is unimportant. The demons are right about God. It means correct doctrine without trust, love and obedience is demonic, not saving. Saving faith includes knowledge, agreement and personal trust (the Reformers’ notitia, assensus, fiducia).

How do I know my faith is more than the demons’ faith? Ask what you do with what you believe. The demons know Jesus is the Son of God and want him to go away (Mark 5:7). Do you want him near? They tremble at God and hate him. Do you, even weakly, love him and want to please him? They believe, and keep on rebelling. Do you fight your sin, and grieve when you fail? Saving faith comes to Christ, rests on him, and wants to follow him. If that is the direction of your heart, however feeble, it is not demonic belief; it is the work of the Spirit.

Should I look at my works to find assurance? Look first and chiefly to Christ: his promises, his finished work, his invitation to all who come. That is the foundation of assurance. Then your works and the change in your life serve as confirming evidence that your faith is real, and the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16; Westminster 18.2). If you look only at your works, you will either become proud or despair. Look to Christ, and then you can look honestly at your life without fear, because your hope does not rest there.

In a sentence. But someone will say, You have faith; I have deeds. Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. You believe that there is one God. Good! Even the demons believe that, and they tremble with fear.

On a Tuesday. Write down the three or four things you believe most firmly about God. Then for each one, ask: what difference did this make to my life this week? If God is sovereign, how did I handle the thing that went wrong? If Christ is Lord, whose will governed my diary? Beyond believing the right things about God, are you trusting him, loving him, obeying him? Let your faith go further than the demons’ faith.

For worship. The demons tremble before the one God, and they are right to. But we may come close. The God whose holiness makes devils shudder has opened his arms to sinners through his Son, so that we can draw near with confidence to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16). The Holy One of God whom the demons named in terror is the friend of sinners, who crushed the serpent’s head and disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15). We do not tremble as they do. We tremble with joy, and we trust.
verseByVerse.note: The confession “God is one” is the Shema, the daily creed of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?

Do you want to be shown, you foolish person. The address is sharp. Want (theleis) means are you willing; shown (gnōnai) means to know, recognise. And foolish (kenē) means empty, hollow, vain: a man with nothing inside. It is aimed with some precision at somebody whose religion consists of a claim: his faith is empty, and so is he. Not an insult but a rebuke, like Jesus’ O foolish ones on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:25).

Do you want to be shown. That introduces evidence. James has argued from a scene (vv. 15–16) and from the demons (v. 19); now he turns to Scripture, and to the two examples his readers would have found most surprising.

That faith apart from works is useless? Useless (argē) is a slight change from dead in verse 17. The word means idle, not working, out of employment. It is the term for land lying fallow or a labourer standing in the marketplace with nothing to do (Matthew 20:3). And there is a deliberate play in it: faith without works (ergōn) does not work (a-ergē). Some manuscripts read dead (as in vv. 17, 26), but useless is better supported.

Dead and idle. The two words together give the whole diagnosis. Dead describes what it is; idle describes what it does, which is nothing. Neither word suggests a faith that is real but underdeveloped, and James leaves no room for the reading that would make works an optional improvement on something already sufficient.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the person addressed is beyond hope. James rebukes in order to restore.

Jesus said whoever says You fool will be liable to judgment. Is James breaking that rule? No. Jesus was forbidding contemptuous insult flung in anger (Matthew 5:22). James is giving a pastoral diagnosis, the way Jesus himself called the Pharisees blind fools (Matthew 23:17) and the Emmaus disciples foolish. The difference is motive and purpose: the angry insult wants to wound and dismiss; the loving rebuke wants to wake someone up and bring him back. A doctor who says this is serious is not being cruel. James speaks sharply because the stakes are eternal.

In a sentence. You foolish person, do you want proof that faith without deeds does not work?

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself whether there is anything in your Christian life that is idle: a gift you are not using, a conviction you have never acted on, a resolution you keep making. Pick one and put it to work this week. And if someone has rebuked you lovingly recently, go back to what they said and take it seriously.

For worship. God does not leave empty people empty. He fills the hungry with good things (Luke 1:53). The Spirit poured into our hearts turns idle faith into working love. And the Lord who rebukes us does it as a Father: the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6). Even his sharpest words are spoken in order to fill us, and he has never given up on a hollow heart that turned to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works;

Was not Abraham our father justified by works. This is the sentence that troubled Luther, and it needs facing directly rather than softened. Abraham our father is the father of the Jewish people and of all who believe (Romans 4:11–12). James has chosen the same man Paul uses to prove justification by faith apart from works (Romans 4:1–5; Galatians 3:6), and appears to say the opposite. Justified (edikaiōthē) here means shown to be righteous, vindicated, proved genuine.

When he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? The resolution is in the chronology, and James supplies it himself two verses later. Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15:6, when he believed the promise about the stars. He offered Isaac in Genesis 22, decades later. So the offering cannot be what made him righteous before God, since he had been counted righteous for years before he climbed the mountain. It demonstrated and vindicated his faith. God said afterward that now he knew Abraham feared him (Genesis 22:12). The test proved the faith genuine.

You see that faith was active along with his works. What then does justified by works mean here? Verse 22 answers it exactly. Two verbs, and both are careful. Faith was active along with (synērgei), working together with, cooperating with his works: they are collaborators, not rivals, and the faith is the active partner. Faith was the source; works were the expression. Abraham’s faith did not sit idle; it went to work.

And faith was completed by his works. Completed (eteleiōthē) means brought to its intended end, matured, perfected, like fruit ripening. Not supplemented, as though something was missing, nor that faith was deficient before; fulfilled, as a seed is fulfilled in a tree. Faith reached its full goal in obedience.

The faith that raised the knife. So Genesis 22 did not create Abraham’s righteousness. It demonstrated and matured the faith of Genesis 15, and it demonstrated it in the one place where faith could be tested to destruction, since the son on the altar was the very promise he had believed God for. Only a man who genuinely trusted God to keep his word could raise that knife. Hebrews tells us what he was thinking: he considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead (Hebrews 11:17–19).

Two senses of justify. James and Paul are using justify in its two ordinary senses. Paul means declared righteous before God; James means shown to be righteous, vindicated, as Jesus said: wisdom is justified by her deeds (Matthew 11:19). We use the word the same way when we say that events justified someone’s confidence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham was declared righteous before God because of his works. Scripture says he was counted righteous when he believed (Genesis 15:6), decades before Genesis 22. His works proved his faith genuine before God and others.

Does the story of Isaac mean God approves of child sacrifice? No. God stopped Abraham’s hand and provided the ram, and his law later condemned child sacrifice as an abomination (Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31). The command was a unique test in redemptive history, never to be repeated, and it was designed to point forward. On that same mountain range, Moriah, God would one day not spare his own Son. What God stopped Abraham from doing, he did himself, for us.

Will God test me the way he tested Abraham? Not with that command; it was unique, and God will never ask you to do what his word forbids. But he does test his people, asking whether we love him more than his gifts. Often the test comes in the thing we most treasure: a child, a career, a hope. God may ask you to hold it with an open hand, to trust him with it, to obey him when obedience seems to put it at risk. The lesson of Moriah is that God can be trusted with our Isaacs. The LORD will provide (Genesis 22:14).

In a sentence. Was not our ancestor Abraham shown to be righteous by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that his faith and his actions were working together, and his faith reached its full goal through what he did.

On a Tuesday. What is your Isaac: the thing you love so much that you are afraid of what obedience might cost it? Name it to God honestly. Then take one step of trust this week: a decision made his way, a grip loosened, a prayer that says, it is yours. Faith that is completed by works usually starts with one such step on a hard morning.

For worship. On Mount Moriah, a father climbed with his son, and the son carried the wood. The son asked where the lamb was, and the father said God would provide. Two thousand years later, on a hill near that same place, another Father gave his only Son, whom he loved, and the Son carried the wood of his own cross, and this time there was no voice from heaven to stop the knife. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Romans 8:32). Abraham’s faith was completed by his works. Our salvation was completed by God’s.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.

And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Here James quotes Genesis 15:6, the very verse Paul builds Romans 4 on (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6), and by quoting it he settles the chronology himself. The statement that Abraham was counted righteous by believing stands; James is showing what happened to it afterwards. Counted (elogisthē) means reckoned, credited, imputed: a legal and accounting word. God credited righteousness to Abraham when he believed.

Fulfilled. And fulfilled (eplērōthē) is the key. The word is used of a prophecy coming true: filled up, brought to full meaning. Genesis 15:6 was a declaration awaiting its demonstration, and Genesis 22 is where it was filled full. The faith that was counted righteous in chapter 15 proved to be the real thing in chapter 22.

And he was called a friend of God. The title (philos theou) comes from 2 Chronicles 20:7 and Isaiah 41:8, and it is still how Abraham is known across the Middle East today: in Arabic, simply the Friend. Notice what James thinks the offering produced: not merit, but intimacy. Genuine faith leads to intimate relationship with God, shown in obedience; Jesus said, you are my friends if you do what I command you (John 15:14–15).

You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. The most debated phrase in James. It is the only place in the New Testament where the phrase faith alone appears, and it is negated, which is why Luther struggled with the letter. But read what James actually denies. Justified here, as in verse 21, means shown or vindicated as righteous. Not by faith alone (ouk ek pisteōs monon) means not by the kind of faith described in verses 14–19: a faith that is on its own, unaccompanied, with nothing beside it, a mere profession. That is the naked claim of verse 14, the faith that only gets said. Such faith does not justify, because it is not genuine faith. A person is shown to be righteous by works that prove the reality of their faith.

Where Christians differ: does this verse deny justification by faith alone? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse as proof against the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone, and cites it to show that justification is a process of being made righteous, to which faith and works both contribute. Verdict: James is not denying that we are declared righteous by faith alone in Paul’s sense; he quotes Genesis 15:6 himself. He is not describing how a sinner is first accepted by God: he says that Abraham was counted righteous when he believed (v. 23), and then shows that faith proved true years later. He is denying that a faith which remains alone, without works, is saving faith. The Reformers said it well: we are justified by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. James and Paul agree: God declares sinners righteous by grace through faith in Christ, on the basis of his righteousness imputed to them; and the faith that receives this always works by love.

A formula worth memorising. The Reformers understood this exactly: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. James is not attacking the article the Reformation recovered. He is attacking the counterfeit that always attaches itself to it. Every true doctrine has a cheap imitation, and the cheap imitation of justification by faith is a belief that costs nothing and changes nothing. James guards the real thing by exposing the fake.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our works merit God’s acceptance, or that justification is a lifelong process of becoming righteous. It means that genuine justifying faith is always shown by works.

If I stop doing good works, will I lose my justification? No. Justification is God’s once-for-all verdict, resting entirely on Christ’s righteousness, and it cannot be reversed: those whom he justified he also glorified (Romans 8:30). Those who are truly justified will persevere, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6). A believer may go through dry and backslidden seasons and fall into serious sin, and he will be disciplined by his Father, but he will not finally fall away. If someone abandons Christ completely and permanently, it shows his faith was never the living kind (1 John 2:19). The answer to coldness is not fear of losing justification but returning to the Saviour who justified you.

Can I really be God’s friend? Yes. Abraham was a sinner who lied about his wife twice, and God called him friend. Jesus says to his disciples: no longer do I call you servants, but I have called you friends (John 15:15). Friendship with God is not reserved for spiritual giants; it is the privilege of everyone justified by faith. It means you may speak to him freely, share your heart, trust his heart, and enjoy his company. And it shows itself, as Abraham’s did, in trusting obedience.

In a sentence. And so the Scripture came true that says, Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness, and he was called God’s friend. You see that a person is shown to be righteous by what they do, and not by a faith that stays on its own.

On a Tuesday. Explain to yourself, in two sentences, how a sinner is made right with God. Then explain how you would know whether someone’s faith was real. If you can say both clearly, you can hold Paul and James together. Then ask what a friend of God would do with this Tuesday: talk to him, trust him with the worry, do the thing he asked.

For worship. Righteousness was credited to Abraham, an old man who believed God about the stars, and it has been credited to everyone who believes in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:24–25). It was not our righteousness that was counted; it was Christ’s. And the God of glory, who needs no one, calls such people his friends. The friend of sinners laid down his life for his friends, and greater love has no one than this (John 15:13). We are justified by faith alone, and the faith he gives is never alone, because he is never absent from it.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, many years before he offered Isaac in Genesis 22; the offering showed the faith was real.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.

And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works. The second example is deliberately chosen to be as unlike the first as possible. Abraham is a man, the father of the nation, the patriarch, a Jew, the friend of God. Rahab is a woman, a Gentile, a Canaanite, and a prostitute, and James does not soften the noun. Between them they cover everybody. If the principle holds at both ends of that range, nobody is outside it. Genuine faith looks the same across every human distinction.

Two people God justified. And there may be a further point in a letter that has just condemned partiality: the congregation seating men by their clothes is shown two people God justified, one of whom they would not have let through the door. Rahab ended up in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). The church that would have sat her on the floor would have been snubbing the great-great-grandmother of King David.

When she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? Her work is specified. She received them (hypodexamenē, welcomed as guests), hid the two spies under flax on her roof, and sent them out (ekbalousa, thrust out, helped them escape) by a different route (Joshua 2:1–21). It was treason against her own city, punishable by death, and it was done on the strength of what she had heard about Israel’s God: the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath (Joshua 2:11). Her faith in Israel’s God led her to risk her life to protect his people. Her actions showed her faith was real. Hebrews 11:31 credits the same act to faith. James and Hebrews are looking at one event from two sides.

But Rahab lied. She lied to the king’s men (Joshua 2:4–5). James commends her for siding with God’s people at the risk of her life, receiving the spies and sending them out safely (Hebrews 11:31), not for the lie as such. Christians differ on whether deceiving those bent on murder is a sin; the more likely reading is that her lie was a sin forgiven, and her faith was what God honoured.

For as the body apart from the spirit is dead. Then the closing image, and it is the sharpest in the letter. Spirit (pneuma) also means breath. A body without breath, without spirit, is a corpse.

So also faith apart from works is dead. The conclusion of the passage, repeating verse 17. Work out the correspondence. Faith is the body; works are the breath. Which means works are not the important half; a body matters more than an exhalation. What breath does is prove there is life in the body. So James is not saying works are the substance of Christianity and faith the accompaniment. He is saying that a faith with no works is a corpse: the shape is all there, the features are recognisable, and nothing is moving.

What it does not mean. It does not commend Rahab’s former life or her lie (see Hebrews 11:31). It commends her faith-driven act of protecting God’s messengers. Nor does it make works the source of faith’s life; it makes them the sign of it.

My past is like Rahab’s. Can my faith be real? Yes, and this verse was written partly for you. God did not wait for Rahab to clean up her reputation before he saved her. She believed with what little she knew, acted on it, and was brought into the people of God and into the family line of the Messiah. Your past does not limit what God can do with you; it magnifies his grace. The question is not where you have been but whom you are trusting now, and whether that trust is starting to move your hands and feet.

What does a living faith look like in an ordinary week? Usually it is quiet. It is the young mother who prays while she changes nappies and is patient with a toddler for Christ’s sake. It is the businessman who refuses the dishonest deal, the teenager who sits with the lonely kid at lunch, the old man who visits the hospital every Thursday, the couple who open their home to the church’s newcomers. Rahab’s work was one dangerous night, but most works of faith are small, repeated, and unseen. They are the breathing of a living faith, and breathing is rarely dramatic. It is only noticed when it stops.

In a sentence. In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute shown to be righteous by what she did when she welcomed the spies and sent them off in a different direction? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your background, your faith can be real and active. What risk might faith call you to take this week for God’s people: standing with a persecuted believer, opening your home, speaking up for a brother who is being slandered, giving more than is comfortable? And check your breathing: if there is no sign of life in your faith this week, do not try harder in your own strength; go back to Christ, the one who breathes life into the dead.

For worship. A scarlet cord hung from Rahab’s window, and when Jericho fell, the house with the scarlet cord stood. She was saved by faith in the God of Israel, marked by a thread of red, and brought into the line that led to Bethlehem. And the one born of that line shed his blood for prostitutes and patriarchs alike, so that all who shelter under it are spared when judgment falls. He breathed his last on the cross, and on the third day he breathed again, and on the evening of his rising he breathed on his disciples and said: receive the Holy Spirit (John 20:22). Living faith breathes because the risen Christ has breathed into it, and what he has made alive he will never let die.
