3.title: The Tongue and True Wisdom
3.overview:
Chapter 3 deals with two linked themes: the tongue and wisdom. The tongue (vv. 1–12) is small but decisive, like a bit, a rudder or a spark, and no human can tame it. Its problem is not speech but the heart: a spring gives what its source supplies.

So James turns to wisdom (vv. 13–18). Earthly wisdom, full of jealousy and selfish ambition, produces disorder. Wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, merciful, impartial and sincere, and it yields a harvest of righteousness sown in peace. The answer to the tongue is not a technique, but a new source.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Not many should become teachers, because teachers are judged more strictly. We all stumble, and the one who controls his speech is mature. The tongue is small, like a bit or a rudder, but it steers everything; like a spark, it sets a forest ablaze. No human can tame it. With it we bless God and curse people made in his likeness, which ought not to be. A spring cannot give fresh and salt water from one opening.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Tongue Cannot Be Tamed

The tongue is small and decisive, and no human can tame it. The problem is the spring, not the water; the answer is wisdom from above.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Too many in the congregation wanted to teach.

Now: We cannot bless God and curse people made in his likeness from the same mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.

Meaning first. James 3 develops two themes from chapter 1: the tongue (1:19, 26) and wisdom (1:5). First, the tongue (vv. 1–12). Teachers will be judged more strictly, because they use words, and everyone stumbles in speech; whoever never stumbles in speech is mature enough to control his whole self (vv. 1–2). The tongue is small but powerful, like a horse’s bit or a ship’s rudder (vv. 3–4). It is like a tiny spark that sets a forest ablaze; it is a world of evil among our members, defiling the whole person and setting life on fire, itself set on fire by hell (vv. 5–6). Every kind of animal has been tamed, but no human can tame the tongue: it is restless and full of deadly poison (vv. 7–8). With it we bless God and curse people made in his image, which should not happen; a spring does not pour out fresh and salt water, nor a fig tree bear olives (vv. 9–12). Second, two kinds of wisdom (vv. 13–18). True wisdom shows itself in good conduct and gentle humility (v. 13). Jealousy and selfish ambition are a false wisdom, earthly, unspiritual and demonic, producing disorder and every evil (vv. 14–16). The wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, reasonable, merciful, fruitful, impartial and sincere, and peacemakers sow a harvest of righteousness (vv. 17–18). The chapter that begins with a fire set by hell ends with a harvest sown from heaven, and the hinge between them is a wisdom that only God can give.

Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers. It is a startling opening, and it tells us something about that congregation: too many of them wanted the job. Teachers (didaskaloi) were those who taught in the church, a recognised and respected role (Acts 13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11). That is understandable in a Jewish setting, where the rabbi was the most honoured figure in the community and teaching was the recognised path to standing. In scattered congregations with no settled structure, the man who could hold a room had an obvious opportunity.

For you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness. Note the pronoun. James does not exempt himself; he puts himself inside the warning, which is the only honest way to issue it. Greater strictness (meizon krima) is literally a greater judgment, and it is a real principle that runs through Scripture: to whom much is given, much is required (Luke 12:48). A teacher handles other people’s souls with his words, and error from the front does damage that error in a private conversation does not. Teachers are responsible both for what they teach and for how they live (Matthew 5:19; 12:36–37; Hebrews 13:17), because their hearers will copy both.

The hinge into the chapter. Why does a warning about teachers open a passage about the tongue? Because teaching is the one occupation conducted entirely with it. The teacher is the man whose whole work is speech, and therefore the man most exposed to the thing James is about to describe.

The wanting. Be clear that this is not discouragement of the gift. The New Testament commands teaching and prizes it. What James discourages is the wanting: the drift toward a visible role for reasons that have more to do with standing than with service. Anyone who has ever been eager to be heard should let the verse do its work before dismissing it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean no one should teach. The church needs teachers: what you have heard from me, entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). It means teaching is a serious responsibility not to be sought for status, and those who teach must be qualified and humble.

I teach Sunday school, lead a small group, or teach my children. Should this verse frighten me off? It should sober you, not silence you. If God has given you the opportunity and the church has entrusted it to you, do it gladly. Parents are commanded to teach their children (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). The warning is for the person who wants the platform more than the people, and for anyone careless with God’s truth. So prepare properly, teach only what Scripture says, admit what you do not know, live what you teach, and let your church’s elders correct you. The greater strictness is a reason for care, not for fear: the same Lord who will judge teachers is the one who forgives them.

How should I choose whom to listen to, especially online? With the same seriousness James shows. Not every confident voice is a qualified one. Ask: does this teacher explain the Bible, or use it for his own ideas? Is his life consistent with his teaching? Is he accountable to a local church and its elders? Does his teaching make Christ great and make you more humble, holy and loving, or more angry, proud and suspicious? And do not let any online teacher replace the pastor who knows your name and will give account for your soul (Hebrews 13:17).

In a sentence. Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.

On a Tuesday. If you teach in any way, whether Sunday school, Bible study, parenting, or online, pray for faithfulness and humility, knowing you will give account. Before you next prepare, ask yourself why you want to do it, and whether the passage has spoken to you before you speak it to anyone else. And pray this week, by name, for those who teach you.

For worship. There is one Teacher who will never be judged, because he is the Judge, and his words were never once careless. No one ever spoke like this man (John 7:46). He taught with authority and lived every syllable, and he never sought his own glory: my teaching is not mine, but his who sent me (John 7:16). He bore the stricter judgment we teachers deserve for every careless word we have spoken in his name. And he still teaches his church through his word, gentle and lowly in heart, the only teacher whose every word is life.

verseByVerse.quote: For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.

For we all stumble in many ways. Again the pronoun includes the writer, and the verb (ptaiomen, as in 2:10) is the ordinary word for tripping: not falling headlong, but catching your foot. It happens repeatedly (polla, many times, in many areas), to everyone, and mostly without intention. Every believer continues to sin: if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). James, the pillar of the Jerusalem church, says we.

And if anyone does not stumble in what he says. In what he says (en logō) is in word, in speech. The tongue is the hardest area to control.

He is a perfect man. Perfect is teleios again, the word from 1:4: mature, complete, having arrived at its end. James is not describing sinlessness but full growth, and this is hypothetical: since we all stumble, no one has reached it. And he is making a diagnostic claim of great practical value: speech is the reliable index of maturity. Not doctrine, not zeal, not attendance, not even generosity, all of which can be produced by effort or temperament. The tongue is the last thing to come under control, so a man who has it in hand has everything else in hand.

Why speech tells the truth. The reason is that speech is largely involuntary. Most of what we say is not decided; it arrives. Which makes it the most honest evidence available about what is actually inside, and it is why the Lord said that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34). What comes out when you are tired, interrupted or contradicted is a fair sample of what is in there.

Able also to bridle his whole body. The bridle image (chalinagōgēsai, rein in, control) is from 1:26, and it introduces the two pictures that follow. James is not saying the tongue is the worst part of a person. He is saying it is the controlling part, and that is the thought the next verses develop. If you can control your tongue, you can control everything else. The tongue is the test of self-control.

Where Christians differ: can a Christian reach sinless perfection in this life? Some holiness and Wesleyan traditions teach that believers can attain entire sanctification, a state of freedom from conscious sin. Verdict: James says we all stumble in many ways, including himself, an apostolic leader. Scripture teaches that believers grow in holiness throughout life but are never sinless until glory (1 John 1:8–10; Philippians 3:12–14; Romans 7:14–25). We pursue maturity earnestly, but we always need daily forgiveness.

What it does not mean. It does not excuse sin because we all stumble. It humbles us and calls us to work at the hardest area, speech.

What counts as stumbling in speech? More than swearing. Scripture names lying, exaggeration, gossip and slander, flattery, boasting, grumbling and complaining, harsh and cutting words, sarcasm meant to wound, crude joking, breaking promises, and careless words spoken in anger (Ephesians 4:25–31; 5:4; Philippians 2:14). It also includes what we fail to say: the encouragement withheld, the truth not spoken, the apology not made. Most of us stumble daily. The point is not to despair but to notice, confess, and ask God to make our words like his.

In a sentence. We all make many mistakes. Anyone who never makes a mistake in what they say is fully mature, able to keep their whole body in check.

On a Tuesday. Keep a quiet watch on your words for one day: not to scold yourself, but to learn. Notice when you exaggerated, interrupted, complained or spoke sharply, and what was happening at the time. At the end of the day, confess them specifically, and where someone was hurt, put it right before you sleep.

For worship. One man never stumbled in what he said. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:22–23). Every word Jesus spoke was true, kind and well-timed, even on the cross: Father, forgive them; today you will be with me in paradise; behold your mother. He was the perfect man James describes, and his perfect words are counted to us who have stumbled in ours. And the same Lord is at work in us now, by his Spirit, to make our speech gracious, seasoned with salt.

verseByVerse.quote: If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.

If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us. Two illustrations, and they make the same point from opposite ends of ordinary experience. A horse weighs half a ton and can kill a man. The bit (chalinos) is a few ounces of iron. And the disproportion is the whole argument.

We guide their whole bodies as well. A small thing in the mouth turns (metagomen, turns, directs) the entire animal. Control the mouth, control the horse.

Look at the ships also, though they are so large and are driven by strong winds. Same disproportion, and now with an added factor: the ship is not merely large, it is under enormous external pressure. Ancient merchant ships could be large; the one that carried Paul held 276 people (Acts 27:37). Gales are pushing it.

They are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs. And still a board at the stern decides where it goes. The rudder (pēdalion) was a steering oar. Both images say the same thing about the tongue: small, and decisive. James has already said the man who controls his speech controls everything (v. 2); these pictures explain why. The tongue is not one member among many. It is the helm.

Who has the rudder? And notice a detail in the second picture: wherever the will of the pilot (euthynontos, the one steering) directs. The rudder is small and powerful, and it is also steered. It does not choose the course; somebody’s intention is behind it. Which is the hopeful note in a chapter that is about to turn very dark. If the tongue is a rudder, the question is who has hold of it. James will say shortly that no human being can tame it, but a rudder was never meant to be tamed. It was meant to be steered.

What it does not mean. The illustrations do not mean the tongue is easy to control. They show its power: small, but it directs everything. The next verses show it is in fact hardest of all to control.

Does this mean I can steer my life by speaking positive words over it? No. Some teachers claim that our words have creative power, so that by declaring health or wealth we bring it into being. That is not what James means, and it is not biblical. Only God speaks things into existence. James means that our words steer our relationships and our character: a habit of complaining steers a life toward bitterness, a habit of lying toward ruin, a habit of encouragement and prayer toward peace. Our words do not command God; they reveal and shape us.

In a sentence. When we put bits into horses’ mouths to make them obey us, we can turn the whole animal. Or think of ships: although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot wants to go.

On a Tuesday. Your tongue is steering your life and relationships. Where is it taking you? Look at your three closest relationships and ask what your words over the last month have done to them: steered toward trust and warmth, or toward distance and irritation? Then ask God to take the rudder, and choose one relationship where you will deliberately steer with kindness this week.

For worship. The winds that drive our lives are strong, but there is a Pilot who has never lost a ship. The disciples woke him in the storm, and he rebuked the wind and said to the sea, Peace! Be still! (Mark 4:39). The Word by whom the worlds were made speaks still, and his word steers all things toward his purpose. Put the helm of your mouth in his hands. He who calmed the sea can calm the tongue, and bring every one of his people safe into harbour.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell.

So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. The summary of the two pictures: a small member (melos, part of the body) that boasts of great things (megala auchei, claims great power), small but with enormous influence, for good or ill. And then the image changes, and the temperature with it.

How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! The bit and the rudder were neutral instruments; a fire is not. James has moved from the tongue’s power to its danger, and every image from here is destructive. Anyone who has lived near dry country knows the picture exactly. A spark, one carelessly dropped thing, and a hillside (hylē, woodland, brushwood) is gone, as the dry hills of Palestine knew in summer. The disproportion is the same as before, but now it runs the wrong way. A single careless word can destroy a reputation, a friendship, a marriage, a church.

And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. Then verse 6, and it is one of the most ferocious sentences in the New Testament. A world of unrighteousness (ho kosmos tēs adikias): a whole universe of wrong contained in one organ. Lies, slander, gossip, flattery, boasting, cursing, false teaching: a whole world of sin in a small space.

The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body. The word for staining (spilousa) means to defile, to spot, the opposite of the unstained of 1:27. What we say defiles our whole person: what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person (Matthew 15:11, 18).

Setting on fire the entire course of life. Literally the wheel of birth (ton trochon tēs geneseōs), the cycle of existence, an unusual phrase perhaps borrowed from popular philosophy. The whole revolving round of a person’s existence, alight from end to end, from beginning to end.

And set on fire by hell. Then the source. The word is Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final punishment (Matthew 5:22, 29–30; 10:28; 23:33; Mark 9:43–48). Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once defiled by child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31), later a symbol of God’s judgment. James is not being poetic. He is saying that destructive speech has a supply line, and it runs from below: its source is in hell itself, in Satan, the father of lies (John 8:44).

Why James goes so far. This is the strongest thing said about the tongue anywhere in Scripture, and it is worth asking why James goes so far. The answer is in his congregation: these were people under pressure, poor, displaced, and quarrelling, and what was actually destroying them was not persecution from outside but what they were saying to each other.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the tongue can only do evil. It can bless, encourage, teach and pray (v. 9). The tongue of the wise brings healing, and death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 12:18; 18:21). But uncontrolled, its potential for evil is immense. And hell does not mean the Valley of Hinnom was literally the place of final punishment; it became the name for the real, conscious, eternal punishment of the wicked.

When I lose my temper and say terrible things, is that the devil? It is your own sin, for which you are responsible, and the devil is glad to fan it. James does not say every harsh word is demonic possession; he says destructive speech serves the devil’s purposes and draws on his fire. That should make us take our words very seriously, and it should also make us run to Christ, who has defeated the devil (Hebrews 2:14). You do not fight hell’s fire with willpower. You fight it with confession, the word of God and the Spirit’s help.

I have already started a fire with my words. What do I do? Act quickly, because fires spread. Go to the person you hurt, privately, and say plainly what you said and that it was wrong, without excuses or blaming. If you spread gossip, go back to those you told and correct it. Ask forgiveness from God and from them. Do what you can to restore the reputation you damaged. You cannot unsay words, but honest repentance can stop a fire spreading and often begins to heal what was burned. And God can rebuild what our tongues have destroyed.

In a sentence. In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it makes great boasts. Think how a whole forest is set on fire by a tiny spark. The tongue also is a fire, a world of evil among the parts of the body. It corrupts the whole person, sets the whole course of life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak, post or send a message this week, ask: will this light a fire? If so, don’t say it. Social media has made every one of us a potential arsonist with a very large forest: words typed in a moment can reach thousands and last for years. Read it twice, imagine the person reading it, and ask whether you would say it to their face with Christ standing beside you.

For worship. The fire of hell that our tongues kindle was met by another fire. On the day of Pentecost, tongues as of fire rested on the disciples (Acts 2:3), and the first thing they did with their tongues was to tell the mighty works of God. The Spirit of Christ came down to set tongues on fire from heaven, not from hell. And the Lord who will judge every careless word bore the fire of judgment in our place, so that tongues which once spread poison might spend eternity in praise. Every word of worship from a redeemed mouth is a forest fire put out and a garden planted.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here translates Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature. The fourfold list is the categories of Genesis 1:26 and 9:2, and it is deliberate: the dominion given to Adam has actually been exercised.

Can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind. Tamed (damazetai) means subdued, brought under control. Humanity has broken horses, trained falcons, charmed snakes and worked with dolphins. Lions, elephants and even fish have been brought under human command. Remarkable mastery over creation.

But no human being can tame the tongue. And there is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward. No human being (oudeis anthrōpōn), no one of mankind. Man rules the animal creation and cannot rule six inches of his own mouth. The claim is absolute, and it needs to be taken at face value rather than softened into it is difficult. James says it cannot be done. Not by resolve, not by technique, not by the accumulated wisdom of a long life. No human effort alone can bring the tongue under control. Only God can (Psalm 141:3; Proverbs 16:1).

It is a restless evil. The same word (akatastaton) he used of the double-minded man’s instability in 1:8. It will not settle; it cannot be left unattended. Like a wild animal pacing in a cage, never at rest, always ready to break out.

Full of deadly poison. The image is the snake: venom (ios), death-bringing (thanatēphorou), like the poison of asps under their lips (Psalm 140:3; Romans 3:13). And it is the one creature in the list that is not tamed but neutralised. The venom is not occasional; the tongue is described as full of it. Words can kill: reputations, relationships, faith, and even lives.

Why James shuts the door. Why does James make a claim so absolute that it appears to leave no way forward? Because he is not writing a self-improvement chapter. If the tongue could be tamed by effort, the sensible response would be effort. He shuts that door deliberately, and the chapter’s answer, when it comes at verse 17, is not a technique for controlling speech but a wisdom from above. The problem is not the mouth. It never was.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should give up trying to control our speech. What humans cannot do alone, God can do through his Spirit. Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23).

If no one can tame the tongue, what can a Christian do? No human being can tame it, but God can change the heart from which words come (Matthew 12:34). Pray: Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth (Psalm 141:3); fill the heart with God’s word; think before speaking; and when the tongue fails, confess and make it right. The Spirit’s fruit includes self-control (Galatians 5:23).

What if someone’s words have poisoned me, and I still hear them years later? Poisonous words from a parent, a spouse, a teacher or a church leader can do deep harm, and Scripture takes that seriously; this whole passage says so. Bring those words to God and set them beside what he says about you in Christ: chosen, forgiven, loved, his child. Let his word answer theirs, again and again, until his voice is louder. Talk to a wise pastor or counsellor if the wound is deep. And if the person is still harming you with words, that is not something you must simply endure; seek help and protection.

In a sentence. Every kind of animal, bird, reptile and sea creature can be tamed and has been tamed by human beings, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

On a Tuesday. Pray Psalm 141:3 every morning this week before you speak to anyone: Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! Then watch for the moment the guard is needed, and pause long enough to let him stand at the door. Memorise one verse that answers your most common sin of speech, and say it to yourself when the temptation comes.

For worship. No human being can tame the tongue, but the Son of God became a human being and did. He who spoke the stars into being learned to speak as a child in Nazareth, and never once in thirty-three years let poison pass his lips. Grace was poured upon his lips (Psalm 45:2). And at the cross he took the venom of every poisonous word we have ever spoken, like the bronze serpent lifted up in the wilderness, so that whoever looks to him is healed (John 3:14–15). What we could not tame, he has conquered, and what he has conquered he is renewing.

verseByVerse.quote: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

With it we bless our Lord and Father. This is the double-mindedness of 1:8 in its most visible form, and note the pronoun once more: we. James includes himself in the indictment. Bless (eulogoumen) means praise, speak well of; Jewish prayers often began, Blessed are you, O Lord, and the synagogue prayers blessed God many times a day. Lord and Father together is a combination found only here in the New Testament. The blessing is genuine. These are people who really do praise God; the same mouth was singing an hour ago. That is what makes the charge land: he is not describing hypocrites who despise God, but worshippers.

And with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. Curse (katarōmetha) means to call down evil on, speak against. And the argument turns on a single phrase: people who are made in the likeness of God (kath’ homoiōsin theou gegonotas). The perfect tense means they have been made and remain in God’s likeness. James reaches back to Genesis 1:26–27 and thereby makes cursing a person a theological offence rather than merely an unkind one. Every human being bears God’s image, even after the fall (Genesis 9:6). To curse a person is to insult the God whose image they bear.

The original and the image. You cannot bless the original and curse the image. The two acts are directed at the same likeness, and one of them must be insincere. It is the argument of 1 John 4:20 in different terms: he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen. And it is why contempt for people is never a small matter: the resemblance is still there in the man you are dismissing, however defaced. Note also the scope. James does not say we curse our enemies, or the wicked. He says people, and the image-bearing is stated without qualification. It covers the difficult neighbour, the political opponent, and the person in the congregation who has genuinely wronged you.

From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. The inconsistency is painfully familiar: praising God on Sunday and slandering people on Monday; singing worship songs and then gossiping in the car park.

My brothers, these things ought not to be so. It is a remarkably restrained conclusion after the fire of verse 6, almost gentle, and addressed to brothers. Ought not (ou chrē) means it is not fitting, it must not be: a real rebuke, because this double-tongued behaviour is incompatible with genuine faith. But James thunders about the tongue in the abstract and speaks softly to the people who have one.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all strong language against evil. Jesus and the prophets denounced sin. It forbids cursing people, wishing them harm, and speaking with malice against those made in God’s image (Romans 12:14; Luke 6:28).

Is all cursing forbidden, then? The psalms and prophets call down God’s judgment on his enemies, and Paul says a false gospel is accursed (Galatians 1:8). That is leaving judgment to God. What James forbids is cursing people out of malice in our own name; Jesus calls his disciples to bless those who curse you (Luke 6:28).

What about swearing and crude language? Scripture says: let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up (Ephesians 4:29), and it rules out filthiness, foolish talk and crude joking (Ephesians 5:4). Using God’s name carelessly breaks the third commandment. Crude and obscene speech cheapens what God made good. But the deeper issue James raises is not vocabulary but contempt. A man can avoid every rude word and still destroy someone with a polite sentence. Watch both: the words, and the heart behind them.

Can I criticise politicians and public figures? Yes, you may disagree with their policies and actions, even strongly, and speak truthfully about wrongdoing. But they too bear God’s image, and we are commanded to pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and to honour everyone (1 Peter 2:17). Mockery, slander, sharing half-truths and wishing them harm are what James forbids. A useful test: would you be comfortable if they heard what you said, and if Christ heard it too?

In a sentence. With the tongue we praise our Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made in God’s likeness. Out of the same mouth come praise and cursing. My brothers and sisters, this should not be.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak about someone you dislike, remember: they bear God’s image. Speak of them as you would speak of God’s handiwork. Think of the person you have spoken most harshly about this month. Pray for them by name, ask God to bless them, and then say one true and good thing about them to someone else.

For worship. God has blessed us with the mouth that we cursed him with. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). He hung on a tree under the curse that our words had earned, and from that tree he blessed the men who cursed him. Now the same mouths that once were full of cursing and bitterness (Romans 3:14) have been given a new song. Every time a redeemed sinner blesses God, the curse is being undone, and one day every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.

Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Three questions from nature, and each expects the answer no. The picture is local and vivid. A spring (pēgē) in dry Palestine was precious, and around the Dead Sea and the Jordan valley there are both sweet springs and brackish ones, and no one confuses them. A spring is defined by what comes out of its opening (opē, crack, hole), and what comes out is determined by what it draws from. A spring gives one kind of water; it cannot give both sweet and bitter.

Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Same logic in the vegetable world: each plant produces according to its kind (Genesis 1:11–12). And the Lord had made the identical point: you will recognise them by their fruits; are grapes gathered from thornbushes? (Matthew 7:16–20; 12:33–35).

Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water. The final line is blunt and it closes off the sentimental reading. A salt spring (halykon) like those near the Dead Sea could not produce drinkable water. There is no arrangement by which a bitter source produces sweet water occasionally. The two-mouthed spring of verse 11 is not merely inconsistent; James is saying it is impossible, and therefore that the blessing and cursing coming from one congregation is evidence of something wrong at the source.

Deal with the spring. What all three pictures have in common is that the output reveals the source, and that no tree or spring has ever been talked into producing something foreign to it. Which is the answer to a question the previous verses raise: if no human can tame the tongue, what is to be done? The answer implied here is that you do not work on the water. You deal with the spring. Speech is a symptom, and the persistent attempt to reform it directly, watching your words, resolving to be kinder, is treating an outflow as though it were the problem.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who sometimes speaks sinfully is not a believer. We all stumble (v. 2). It means the pattern of our speech reveals the nature of our heart (Luke 6:45). A heart renewed by God will increasingly produce good speech; persistent evil speech reveals an unrenewed heart.

So how does the spring actually change? Only God can change a heart, and he does it through the gospel and his Spirit. In practice, that means feeding the spring: filling your mind with Scripture, so that his words are what flow out (Colossians 3:16); confessing the bitterness, envy or fear underneath the words, not just the words themselves; and praying for a clean heart (Psalm 51:10). Ask what is behind your harshest words. Usually it is pride, hurt, or fear. Take that to Christ. Sweet water comes from a heart that has been forgiven much and knows it.

In a sentence. Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring? My brothers and sisters, can a fig tree bear olives, or a grapevine bear figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.

On a Tuesday. Next time harsh words come out of you, do not only apologise for the words. Stop and ask what was in the spring: what was I afraid of, what did I want, where was my pride wounded? Write it down. Over a few weeks you will see a pattern, and that pattern is what to bring to God in prayer.

For worship. There is only one spring whose water is entirely sweet. Jesus stood up at the feast and cried: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water (John 7:37–38). He does not ask us to sweeten our own salt springs. He gives us a new spring, his own Spirit, welling up to eternal life. When he renews the source, the water becomes sweet, and the tongue that once poured out bitterness begins to pour out praise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James asks who among his readers is truly wise and understanding, and answers that wisdom proves itself in a good life lived with gentle humility. Where bitter envy and self-promotion fill the heart, boasting about wisdom is a lie against the truth. That kind of “wisdom” does not come from God; it is earthly, merely natural and even devilish, and it breeds disorder and every kind of wrong. God’s wisdom is marked first by purity, then by peace, gentleness, willingness to listen, mercy, good fruit, fairness and sincerity. Those who make peace sow seeds that grow into a harvest of righteousness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wisdom Shown, Not Stated

Wisdom is proved by good conduct in meekness. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, and almost every mark of it concerns how we treat others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition lay behind the quarrelling.

Now: The eagerness to be seen as wise is itself evidence against the claim.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.

Who is wise and understanding among you? The question returns to verse 1 and the men who wanted to teach. Very well: here is how the claim is tested. Wise (sophos) is one who has practical, godly wisdom; understanding (epistēmōn) is knowledgeable, expert, skilful. Perhaps aimed at the would-be teachers who claimed wisdom.

By his good conduct let him show his works. And the test is not what you would expect. Not an examination, not a doctrinal statement, not fluency. Show (deixatō), as in 2:18; good conduct (kalēs anastrophēs) is literally a beautiful way of life. Wisdom in the Bible is never primarily information. It is skill in living (the Hebrew word is used of craftsmen who work metal and cloth), and so the evidence for it is necessarily a life rather than an argument. A man may be able to explain wisdom faultlessly and not have any.

Show me. This is the whole letter’s method applied to a new subject. Faith is shown by works (2:18); wisdom is shown by works; and in both cases the demand is the same: show me. Not by clever words or impressive knowledge, but by a beautiful life.

In the meekness of wisdom. The phrase is the sting. Meekness (prautēs), as in 1:21, is not timidity but strength under control: the word used of a broken horse, all the power still there and now answering the rein. Moses was very meek, more than all people on the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3); Jesus was gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). So the mark of the genuinely wise man is that he is not pushing. He does not need to win the room, correct everyone present, or be recognised as the wisest person in it. And that is precisely diagnostic in a congregation where too many wanted to teach: the eagerness to be seen as wise is itself evidence against the claim.

What it does not mean. It does not mean wisdom is anti-intellectual. Understanding matters. But wisdom is measured by how we live, not by how much we know.

How can I tell whether a church leader or teacher is truly wise? Look at the life, not only the gifts. Is he humble and teachable? Does he listen before he speaks? How does he treat people who cannot help him, the elderly, children, the awkward, the critic? Is his home in order? How does he handle being contradicted? Paul’s lists of qualifications for elders are mostly about character, not ability (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). A brilliant speaker who is harsh, proud and quarrelsome is not wise, however impressive he sounds.

Isn’t meekness just weakness? Not in Scripture. Moses confronted Pharaoh and was called the meekest man on earth. Jesus overturned the money-changers’ tables and called himself gentle and lowly. Meekness is power yielded to God: strong enough to fight, humble enough not to fight for itself. The meek person can stand firm on the truth and still be gentle in manner, can be wronged without retaliating, and can lose an argument without losing his peace. That takes more strength, not less.

In a sentence. Who is wise and understanding among you? Let them show it by their good life, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom.

On a Tuesday. Think of the wisest person you know. Is it their knowledge or their humble, good life that makes them wise? Aim for the same. In your next disagreement, at home, at work or in church, try being the one who asks questions and listens, and does not need to have the last word.

For worship. The wisest man who ever lived was meek. One greater than Solomon came (Matthew 12:42), and he showed his wisdom not by dazzling the learned but by washing feet. He confounded the scholars at twelve and spent the next eighteen years in a carpenter’s shop. He could silence his enemies with a sentence, and he did not open his mouth before his accusers. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and he is gentle with every fool who comes to him to learn.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.

But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts. Two words, and they name what was actually happening. Jealousy is zēlos, zeal, which can be a virtue and here is qualified as bitter (pikros), like the salt water of verse 11. It is the passion for a cause that has curdled into passion against a person: envy, rivalry. And selfish ambition is eritheia, originally the word from the world of hired political canvassing: working a crowd for your own advancement. Wanting to get ahead, be recognised, win.

In your hearts. Note where they are located: in your hearts. This is the spring of verse 11. The quarrelling tongues have a source, and James has found it.

Do not boast and be false to the truth. That is, do not claim to be wise while this is going on inside you. Boast (katakauchasthe) means brag, exult over; be false to (pseudesthe) means lie against. The claim is not merely mistaken; it is a lie told about reality. Claiming to be wise while full of envy is a lie against the truth.

This is not the wisdom that comes down from above. True wisdom comes from God (1:5, 17). This is a counterfeit.

But is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. Then the verdict, in three descending words. Earthly (epigeios): it belongs to this world, with its values, and reaches no higher. Unspiritual (psychikē) is literally soulish, natural, the merely human faculties of unregenerate nature operating without the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:14; Jude 19). And demonic (daimoniōdēs, devilish, like demons), which is where the descent ends: its ultimate source is the devil, whose original sin was pride and ambition. And it connects to verse 6: the tongue set on fire by hell, and the wisdom behind it coming from the same place.

For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice. The word for disorder (akatastasia) means instability, upheaval, confusion, the same family as the restless tongue of verse 8 and the unstable man of 1:8. Vile (phaulos) is worthless, evil. And the sequence is worth noting: the private ambition produces public chaos, and the chaos then makes room for everything else. Envy and ambition produce chaos in churches, families and workplaces, and open the door to every evil.

What it does not mean. It does not condemn all ambition. Wanting to serve God well and use our gifts fully is good: earnestly desire the higher gifts (1 Corinthians 12:31), and if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task (1 Timothy 3:1). It condemns selfish ambition, which seeks one’s own glory at others’ expense.

How do I fight envy when a friend succeeds where I have not? Name it honestly before God; envy hides behind criticism and loves to call itself discernment. Remember that God gives his gifts as he wills, and that your worth is not set by comparison but by his love for you in Christ. Then do the opposite of what envy wants: thank God for your friend’s blessing, pray for them, and tell them you are glad. Rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15). Feelings often follow obedience. And look at what God has given you, because envy blinds us to our own gifts.

Our church is in conflict, and I think ambition is behind it. What should I do? Start with your own heart: is there any selfish ambition or bitterness in you? Then refuse to feed the fire: do not gossip, take sides on social media, or spread rumours. If you have a concern, take it privately and humbly to the person or to the elders (Matthew 18:15). Pray for the leaders and for peace. Be a peacemaker, not a party member. If there is real sin or abuse, it must be dealt with properly and openly, not covered up. Truth and peace together are the goal.

In a sentence. But if you harbour bitter envy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast about it or deny the truth. Such wisdom does not come down from heaven, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where you have envy and selfish ambition, there you find disorder and every evil practice.

On a Tuesday. Is there envy or selfish ambition in your heart toward a colleague, a sibling, another believer? A good test is to ask whose success makes you quietly unhappy, and whose failure would secretly please you. Confess it, and pray for their good, specifically and by name, every day this week.

For worship. The wisdom of this world crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). Envy handed him over: Pilate knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up (Matthew 27:18). Selfish ambition sat among his disciples at the Last Supper, arguing about which of them was the greatest. And he answered both by taking a towel and dying on a cross. He did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7). The one with every right to ambition laid it down, and so broke the power of the demonic wisdom that killed him.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

But the wisdom from above is first pure. Now the alternative, and it is the answer to the whole chapter. Not a technique for controlling the tongue, which James has said cannot be done, but a wisdom that comes from somewhere else. The wisdom from above comes from the same direction as every good gift in 1:17, and it is the same thing offered to anyone who asks in 1:5. It is not achieved. It is given. First (prōton) means first in priority, not merely first in the list: above all, the foundation of the others. Pure (hagnē) means holy, morally clean, without mixed motives. True wisdom begins with a pure heart before God.

Then peaceable. The order is deliberate. Purity is not negotiable, and it comes before peaceableness, which forbids the false peace that keeps quiet about sin to avoid trouble. But having secured the order, James lets peace govern everything after it. Peaceable (eirēnikē) is peace-loving, seeking harmony, the opposite of the jealousy and disorder of verses 14–16. Never peace at the expense of truth or holiness, and never truth without the longing for peace.

Gentle. The word is epieikēs, almost untranslatable: gracious, considerate, forbearing, the man who does not insist on the last inch of his rights. It is a qualification for elders (1 Timothy 3:3).

Open to reason. The word (eupeithēs) means easily persuaded, willing to yield, teachable. An extraordinary thing to require of wisdom, and exactly what the quarrelling teachers lacked. Not stubborn, but willing to listen and be corrected.

Full of mercy and good fruits. Mercy (eleos) is compassion in action, as in 2:13, and good fruits are practical good deeds. And there is the works test again.

Impartial. The word (adiakritos) means without wavering, undivided, unprejudiced. It reaches back both to chapter 2 and the gold ring, not showing favouritism (2:1–9), and to chapter 1, not double-minded (1:6–8).

And sincere. Sincere is anypokritos: without a mask, without hypocrisy, genuine, not play-acting. It is the opposite of the double-mindedness that has run through the whole letter.

What the list leaves out. Read the list and notice what is absent. Not one of these qualities is intellectual. Heavenly wisdom is described almost entirely in terms of how a person treats other people, which is what you would expect from a writer who has just said that wisdom is shown by conduct. And this list of qualities describes Jesus himself, who became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30). Read it with his name in place of wisdom, and it is a portrait.

And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace. The metaphor closes the chapter that opened with fire. Harvest (karpos) is fruit; sown (speiretai) is the farmer’s word. Fire destroys in an afternoon; sowing produces slowly and only in the right conditions. And the peacemakers are not merely those who avoid conflict but those who make peace (poiousin eirēnēn), which is work, and which is what the whole congregation had stopped doing. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God (Matthew 5:9; Hebrews 12:11). In contrast with envy, which produces disorder, peace produces righteousness.

What it does not mean. Peaceable does not mean avoiding all conflict. Purity comes first; sometimes faithfulness requires confronting error. But the manner is gentle, reasonable and merciful.

Does open to reason mean I should change my convictions whenever someone disagrees? No. Wisdom is first pure; it does not bend on what God has clearly said. But on everything else, and on how we hold what God has said, it is willing to listen, to learn, and to admit error. The wise person can say: I had not thought of that; you may be right; I was wrong. The foolish person cannot. The test is whether you hold your opinions as firmly as God’s word, which is a sign that you have confused the two.

How do I actually make peace? Begin by being at peace with God through Christ, because peacemakers are those who have been reconciled (Romans 5:1). Then go first: do not wait for the other person to come to you (Matthew 5:23–24). Listen to understand, not to win. Own your part honestly, without adding but. Speak the truth gently. Look for what you can agree on. If two other believers are in conflict, do not carry stories between them; help them talk to each other, or bring in a wise elder. And keep sowing: peace often grows slowly, like a harvest.

In a sentence. But the wisdom that comes from heaven is first of all pure; then it is peace-loving, considerate, willing to listen, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere. Peacemakers who sow in peace reap a harvest of righteousness.

On a Tuesday. Read the list slowly and score yourself honestly on each quality, especially open to reason and gentle. Then pick the weakest one and ask God for it, as he promised (1:5). And think of one broken or strained relationship where you could sow peace this week: a message, an apology, an invitation. Sow it, and leave the harvest to God.

For worship. Read the list slowly and see Jesus in each quality. Pure: he knew no sin. Peaceable: he is our peace, who made the two one and broke down the dividing wall (Ephesians 2:14). Gentle: a bruised reed he did not break. Open to reason: he answered honest questions with patience, from Nicodemus by night to doubting Thomas. Full of mercy and good fruits: he went about doing good. Impartial: he ate with Pharisees and prostitutes alike. Sincere: no deceit was found in his mouth. And he is the great Peacemaker, making peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), sowing himself in the ground like a seed so that a harvest of righteousness could rise from his grave. The wisdom from above came down in a manger, and it is still given to everyone who asks.
