4.title: Submit to God: Pride, the World, and the Brevity of Life
4.overview:
Chapter 4 goes to the root of the church’s failures. Quarrels come from desires at war within each person. Those desires come from friendship with the world, which is spiritual adultery against God. The remedy is humble submission: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, grieve over sin, humble yourselves. At the centre stands Proverbs 3:34: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” And “he gives more grace.”

The chapter ends with two warnings against taking God’s place: judging a brother, which sets us over the law, and planning as if tomorrow were ours, which forgets that we are a mist. The humble say, “If the Lord wills.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Quarrels, Adultery, and More Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your fights come from desires at war inside you. You want and do not have, so you quarrel; you do not ask, or you ask to feed your desires. Friendship with the world is hostility to God. But God yearns jealously over us, and gives more grace: he opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. So submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse your hands and hearts, grieve over sin, and humble yourselves, and he will lift you up.
verseByVerse.theology:
But He Gives More Grace

Quarrels come from desires at war within us, and friendship with the world is spiritual adultery. Yet God gives more grace — to the humble.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers prayed, but to fund the very desires that divided them.

Now: Submit to God, resist the devil, draw near — and he will draw near to you.

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.

Meaning first. James 4 diagnoses the root of conflict and calls for humble repentance. Quarrels in the church come from selfish desires at war within; people crave and do not get, so they fight; they do not ask God, or ask with wrong motives, to indulge their pleasures (vv. 1–3). This is spiritual adultery: friendship with the world is hostility to God (v. 4). God jealously longs for the spirit he made to dwell in us, but he gives more grace, opposing the proud and giving grace to the humble (vv. 5–6). So: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse your hands and purify your hearts, grieve over sin, and humble yourselves, and he will lift you up (vv. 7–10). Do not slander or judge one another, because that is to set yourself above the law and to usurp the place of the one Lawgiver and Judge (vv. 11–12). And do not boast about your plans as if you controlled the future; your life is a mist; say instead, If the Lord wills (vv. 13–16). Whoever knows the good he ought to do and does not do it sins (v. 17). At the centre of the chapter, between the quarrels and the boasting, stand four words that turn everything: but he gives more grace.

What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? The question is diagnostic, and James asks it the way a doctor asks where the pain is. Quarrels (polemoi, wars, battles) and fights (machai, conflicts, disputes) are military words for church conflicts. Chapter 3 traced the quarrelling tongues to jealousy and selfish ambition in the heart (3:14–16); now he goes deeper still.

Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? The word is hēdonai, pleasures, desires for pleasure, from which we get hedonism. At war (strateuomenōn) means waging a military campaign. And note the location: within you, literally in your members. The war is not between the factions in the congregation. It is within each person, and the fighting outside is that inner war showing. Desires fight against God and against each other within us (Romans 7:23; 1 Peter 2:11).

The issue is downstream. That is the observation the chapter turns on, and it is worth pausing over, because it is not how we usually analyse a church quarrel. We look for the issue and the opposing sides. James says the issue is downstream. A man at war inside himself will find something to fight about outside, and if you settle the presenting question he will find another one. The music, the building, the rota, the budget: these are rarely the real war. They are only where it broke out.

You desire and do not have, so you murder. Then verse 2, and it is brutally compressed. Desire (epithymeite) is crave, lust. Murder (phoneuete) is startling and has troubled readers. Some have proposed an emendation to envy, but the manuscripts do not support it. More likely James is doing what his brother did in the Sermon on the Mount: tracing the sin back to its root, where hatred is already murder (Matthew 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15). He is not accusing them of homicide. He is naming what the desire is on its way to: hatred, character assassination, destroying others with words. Or he may be describing exactly where unchecked desire leads, as it led Cain.

You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. Covet (zēloute) is envy, be jealous. Note the pattern repeated twice: desire, then frustration, then violence. The violence is not the primary problem; it is what unmet desire does when it is thwarted. And the frustration is essential to the mechanism: these people are not getting what they want, which is precisely why the room is on fire.

You do not have, because you do not ask. Then the diagnosis lands. After all that heat, the simplest possible sentence. They have organised their whole inner life around getting, and it has not occurred to them to ask (aiteisthai, request, pray) the God who gives generously to all without reproach (1:5). Prayerlessness is the root of much conflict. We try to grab what God would give if we asked.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all desire is wrong. God made us with desires, and he delights to satisfy good ones: delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart (Psalm 37:4). The problem is desire for pleasure that rules us and sets us against others.

But surely some church conflicts are about real issues, like truth? Yes. Some disagreements are about the gospel itself, and then faithfulness requires standing firm (Jude 3; Galatians 2:11). But even then James’s question is worth asking: what is going on in me? It is possible to be right about the issue and wrong in the heart, fighting for truth with pride, anger and a desire to win. And most church quarrels, honestly examined, are not about the gospel at all but about preferences, status and being heard. Ask God to show you which yours is.

Does you do not ask mean that if I pray I will get whatever I want? No. The next verse rules that out. James is saying that many of our battles would end if we took our desires to God instead of fighting for them. When we bring a desire to God honestly, one of three things happens: he gives it, he gives something better, or he changes the desire. All three end the war inside. What does not end the war is grabbing.

In a sentence. What causes fights and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from your desires that battle within you? You want something but don’t get it, so you are ready to kill. You covet but cannot have what you want, so you quarrel and fight. You do not have because you do not ask God.

On a Tuesday. Think of a recent conflict, at home, at work or in church. Underneath the argument, what did you want: respect, control, comfort, to be right, to be noticed? Name the desire. Then bring that desire to God in prayer instead of fighting for it. You may find the quarrel looks very different afterwards.

For worship. There is one man in whom there was no war within. Jesus desired one thing above all, his Father’s will, and every other desire was ordered under it. When his followers fought over seats in the kingdom, he did not fight back; he knelt and washed their feet. When he was struck, he did not strike. And on the cross he made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), between God and us and between us and each other. The war inside us will not end by our own resolve. It ends at the feet of the Prince of Peace.

verseByVerse.quote: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.

You ask and do not receive. James anticipates the protest immediately. Somebody will say: but I have asked. And he answers it without softening. Some do pray, but their prayers go unanswered.

Because you ask wrongly. So the problem is not that God is deaf, and not that prayer does not work. The petition itself is defective, and the defect is named exactly. Wrongly (kakōs) means badly, with evil intent. The problem is the motive, not the asking.

To spend it on your passions. The verb (dapanēsēte) means to squander, use up, and it is the word used of the prodigal son spending everything in the far country (Luke 15:14). Passions is the same word for pleasures as verse 1. They want God to fund their selfish pleasures.

Prayer converted. Here is the thing to see. These people are praying. They have not abandoned the practice; they have converted it. Prayer has become the means by which they hope to fund the very appetites that are tearing the congregation apart, and God, mercifully, declines. God is not a vending machine for our cravings.

A kind refusal. That last word matters. An unanswered prayer of this kind is not God’s indifference; it is his kindness. A father who financed every appetite his children presented to him would not be generous, he would be negligent. James has already said God gives without reproach (1:5); he now says God does not give this.

What would I do with it? And the verse quietly explains something that troubles many Christians. When a prayer has gone unanswered for years, the honest question is not only why is God silent? but what would I do with it if I got it? James does not apply that question to genuine need; he has just told them to ask. But he insists it be asked of desire.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we may never pray for personal needs or good things for ourselves. Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread (Matthew 6:11). It means our motive should be God’s glory and the good of others, not merely our own pleasure, and we ask according to his will (1 John 5:14).

How do I know whether my motives are right? Ask what you want the thing for. If God gave it, would it draw you closer to him or make you need him less? Would it serve others, or only you? Could you pray, your will be done, and mean it? Motives are rarely pure; most of us want good things for mixed reasons. Do not wait for perfect motives before you pray. Bring the mixture to God and ask him to purify it as you pray. Praying honestly is one of the ways he changes our motives.

I have prayed for years for something good, a child’s salvation, healing, a marriage. Are my motives wrong? Not necessarily. James is speaking about prayers to fund selfish pleasure, not about prayers for the good of others or for God’s glory. Many faithful prayers are answered slowly, or in ways we do not see, or not in this life. Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac. Keep praying; Jesus told a parable so that we would always pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Unanswered prayer is a reason to examine your heart, yes, but also a call to trust the wisdom of a Father who knows what you do not.

In a sentence. When you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, wanting to spend what you get on your own pleasures.

On a Tuesday. Before you pray today, ask: why do I want this? Pray first for God’s will and glory, as the Lord’s Prayer does, then bring your requests to him. Take your most frequent personal request and write next to it what you would do with the answer. If the honest answer embarrasses you, tell God that too.

For worship. Our Father does not answer every prayer the way we ask, because he loves us too much to give us what would ruin us. And when his own Son prayed, let this cup pass from me, the answer was no, so that every prayer of his people might be heard for his sake. The Son was refused so that we could be received. He ever lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25), and he takes our muddled prayers, cleanses them, and presents them to the Father as his own.

verseByVerse.quote: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.

You adulterous people! The Greek is feminine, literally adulteresses (moichalides), and that is not an insult about women. It is the language of the prophets, where Israel is the bride and idolatry is infidelity. The covenant was like a marriage, and Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel all speak this way (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3:20; Ezekiel 16). Jesus called his generation adulterous (Matthew 12:39; 16:4). And the church is the bride of Christ (Ephesians 5:25–32; 2 Corinthians 11:2). James is invoking the whole tradition in one word. To love the world is to cheat on God.

A marriage being broken. Which reframes everything in the chapter. The quarrelling, the coveting, the misdirected prayers: these are not merely bad behaviour. They are a marriage being broken.

Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? The word for friendship (philia) carries the sense of affection and shared outlook: agreement, alliance, having the same tastes. And the world (kosmos) here is not the planet or the people in it, but human society organised apart from and against God, with its values of pride, greed, pleasure and self (1:27; 1 John 2:15–17). Enmity (echthra) is hostility. The claim is deliberately stark, and there is no middle category offered. James does not say friendship with the world leads to enmity, or risks it. He says it is enmity. There is no neutral ground. You cannot be friends with both.

Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God. Then he repeats the point in the second half of the verse so that nobody can miss it. Note the verb: wishes (boulēthē, decides, chooses). It is not about being caught, or living in the world, or enjoying good things; the God of this letter gives every good gift (1:17). It is about where the affections are pointed. The wishing is the adultery. And makes himself (kathistatai, establishes himself, sets himself up): the reflexive is important. God has not declared war on him. He has taken up a position, and the enmity is his own construction, which is exactly why the next verses can offer him grace rather than sentence. Abraham was the friend of God (2:23); the worldly make themselves God’s enemies.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should hate the people of the world. God loves the world of people (John 3:16), and we are sent into it (John 17:15–18). It means we must not love the world’s values and ways, or seek its approval above God’s.

What counts as worldliness? Is it films, clothes, music? Worldliness is less about particular things than about the heart’s loyalty. John defines it as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and pride of life (1 John 2:16): wanting what pleases the body, what looks good, and what makes us important. A Christian can avoid every questionable film and still be thoroughly worldly in his love of money or status. Ask: where do I get my sense of worth? Whose approval do I most want? What would I be most devastated to lose? If the answer is anything other than God, that is where the world has your heart.

Can a Christian become an enemy of God? James writes to church members as a warning, and the warning is real. A professing Christian who settles into love of the world shows that his heart is drifting from God, and if he persists without repentance, he shows that his profession was never genuine (1 John 2:19). But a true believer who has strayed will be drawn back; God disciplines his children and does not let them go (Hebrews 12:6; John 10:28). The very next verses are the door back: he gives more grace. If you are troubled by your worldliness, that trouble is his jealous love calling you home.

In a sentence. You unfaithful people! Don’t you know that friendship with the world means hostility toward God? So anyone who chooses to be a friend of the world becomes an enemy of God.

On a Tuesday. Where are you seeking the world’s friendship: its approval, pleasures or values? Look at what you worry about, what you daydream about, and what you spend your spare money and time on. Those are the clearest maps of the heart’s affections. Choose one place where you will choose friendship with God instead this week, and tell him so.

For worship. The God we betrayed is a husband who does not give up. When Israel played the harlot, he told Hosea to go and buy back his unfaithful wife, and said: I will betroth you to me forever (Hosea 2:19). And when the time came, the Bridegroom paid the price himself. Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might present the church to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). We are the adulteress whom he redeemed and is making pure. His faithfulness is greater than our unfaithfulness.
verseByVerse.note: The prophets called Israel’s unfaithfulness to God “adultery.”

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”? But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”? But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says. To no purpose (kenōs) means emptily, in vain. Scripture is never empty.

He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us. Verse 5 is the hardest sentence in the letter to translate, and honesty is better than confidence here. The ESV margin offers other readings, and no Old Testament text says this in these words. James appears to be summarising the general teaching of Scripture rather than quoting a verse (Exodus 20:5; 34:14; Deuteronomy 32:16; Zechariah 8:2). There are three main readings: first, God yearns jealously for the human spirit he placed in us at creation (Genesis 2:7); second, God yearns jealously for the Holy Spirit he made to dwell in believers; third, the human spirit God made to dwell in us longs enviously, an indictment of sinful desire. The first fits the context best: God, like a faithful husband, jealously wants our whole heart. He will not share us with the world (v. 4).

Whose spirit is meant? The ESV reads God as the one who yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us, the human spirit he gave us, which he wants wholly for himself; others read it as the Holy Spirit, who yearns over us. The first fits the context of divided loyalty best: God will not share us with the world.

The jealousy of love. Divine jealousy is not the petty thing the word suggests in human relationships. It is the proper response of a husband to a wife who is leaving, and a God who felt nothing about our adultery would not be more loving but less. Indifference is not the opposite of jealousy; it is the opposite of love. Godly jealousy is not petty envy but the passionate love that rightly wants exclusive devotion.

But he gives more grace. Then verse 6, and after the severity of verses 1–5 it arrives like a door opening. Four words, and they are the turning point of the chapter and arguably of the letter. More grace (meizona charin, greater grace): greater than the adultery, greater than the quarrelling, greater than the appetite that has been running the whole congregation. Whatever the sin has cost, the supply is larger. God’s demand is total, but his grace is greater. He gives grace to meet his demand, enough grace for every failure and every temptation: my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).

Therefore it says, God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, and Peter uses it too (1 Peter 5:5): evidently a text the early church leaned on. And it names the one condition. Grace is not scarce; it is more. But it is given downhill, and it will not flow to a man who has arranged himself above it. The word for opposes (antitassetai) is military: to set oneself in battle array against. God does not merely withhold from the proud. He lines up against them. And the humble (tapeinois, lowly) are where grace collects, like water flowing to the lowest place.

What it does not mean. God’s jealousy does not mean he is insecure or selfish. He alone is worthy of total devotion, and our good lies in giving it to him.

How can God be jealous, if jealousy is a sin? Jealousy is sinful when it wants what is not ours, or resents another’s good. But there is a right jealousy, for what truly belongs to us. A husband who did not care if his wife loved another man would not be admirable. God’s jealousy is his holy, protective love for those who are his by creation and redemption. He is jealous for us, not of us; he wants our whole heart because he is our true good, and because anything else we give it to will destroy us. His name is Jealous (Exodus 34:14), and it is a name of love.

How do I become humble? Not by trying to feel small, and not by putting yourself down, which is often pride in disguise. Humility grows by looking at God: his holiness, his greatness, his grace. Isaiah saw the Lord and said, woe is me (Isaiah 6:5). It grows by looking at the cross, where we see what our sin cost and what we were given freely. And it shows itself in practice: admitting you are wrong, asking for help, serving where no one sees, rejoicing in others’ success, receiving correction without defending yourself. Humility is not thinking less of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less, because you are thinking of him.

In a sentence. Or do you think Scripture means nothing when it says that God jealously longs for the spirit he has caused to live in us? But he gives us more grace. That is why Scripture says: God opposes the proud but shows favour to the humble.

On a Tuesday. Think of the sin you are most ashamed of, the one you feel you have used up God’s patience on. Read these four words again: he gives more grace. Then do the humble thing: confess it plainly, without excuses, and receive the grace. And look for one place this week to take the lower seat: let someone else have the credit, the last word, or the better place.

For worship. He gives more grace. When we have exhausted our resolutions, he gives more. When we have betrayed him again, he gives more. Grace upon grace has come to us from his fullness (John 1:16). And the source of this endless supply is a cross, where the one who opposes the proud became the most humbled man in history, so that the proud who repent could receive grace. The jealous love of God and the boundless grace of God met at Calvary, and they meet in every sinner who comes home. His grace is not a reservoir that runs low. It is an ocean.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 5 is hard to translate; the ESV margin offers other readings. No single Old Testament verse matches it; it seems to sum up Scripture’s teaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.

Submit yourselves therefore to God. Now ten imperatives in four verses, the densest cluster of commands in the letter, all aorist imperatives: decisive actions. And they all unpack the single word at the end of verse 6: the humble. Submit (hypotagēte) is a military word again: to arrange yourself under, like soldiers under a commander. It is the opposite of the proud man’s posture, and it is first because everything else follows from it. The first step of humility is surrender to God’s authority.

Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Resist (antistēte) is stand against, oppose. Note the order: submit first, then resist. A man who has not submitted to God has no standing from which to resist anything. And the promise is remarkable: not that the devil will be defeated after a long struggle, but that he will flee (pheuxetai, run away). He does not have the resources for a siege. The devil is real and active (1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11–13), but he is a defeated enemy (Hebrews 2:14). When believers stand firm in God’s strength and word, as Jesus did in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11), he flees.

How does a believer resist the devil? By standing firm in faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), putting on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:11–17), and answering his lies with God’s word, as Jesus did in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11). It does not mean shouting at Satan or using formulas; even the archangel said only The Lord rebuke you (Jude 9). The first command is Submit yourselves therefore to God.

Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Draw near (engisate, come close) is priestly language: it is what a priest did when he approached the altar (Hebrews 7:19). James applies to ordinary believers the vocabulary of the sanctuary. God responds to those who come to him (Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7). And the promise should be read carefully. It is not that God waits at a distance until we have travelled far enough. The whole chapter has just said he yearns jealously over us and gives more grace. The drawing near is a response to a God who is already leaning toward us, and the prodigal’s father, who ran (Luke 15:20), is the right picture.

Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Then two commands with two vocatives, and they are addressed to church members. Cleanse (katharisate) your hands: outward actions. Priests washed their hands before approaching God (Exodus 30:19–21). Sinners (hamartōloi) is a strong word, used deliberately to shock.

And purify your hearts, you double-minded. Purify (hagnisate) is make holy, sanctify; hearts are inner motives and loyalty. Hands and hearts: outward conduct and inward loyalty, and both are required. Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? He who has clean hands and a pure heart (Psalm 24:3–4). And there is dipsychos again, the two-souled word of 1:8. It is his diagnosis for the whole letter, and here at last it is given a remedy: not effort, but purification, and it comes after he gives more grace.

Where Christians differ: does our drawing near come first, then God’s? Some read draw near to God, and he will draw near to you as teaching that human initiative comes first, and God responds. Verdict: this command is addressed to believers already born again by God’s will (1:18), and James has just said God gives more grace (v. 6). God’s grace always comes first: no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). Within a relationship already begun by grace, God calls us to draw near and promises to meet us. Our drawing near is itself the fruit of his drawing us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we cleanse ourselves by our own power. Christ’s blood cleanses (1 John 1:7, 9). But we must turn from sin in repentance, by grace.

I have tried to draw near, but God still feels far away. What now? Feelings are not the measure of God’s nearness. He has promised to draw near, and he keeps his promises whether you feel it or not. Many saints have walked through long seasons of spiritual dryness; the psalmists cried, how long? (Psalm 13:1). Keep doing what draws near: read his word, pray honestly, gather with his people, take the Lord’s Supper, confess known sin. Check for anything you are holding back from him. And rest on the fact that in Christ you have already been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). Your nearness to God rests on Christ’s work, not on your sense of it.

In a sentence. So submit yourselves to God. Stand against the devil, and he will run from you. Come near to God, and he will come near to you. Wash your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you who are divided in loyalty.

On a Tuesday. Where is the devil pressing you right now: a lie about God, an accusation, a temptation, a fear? Resist him today by submitting to God and holding firm to his word. Find one verse that answers the lie directly and say it aloud when the pressure comes. Then take ten minutes, unhurried, simply to draw near: no list, just coming to God because he has promised to come to you.

For worship. We can draw near only because someone drew near for us. Our great High Priest passed through the heavens, and through his blood we have confidence to enter the holy places, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). He resisted the devil in the wilderness and crushed him at the cross. He washed our hands and purified our hearts with his own blood. And when we take one trembling step toward the Father, we find he has been running toward us all along, with a robe and a ring and a feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.

Be wretched and mourn and weep. It is the most severe thing in the letter, and it sits oddly in a New Testament that commands rejoicing. James himself opened by telling them to count trials all joy. So what is going on? Be wretched (talaipōrēsate) means feel your misery, lament; mourn (penthēsate) is to grieve as for the dead; weep (klausate) is to cry aloud. This is deep, heartfelt sorrow over sin (Joel 2:12–13). Jesus said, blessed are those who mourn (Matthew 5:4).

Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. The answer is that this is a call to repentance, and repentance has an appropriate emotional weather. James is addressing people who have been quarrelling, coveting and committing spiritual adultery, and doing it cheerfully. The laughter (gelōs) he wants turned to mourning is the careless laughter of people who are not taking their condition seriously, who enjoy worldly pleasures without thought of God (Luke 6:25; Ecclesiastes 7:2–6). Gloom (katēpheia) is dejection, literally downcast eyes, shame: the posture of the tax collector who would not lift up his eyes to heaven (Luke 18:13).

Godly grief. This is not a call to permanent gloom, and it is not a recommendation of misery as a spiritual state. It is the recognition that there is a grief which is the right response to your own sin, and that a person who can survey what James has just described without any of it has not understood. Paul calls it godly grief, and says it produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Humble yourselves before the Lord. The tenth imperative, and it closes the sequence by returning to the proverb of verse 6. Humble yourselves (tapeinōthēte) is make yourselves low; before the Lord (enōpion kyriou) is in his sight. It is the summary of all the commands.

And he will exalt you. Note who does the humbling and who does the exalting. The humbling is commanded; it is ours, and it is active. The exalting (hypsōsei, lift up, raise high) is promised, and it is his. That order is the whole of biblical spirituality, and it is the exact reverse of the arrangement everyone defaults to, in which we exalt ourselves and hope God will not humble us (Matthew 23:12; Luke 14:11; 1 Peter 5:6). And it is a promise, not merely a condition. The man who goes low is not left there. James does not say humility is its own reward; he says God lifts the person who takes the low place, which is the pattern of Christ himself (Philippians 2:8–9). The way up is down. Sorrow for sin leads to joy in forgiveness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never laugh or be joyful. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22). It means joy must not be the careless joy of the worldly who ignore sin. True joy comes after true repentance.

How much grief is enough? I feel I can never grieve enough over my sin. Godly grief is not measured by quantity of tears, and you do not earn forgiveness by feeling bad enough. Christ’s blood, not your sorrow, pays for sin. Godly grief turns you to God; once it has done that, its work is done, and the next step is to receive forgiveness and be lifted up. If you find yourself endlessly mourning sins already confessed, that is not humility; it is failing to believe the promise (1 John 1:9). Mourn honestly, then let God exalt you. He wants his children forgiven and glad, not perpetually downcast.

Is there a place for this kind of mourning in church life today? Yes, and many churches have lost it. Times of honest confession in worship, days of prayer and humbling when a church has sinned or is in crisis, grief over a nation’s or a family’s sin: these are biblical (Nehemiah 9; Daniel 9). A church that only ever celebrates may be skipping the repentance that makes the celebration real. The joy of the gospel is deepest in people who have felt the weight of their sin.

In a sentence. Grieve, mourn and weep. Change your laughter to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up.

On a Tuesday. Take time today to grieve honestly over your sin before God. Not sin in general, but the specific things in this chapter you recognise: the quarrel, the coveting, the worldly loyalty, the careless laughter. Then receive his forgiveness, as freely as he offers it, and let him lift you up. End by thanking him aloud.

For worship. He was the Man of Sorrows, acquainted with grief, who wept over Jerusalem and at the tomb of his friend. He took the lowest place of all, obedient to death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9). He mourned so that we could be comforted; he was humbled so that we could be lifted up. And one day he will wipe away every tear from our eyes, and the laughter that was turned to mourning will be turned back into everlasting joy (Isaiah 35:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not slander one another. Judging a brother sets you over the law instead of under it; there is one Lawgiver and Judge. And do not plan as though tomorrow were yours. You are a mist. Say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.” Boasting about the future is evil, and whoever knows the right thing to do and does not do it, sins.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sin as Knowledge Not Acted On

Speaking against a brother sets us over the law instead of under it. And whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The merchants' plan was complete except for God.

Now: Plan, but hold every plan under “if the Lord wills” — life itself included.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?

Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The word (katalaleite) means to talk down, to speak against: slander, criticise, run down. It covers the whole range from slander to the accurate but damaging remark, not just lying, but any speech that tears down another person behind their back. It is the tongue of chapter 3 turned on the congregation.

The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother. Judges (krinōn) is condemns, sits in judgment: setting yourself up as the judge of another’s worth or motives.

Speaks evil against the law and judges the law. Then an argument that is easy to miss and is remarkably shrewd. How does criticising a person become criticising the law? Because the law says love your neighbour as yourself, the royal law of 2:8, and Leviticus 19:16–18, the same paragraph, also forbids slander. If you set that aside in order to condemn somebody, you have not merely disobeyed it. You have passed judgment on it, ruling that in this case it does not apply. You treat the law as if it did not apply to you, as if you were above it.

But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. And there is the whole letter’s theme again, in a new setting. Chapter 1 divided the world into hearers and doers; here it is doers and judges. You cannot be both, because a judge stands over the law and a doer stands under it. The point of the law is to obey it, not to sit over it (1:22–25).

There is only one lawgiver and judge. Lawgiver (nomothetēs) is the one who gives the law. For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us (Isaiah 33:22). God alone gives the law and judges by it. To judge others is to usurp God’s place.

He who is able to save and to destroy. The credentials are decisive. The one qualified to judge is the one who can act on the verdict either way, and that describes exactly one person. Only God has power over eternal destiny (Matthew 10:28; Deuteronomy 32:39).

But who are you to judge your neighbor? The question (sy de tis ei, emphatic) is not rhetorical bluster; it is a genuine matter of jurisdiction, a rebuke to arrogance (Romans 14:4). And note the last word: neighbour, which pulls Leviticus 19:18 back into the sentence one final time. The person you are judging is the person you were commanded to love.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all moral discernment, church discipline, or loving correction. Jesus calls us to judge with right judgment (John 7:24), and the church must deal with sin (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5). It forbids slander, harsh condemnation, and usurping God’s role as final judge of hearts.

Does this forbid all judging? No. James forbids slander and condemning a brother as if we were his final judge. Scripture still calls us to judge teaching and conduct by God’s word (1 John 4:1), and the church to exercise discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). What is forbidden is taking God’s seat.

If what I say about someone is true, is it still slander? It can be. James’s word covers accurate but damaging talk behind someone’s back. Ask: why am I saying this, and to whom? If you are telling people who have no need to know, in order to lower someone in their eyes, it is sin even if every word is true. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). If the matter is serious, go to the person, or to those with responsibility to act. If it is not serious, let it go.

But what if I need to warn others about someone dangerous? That is not slander; it is love for the vulnerable. If someone is abusing, defrauding or endangering others, the truth must be spoken to those who need to know: the authorities, the elders, those at risk. Protecting the weak is commanded (Proverbs 31:8–9). Covering up harm in the name of not judging is itself a grave wrong. The difference lies in motive and audience: slander wants to damage a reputation; a warning wants to protect people. Speak the facts plainly, to the right people, and leave the final judgment of the heart to God.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against a fellow believer or judges them speaks against the law and judges it. When you judge the law, you are not keeping it, but sitting in judgment on it. There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the one who is able to save and destroy. But you, who are you to judge your neighbour?

On a Tuesday. This week, refuse to speak negatively about anyone behind their back. If you have a concern, go to them, or to God. When someone else begins to run a person down in your hearing, change the subject gently, or say something good and true about them. And notice the moment you are tempted to judge someone’s motives; ask yourself whether you would want your own motives judged on so little evidence.

For worship. There is one Lawgiver and Judge, and he is able to save and to destroy. And the Judge chose to save. He came not to condemn the world but that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). The one who alone has the right to judge took the judgment himself, and stood silent before human judges who condemned him falsely. Because he was judged in our place, those in him will never face condemnation, and he who sits on the judgment seat is the one who was slain for us. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, who is interceding for us (Romans 8:34).

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”

Come now, you who say. It is the prophet’s summons (age nyn), an abrupt call to attention, a phrase for calling someone to account, and James will use it again at 5:1. Now he addresses merchants and businesspeople.

Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit. Then he quotes the business plan, and it is entirely reasonable. Travelling merchants were common in the Roman world. Look at how complete it is. The timing, the destination, the duration, the activity and the outcome: five elements, all settled, detailed and confident. And there is nothing wrong with any of them. Trade is not condemned here, profit is not condemned, and planning is not condemned; Scripture commends the ant who prepares her bread in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8). What is missing is one word, and James supplies it in verse 15. The problem is the attitude: no thought of God.

Yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. That is not pessimism, it is arithmetic. The plan assumes access to information nobody has. Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring (Proverbs 27:1). Jesus’ parable of the rich fool makes the same point: fool, this night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:16–21).

What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. The word (atmis) is used of steam, vapour or morning haze: the vapour over a field that is gone once the sun is properly up, like breath on a cold morning or steam from a pot. Not a short life. A brief appearance. Here for a moment, then gone (Job 7:7; Psalm 39:5; 102:3; 144:4).

Instead you ought to say, If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that. And the correction is smaller than we expect. James does not tell them to cancel the trip or abandon the trade. He tells them to add a clause, and the clause (ean ho kyrios thelēsē) covers not only the doing but the living: if the Lord wills, we will live, and then we will do. Paul used similar words (Acts 18:21; 1 Corinthians 4:19; 16:7). God’s providence governs all things, including our tomorrows.

Not a formula. This is not a formula to be attached to sentences. It is an acknowledgement to be held in the mind, and a man can say the words with no such acknowledgement while another plans his whole year in that spirit without saying them once.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid planning or business. The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance (Proverbs 21:5). It forbids planning that leaves God out, as though we were in control. Nor does saying if the Lord wills automatically make plans godly; the attitude matters.

Is it wrong to save, buy insurance or plan for retirement? No. Scripture commends wise preparation; Joseph stored grain for the famine, and a good man leaves an inheritance (Proverbs 13:22). The question is not whether you plan but in what spirit. Do your savings make you feel independent of God, or are they held as his, available for his purposes? Are you storing up for yourself, like the rich fool, or are you rich toward God? Plan carefully, hold the plan loosely, give generously along the way, and trust him with what you cannot control.

How do I hold my plans loosely without becoming passive or anxious? Make your plans as wisely as you can, and then pray over them, offering each one to God. When plans fail, as many will, receive it as his will rather than as a disaster. The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (Proverbs 16:9). This is not fatalism; it is trust. It frees you from the anxiety of having to control tomorrow, and from the pride of thinking you can. You do your part today, and leave tomorrow to the one who holds it.

In a sentence. Now listen, you who say, Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, do business and make money. Why, you do not even know what will happen tomorrow. What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. Instead, you ought to say, If it is the Lord’s will, we will live and do this or that.

On a Tuesday. Look at your calendar and plans for this week. Pray over them, surrendering each to the Lord’s will. Then look further ahead, at the big plan, the house, the career move, the retirement, and ask honestly whether God is in it or only around it. And when something you planned falls through this week, practise saying, and meaning: the Lord did not will it, and he is good.

For worship. Our lives are a mist, but the Lord who holds them is not. From everlasting to everlasting you are God (Psalm 90:2). Our tomorrows are unknown to us and fully known to him, and every one of them is already in his hand. My times are in your hand (Psalm 31:15). And the Son of God himself, who had all knowledge, lived as a man saying, not my will but yours. Because he gave his brief life for us, our mist of a life is bound up in his endless one, and when the sun rises on the last day, those in him will not vanish but shine.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.

As it is, you boast in your arrogance. Boast (kauchasthe) is brag, glory. The word for arrogance (alazoneia) originally described the wandering quack: the travelling impostor who claimed powers he did not have. It is exactly right for a man announcing what next year holds. They boast about their plans as if the future were theirs to command: the pride of life (1 John 2:16).

All such boasting is evil. Not unwise, not naive. Evil (ponēra), wicked, because it is a claim to a knowledge and a control that belong to God alone, made by a mist. Boasting about the future denies God’s sovereignty. It is practical atheism: living as though God did not rule.

So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin. Then verse 17, which reads like a detached proverb and is not. The so ties it to what precedes. These men now know about the mist and the if the Lord wills. They have been told. From this point their planning cannot be excused as thoughtlessness, and James closes the exit. The right thing (kalon) is the good, what is fitting; fails to do it (mē poiounti) is simply does not do.

Sin as omission. And the definition of sin here is worth weighing, because it is not the usual one. Sin is normally defined as doing what is forbidden. James defines it as not doing what is known to be right: sin as omission, and specifically as knowledge that has not been acted on. Sin is not only doing what is wrong, sins of commission, but also failing to do what is right, sins of omission.

The whole letter in a sentence. Which is the whole letter compressed into a sentence. The man who hears and does not do is deceiving himself (1:22); the man who says and does not give is useless (2:16); the man who knows and does not act is sinning. James’s consistent charge is never that his readers are ignorant. It is that they are informed. And that is a sobering thought for anyone who reads much, hears much, and has a shelf of books. The verse creates a liability that grows with every sermon understood and every chapter agreed with. Knowledge increases responsibility (Luke 12:47). Knowing more is not a neutral achievement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignorance excuses all sin. Sins of ignorance are still sins (Leviticus 4; Luke 12:48). It means knowing what is right and not doing it is especially serious.

There is so much good I could do. Am I sinning all the time by not doing it? No. James is not saying you must do every good thing in the world, which no one can. He means the specific good that God puts in front of you and that you know you ought to do: the call you should make, the apology you owe, the need right in front of you, the duty of your own calling. God gives each of us particular responsibilities and limits; even Jesus did not heal everyone in Israel. Ask: what has God clearly put in my path? Do that, and trust him with the rest. This verse should lead to obedience, not to paralysis.

What about the good I failed to do in the past? Bring it to Christ. Sins of omission are forgiven like any other sin through his blood (1 John 1:9). Where you can still put something right, do it; where you cannot, leave it with him. Then let this verse shape tomorrow rather than haunt yesterday. The purpose of the warning is not to load you with guilt but to move you to act now, while it is still today.

In a sentence. As it is, you boast in your proud plans. All such boasting is evil. So then, if anyone knows the good they ought to do and does not do it, it is sin for them.

On a Tuesday. What good thing do you know you should do but have been putting off? The letter, the visit, the confession, the gift, the conversation about Christ. Do it today. If it is too big for today, take the first step today. And next time you finish reading Scripture or hear a sermon, before you close the book, name the good you now know, and decide when you will do it.

For worship. Only one man never failed to do the good he knew. Jesus knew all things, and he did all his Father’s will: I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). He left no good undone, no duty unfulfilled, no need overlooked that his Father had set before him. And he bore our sins of omission as well as our sins of commission, the good we left undone along with the evil we did. His perfect doing is counted as ours. He did not boast about tomorrow; he gave himself for our tomorrows, and rose to make them his.
