5.title: Patient Until He Comes: Wealth, Endurance, and Prayer
5.overview:
The last chapter moves from prophetic warning to pastoral tenderness. It opens with the letter’s most severe passage (vv. 1–6), a woe against rich oppressors who withheld wages and lived in luxury while the righteous suffered. Their judgment is certain.

Then James turns gently to the suffering church (vv. 7–20). Be patient like a farmer waiting for the rains, because the Lord is coming and the Judge is at the door. Do not grumble or swear. Pray in every condition: in suffering, in gladness, in sickness, confessing sins to one another. Elijah was a man like us, and his prayers were heard. And the letter ends by sending ordinary believers after the one who has wandered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James addresses the rich oppressors as the prophets did. Weep and howl: your wealth has rotted, your clothes are moth-eaten, your gold has rusted, and the rust will testify against you. The wages you withheld from your harvesters cry out, and the Lord of hosts has heard. You have fattened yourselves for a day of slaughter, and condemned the righteous who did not resist.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rust That Testifies

Hoarded wealth will testify against those who kept back the wages of their labourers. The cries of the harvesters have reached the Lord of hosts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A day-labourer's withheld wage meant a family without supper.

Now: Comfort bought by someone else's hunger is not a blessing but fattening for a day of slaughter.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days.

Meaning first. James 5 closes the letter with three themes. First, a prophetic denunciation of the oppressive rich (vv. 1–6): they should weep, because their hoarded wealth is rotting, their unpaid workers’ wages cry out to the Lord of hosts, and they have fattened themselves for the day of slaughter and condemned the innocent. Second, a call to patient endurance (vv. 7–12): believers suffering under such oppression must wait patiently for the Lord’s coming, like a farmer waiting for the rains; they must not grumble against one another, since the Judge stands at the door; they should look to the prophets and to Job, and see that the Lord is compassionate; and they must speak with simple honesty, without oaths. Third, prayer in every situation (vv. 13–18): pray in suffering, sing in joy; the sick should call the elders to pray and anoint them, and the prayer of faith will raise them up, with forgiveness for sins; confess sins to one another and pray for one another, for the prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah’s was. The letter ends with a call to rescue the wandering: whoever brings a sinner back from error saves a soul from death and covers many sins (vv. 19–20). Over the whole chapter stands the coming Lord: the Judge at the door, the compassionate and merciful God of Job, who hears the cries of harvesters and the prayers of ordinary people.

Come now, you rich. The phrase (age nyn) is the prophet’s summons, as in 4:13. You rich (hoi plousioi) are probably wealthy unbelievers who oppressed the poor believers (2:6–7). This is prophetic denunciation in the manner of Amos and Isaiah, who addressed foreign nations and the oppressors of Israel directly while God’s people listened (Isaiah 13; Amos 4:1). James is almost certainly not addressing members of the congregation here. He addresses the oppressors, and the believers overhear and are comforted that God sees.

Weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. The verb is violent: howl (ololyzontes) is to shriek, wail, the noise of open grief, a word used of the anguish of those under God’s judgment (Isaiah 13:6; 15:3). Miseries (talaipōriai) are distresses. And they are coming, not have come. The judgment is future and certain, and the weeping is commanded now on account of it.

Your riches have rotted. Then three assets, in ascending order of durability, and all three have failed. Riches is the general word, and rot (sesēpen, perfect tense: already rotted) is what happens to grain and produce. Riches in the ancient world often meant stored food, grain and oil, which could spoil, like the rich fool’s barns (Luke 12:18–20).

And your garments are moth-eaten. Fine clothing was stored wealth in that world, a major form of savings, and a moth needs no thief. Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy (Matthew 6:19–20).

Your gold and silver have corroded. That third one is chemically impossible, and James knows it. Gold does not corrode (katiōtai, rusted, tarnished); that is precisely why it has been money for five thousand years. He is making a point by overstatement: the one asset that cannot decay has decayed. Nothing they own has survived. Even the most durable wealth is ultimately worthless.

And their corrosion will be evidence against you. The word (martyrion) is a legal term: testimony for the prosecution. The rust is a witness, and what it testifies to is that the wealth sat unused. Metal that is spent does not corrode. This corroded because it was hoarded while the men who earned it went hungry.

And will eat your flesh like fire. The image turns on them bodily: the corrosion that consumed the treasure will consume (phagetai) the owner. The wealth they trusted will become the instrument of their judgment.

You have laid up treasure in the last days. That is the final irony. Laid up treasure (ethēsaurisate) is hoarded. And the last days (en eschatais hēmerais) are the final age before judgment, which began with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). They were accumulating in the very period when it could least be of use, like a man buying property in a town he knows is to be flooded. The folly is not the wealth. It is the timing: hoarding wealth when the end is near, instead of laying up treasure in heaven.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all wealth is evil or all rich people are condemned. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly. James condemns hoarding, oppression, fraud and self-indulgence.

If I am comfortably off, is this passage about me? Its first target is the unbelieving rich who exploited the church, but it searches anyone with more than they need, which includes most readers in the West. The questions it asks are not how much you have, but how you got it, whether you are hoarding it, and whether anyone has gone without because of you. Paul gives the positive command: the rich are to do good, to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, so storing up treasure as a good foundation for the future (1 Timothy 6:17–19). Wealth held open-handed is a tool for the kingdom. Wealth clutched is a witness for the prosecution.

How do I know if I am hoarding rather than saving wisely? Saving for real needs, a home, your children, old age, emergencies, is wise and biblical (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). Hoarding is keeping far beyond need out of fear or love of money, while needs around you go unmet. Some honest tests: Do I give generously and regularly, or only from what is left over? Does my security rest in my savings or in God? If God asked me to give a large part away, would I feel grief or freedom? Is there a need in front of me that I could meet and am refusing to? Talk it through with a wise believer; money is the area where we deceive ourselves most easily.

In a sentence. Now listen, you rich people, weep and wail because of the misery that is coming on you. Your wealth has rotted, and moths have eaten your clothes. Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and eat your flesh like fire. You have hoarded wealth in the last days.

On a Tuesday. Is there wealth you are hoarding that could help someone in need? Open your wardrobe, your garage, your savings account, and ask what is sitting there unused while someone else goes without. Put something to work for God’s kingdom this week: give it, lend it, share it. Let nothing you own become a witness against you.

For worship. The Judge who will call the hoarders to account is the one who emptied himself of every treasure. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). He had nowhere to lay his head, and he was buried in a borrowed tomb. And he has laid up for us an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4), where moth and rust do not destroy and thieves do not break in and steal. Gold will corrode in the last day, but those who belong to him will shine like the stars for ever. He is our treasure, and he does not rust.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.

Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud. Now the specific charge, and it is not vague. The labourers (ergatai) are day-labourers in the harvest. Kept back by fraud (apesterēmenos) is withheld, defrauded. The Old Testament is explicit about this. A hired man was to be paid the same day, before sunset, because he is poor and counts on it (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). A day-labourer had no savings; the wage bought that evening’s food. To withhold it overnight was not a cashflow decision. It was a family going without supper.

Are crying out against you. Crying out (krazei) is shouting, screaming. There are two cries: the wages themselves cry, and so do the men. The image is the one used of Abel’s blood crying to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10): the unpaid wages cry for justice.

And the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. Lord of hosts (kyriou Sabaōth) is the military title: the LORD of armies, God as the commander of heaven’s armies, the mighty warrior who defends the oppressed (Isaiah 5:9; Romans 9:29). James chooses it deliberately. The defrauded workers have no advocate, no court and no standing. Their case has been heard by the commander of heaven’s armies. I have surely seen the affliction of my people, God said at the burning bush, and have heard their cry (Exodus 3:7; Deuteronomy 24:15).

You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. The two words are soft living (etryphēsate, lived delicately) and wanton pleasure (espatalēsate, lived for pleasure, as in 1 Timothy 5:6), like the rich man in Jesus’ parable who feasted sumptuously every day while Lazarus lay at his gate (Luke 16:19). And the contrast is the whole point: this luxury was funded by that unpaid wage. James is not condemning wealth in the abstract but a specific transfer: comfort at one table bought by hunger at another.

You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. A terrible image. Like cattle fattened for the slaughter, they have stuffed themselves, not realising that the day of judgment is coming (Jeremiah 12:3; 25:34). The beast is grazing contentedly, and it does not know what the day is for. They took their prosperity as evidence of favour; James says it was fattening. Their luxury is preparing them for destruction.

You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. Condemned (katedikasate) is a courtroom word, sentenced in court: the machinery of law used against a man who could not afford it (2:6). Murdered (ephoneusate): the rich used the courts to strip the poor of land and livelihood, effectively killing them. The righteous person (ton dikaion) is the innocent poor generally, and perhaps also an allusion to Jesus, the Righteous One (Acts 3:14; 7:52), killed by the powerful.

He does not resist you. And the last sentence is the most terrible: he is not resisting (ouk antitassetai). There was never a contest. The righteous poor are helpless, or choose not to retaliate, like Jesus, who was oppressed and afflicted, yet opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7; Matthew 5:39). Some take it as a question: does not God oppose you? That would echo 4:6, where the same verb says God opposes the proud. Either way, the powerless man’s silence is not the end of the matter.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should take revenge. James immediately calls for patience (v. 7). God will judge. Nor does it make all employers wicked; it condemns injustice.

What does this mean for me as an employer, a customer or a manager? If you employ or pay anyone, pay them fairly and on time, and do not use your power to squeeze those who cannot push back. That includes the cleaner, the builder, the freelancer whose invoice sits unpaid for months. Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1). As a customer, it is worth asking, as far as you reasonably can, whether the cheapness of what you buy depends on someone else’s exploitation. No one can know everything, but a Christian should care, and act where he can.

Is God on the side of the poor? God is on the side of justice, and Scripture repeatedly shows him as the defender of the poor, the widow and the oppressed, who hears their cry when no one else does (Psalm 146:7–9). But that does not mean the poor are saved by being poor, or the rich condemned by being rich; salvation is by grace through faith in Christ for all. What it means is that the oppressed have a Judge, and oppressors will answer to him. The church should share his heart: speaking up for the voiceless, and refusing to flatter the powerful.

In a sentence. Look! The wages you failed to pay the workers who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty. You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened yourselves for the day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the innocent, who were not opposing you.

On a Tuesday. If you employ or pay anyone, are you paying them fairly and promptly? Check this week whether there is any bill, wage or debt you owe that you have been sitting on, and pay it. If you are the one who has been defrauded, bring your cry to the Lord of hosts, plainly and in detail. He hears the cries of the underpaid.

For worship. The Lord of hosts hears the cry of a farmhand. The God who commands the armies of heaven bends his ear to the man who was cheated of a day’s pay. And the Righteous One did not resist those who condemned him. He stood silent before a rigged court, was condemned by the powerful and murdered by the rich and religious, and in his silence he bore the sins of oppressors and oppressed alike. His blood cries out like Abel’s, but it speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24): not vengeance, but forgiveness for all who come to him.
verseByVerse.note: The Law required day-labourers to be paid the same day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–20 — Patience, Prayer, and Going After the Wanderer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James urges suffering believers to wait patiently for the Lord’s coming, as a farmer waits through the seasons for the rain and the crop, strengthening their hearts because the coming is near. They must not grumble against one another, for the Judge is already at the door. They can look to the prophets and to Job, whose endurance showed how compassionate and merciful the Lord is. They are not to bolster their words with oaths, but let a plain yes or no be enough. Anyone suffering should pray; anyone cheerful should sing praise. The sick should call the church’s elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the Lord’s name; the prayer of faith will restore them, and any sins will be forgiven. Believers should confess sins to one another and pray for one another, for the prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah’s was, though he was an ordinary man. Finally, anyone who brings back a believer who has wandered from the truth rescues that person from death and covers many sins.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prayer of Faith

Be patient as the farmer waits for the rains, because the Lord is coming. Pray in every condition; the prayer of faith is prayer submitted to God's will, and Elijah was a man like us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Pressed from outside, the congregation was grumbling against one another.

Now: The letter ends by sending ordinary believers after the one who has wandered.

verseByVerse.quote: Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.

Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. The address changes back to the congregation, and everything softens. Therefore: because God will judge the oppressors. The word here is not the hypomonē of chapter 1, which is endurance under weight. It is makrothymia: long-tempered, slow to burn, bear patiently, do not retaliate, the patience shown toward difficult people. Which is exactly right after verses 1–6. Having heard their oppressors denounced, the natural next move is to take matters up themselves. James says: wait.

Until the coming of the Lord. And that is the ground of it. Coming (parousia) means presence, arrival, a word used of a king’s official visit: Christ’s return (Matthew 24:27; 1 Thessalonians 4:15; 2 Peter 3:4). He is not telling them the injustice does not matter or that it will resolve itself. He has just said the Lord of hosts has heard. The waiting is not for nothing to happen; it is for someone else to act. On that day all wrongs will be put right.

See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth. Waits (ekdechetai) is expects, waits eagerly; precious (timion) is valuable, because his livelihood depends on the harvest.

Being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. The picture is precisely local. In Israel the early rain came in autumn, softening the ground for sowing, and the late rain in spring, swelling the grain before harvest (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24; Joel 2:23), and between them lie months in which nothing can be done. The farmer’s patience is not passivity: he has ploughed and sown, and he will reap. But there is a stretch in the middle where all the activity in the world would not bring the harvest forward by a day, and the mark of a farmer is that he knows it. The harvest is certain, but it comes at its proper time.

You also, be patient. Establish your hearts. Establish (stērixate) means to make firm, strengthen, to prop. Settle your hearts firmly, so you do not waver. Waiting is not merely refraining; it requires something to be shored up.

For the coming of the Lord is at hand. Is at hand (ēngiken) is perfect tense: has drawn near, and is near. Not far off. That is the whole reason the waiting is bearable. The early church lived in expectation of Christ’s return (Romans 13:11–12; Philippians 4:5; 1 Peter 4:7; Revelation 22:20). The New Testament’s consistent posture is imminence: not a date, but a nearness that makes patience reasonable rather than resigned. Since his first coming, the end has been near, and his return could happen at any time.

Where Christians differ: was James wrong about the nearness of Christ’s return? Critics argue that the early church expected Jesus to return within their lifetime and was mistaken. Verdict: near in the New Testament describes the character of the whole age since Christ’s resurrection: the next great event in God’s plan is Christ’s return, and nothing must happen first that would prevent it from being near. God’s timetable is not ours; with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay is God’s patience, giving time for repentance. Christ will come once, visibly and gloriously, to judge and to renew all things; believers in every generation must live ready.

Was James wrong, since two thousand years have passed? At hand means that Christ’s coming is the next great event in God’s plan and could come at any time, not that it would come within a few years. Peter answers the same objection: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and his delay is patience, giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should set dates for Christ’s return; concerning that day and hour no one knows (Matthew 24:36). It means they should live in constant readiness.

What will actually happen when he comes? Scripture describes one visible, glorious return of Christ at the end of this age, seen by all (Acts 1:11; Revelation 1:7). There is no secret coming beforehand. At his coming the dead will be raised, believers who are alive will be changed and caught up to meet him, and he will judge the living and the dead (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52; Matthew 25:31–46). The wicked will go away into eternal punishment, and the righteous into eternal life; and God will make all things new, a new heaven and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). That is the harvest the farmer waits for.

If I am suffering injustice now, does patience mean I should not seek justice? No. Patience forbids revenge and bitterness, not lawful justice. Paul appealed to Caesar and insisted on his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 25:11). If you are wronged, you may use proper means: the courts, the police, the employment tribunal, the church’s elders. If you are being abused, get to safety and report it. What James forbids is taking vengeance into your own hands, and the despair that thinks God has forgotten. Pursue justice by right means, and leave the final reckoning to the Lord, who will repay (Romans 12:19).

In a sentence. Be patient, then, brothers and sisters, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer waits for the land to yield its valuable crop, patiently waiting for the autumn and spring rains. You too, be patient and stand firm, because the Lord’s coming is near.

On a Tuesday. If you are suffering injustice, wait patiently for the Lord, and do your sowing while you wait: keep praying, keep doing good, keep your heart propped up with his promises. Find one promise of his coming and put it where you will see it every morning. And ask yourself honestly whether you would be glad if he came today. If not, what would you want to put right first? Do that.

For worship. The Lord is coming. The one who came first in weakness, to a manger and a cross, will come again in glory, with the clouds, and every eye will see him. He will wipe away every tear, judge every wrong, and raise his people from the dust. The farmer’s waiting ends in harvest, and the harvest is Christ himself, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, and all who belong to him gathered in. He who testifies to these things says, Surely I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! (Revelation 22:20).
verseByVerse.note: In Israel the early rain came in autumn, at sowing, and the late rain in spring, before harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.

Do not grumble against one another, brothers. The word (stenazete) means to groan or sigh, and it is not the sound of open quarrelling but of muttering. The complaint under the breath, the remark to one person about another. Under pressure, believers can turn on each other, like Israel grumbling in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:10).

Pressure goes sideways. The placing is shrewd. James has just told them to be patient toward their oppressors, and he knows exactly where that pressure goes. Pressure from outside that cannot be discharged outward is discharged sideways, onto the people nearest. A congregation under strain from without turns on itself, and the form it takes is rarely dramatic. It is grumbling. The same thing happens in families under financial pressure, in churches in decline, in teams under a difficult boss.

So that you may not be judged. The warning connects directly to 4:11–12, where judging a brother usurped the one Lawgiver’s office. To grumble is to pass sentence privately, and the man who convenes his own court will find himself in somebody else’s. Judge not, that you be not judged (Matthew 7:1).

Behold, the Judge is standing at the door. It is one of the most vivid sentences in the letter, and it does two things at once. The Judge is Christ (Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1), and standing at the door (pro tōn thyrōn hestēken) means he has taken his stand before the doors, about to enter (Matthew 24:33; Revelation 3:20). It is a comfort: the oppressed of verses 1–6 are told their Judge has not merely heard the case; he has arrived at the building. And it is a warning to the same people in the same breath. He is at the door of their room too, and he is about to walk in on the muttering. James gives them no opportunity to enjoy the judgment of their enemies without noticing where they are standing themselves.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid honestly bringing grievances to God in prayer, as the psalms do, or addressing real issues with others in love. It forbids a complaining, resentful spirit toward fellow believers.

What is the difference between grumbling and lament? Lament takes the complaint to God; grumbling takes it to everyone except God, and except the person concerned. Lament is honest about pain and ends in trust: how long, O LORD? but I have trusted in your steadfast love (Psalm 13:1, 5). Grumbling is resentful and goes round in circles. Lament seeks God’s help; grumbling seeks allies. If you have a real grievance against a brother, go to him (Matthew 18:15). If you have a grief you cannot fix, take it to God. Either way, stop muttering.

In a sentence. Don’t grumble against one another, brothers and sisters, or you will be judged. The Judge is standing at the door!

On a Tuesday. Is there a fellow believer you have been grumbling about? Stop, pray for them, and deal with any real issue in love. For one week, every time you notice yourself about to mutter, turn it into a prayer instead: for the person, and for your own heart. And if you lead anything, a family, a team, a church ministry, watch for the grumbling that comes from pressure, and take some of the pressure off.

For worship. The Judge at the door is the Saviour who knocks. Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Revelation 3:20). He stands at the door of every grumbling church not only to judge but to come in and eat with us. He bore with the grumbling of Israel for forty years, and the grumbling of his disciples for three. His patience with us is the reason we can be patient with one another.

verseByVerse.quote: As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.

As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets. An example (hypodeigma) is a pattern, a model. Suffering (kakopathia) is enduring hardship; patience (makrothymia) is long-tempered endurance. The choice is pointed. The prophets, like Jeremiah, Elijah and Isaiah, suffered rejection, imprisonment and death (Matthew 5:12; 23:29–37; Hebrews 11:32–38).

Who spoke in the name of the Lord. The prophets were not men who suffered despite their faithfulness; they suffered because of it, and specifically because they spoke in the Lord’s name. Even God’s own messengers suffered. Faithfulness does not guarantee an easy life. James is telling a congregation being oppressed for their faith that they are in the succession, not the exception.

Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. And here the word returns to hypomonē, the endurance of chapter 1, and to blessed (makarizomen, we call happy), which picks up 1:12 exactly. The letter is closing its own circle. Looking back, we honour those who endured.

You have heard of the steadfastness of Job. The example repays thought, because Job was not patient in the sense the phrase has acquired in English. He protested at length, demanded an audience, and told God he had a case to argue. What he did was not let go, which is what hypomonē means. He never cursed God or abandoned faith: the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD; though he slay me, I will hope in him; I know that my Redeemer lives (Job 1:21–22; 2:10; 13:15; 19:25–27). James’s idea of steadfastness plainly has room for a man who complains bitterly and will not walk away. Endurance is not silence but holding on.

And you have seen the purpose of the Lord. The phrase (telos) means the end, the outcome, the goal: how it turned out. God restored Job, doubled his blessings, and revealed himself to him (Job 42:10–17). Job could not see it from inside; the reader of the book can, and that is the advantage James is handing them. God had a purpose in Job’s suffering, though Job did not know it at the time.

How the Lord is compassionate and merciful. That is a remarkable conclusion to draw from the book of Job, which contains no explanation of his suffering at all. James does not say the Lord explained himself. He says the end of the story showed what he was like. Compassionate is polysplanchnos, full of tender mercy, a word perhaps coined by James; merciful (oiktirmōn) is pitying. And the two ideas he chooses are the ancient self-description of God at Sinai: the LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious (Exodus 34:6; Psalm 103:8). Behind the suffering was a compassionate God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every sufferer will receive double earthly blessing like Job. The ultimate end for believers is eternal glory: the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us (Romans 8:18). Nor does it mean God causes suffering carelessly; he is compassionate even in allowing it.

Is it all right to complain to God the way Job did? Yes, if you complain to him and not away from him. The book of Psalms is full of honest complaint, and God included it in Scripture to teach us how to pray in the dark. Job’s friends, who defended God with tidy explanations, were rebuked; Job, who wrestled honestly, was vindicated (Job 42:7). What God did correct in Job was the edge of accusation, the demand that God answer to him (Job 38–40). So pour out your heart, ask your questions, and then, like Job, put your hand over your mouth before his majesty and keep trusting.

Will God give me back what I lost, as he did for Job? He may, in this life, in some measure; he often does restore. But he has not promised that every loss will be repaid here. The deeper promise is that nothing is finally lost for those in Christ. The children Job buried were not replaced by the new ones, but Job looked for a Redeemer who would stand on the earth at the last. Our end, our telos, is resurrection, reunion, and a world made new. The compassion of the Lord will be seen fully not at the end of a chapter but at the end of the story.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, as an example of patience in the face of suffering, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. As you know, we count as blessed those who have persevered. You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen what the Lord finally brought about. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

On a Tuesday. Read Job 42 today, and then Job 19:25–27. If you are in the middle of your own Job chapter, tell God honestly how it feels, and then tell him, even through clenched teeth, that you are staying. And if someone you know is suffering, do not be Job’s friends. Sit with them, listen, weep with them, and resist the urge to explain.

For worship. The end of the Lord in Job’s story is a glimpse; the end of the Lord in history is a cross and an empty tomb. There we see how compassionate and merciful he is. The Son of God took Job’s place and more: stripped of everything, mocked by his friends, abandoned, crying out, why have you forsaken me? And he did not let go. Because he endured to the end, every steadfast saint is blessed. I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth, and in my flesh I shall see God (Job 19:25–26).

verseByVerse.quote: But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.

But above all, my brothers, do not swear. The phrase is arresting. Above all (pro pantōn, before all things) what? Not the whole letter; James can hardly mean this matters more than faith and works. It is most likely a way of flagging a final point of importance, or perhaps above all in the context of suffering: under pressure, people make rash oaths or call on God in frustration. Swear (omnyete) is take an oath. And it echoes his brother almost word for word (Matthew 5:33–37).

Either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath. The oath-taking in view is not courtroom testimony, and it is not blasphemy. It is the habit of reinforcing your own speech: swearing by heaven, by earth, by the temple, by your own head. Jews avoided using God’s name in oaths, swearing by heaven or earth instead, and a graded system grew up in which some oaths were held binding and others were understood to be escape routes (Matthew 23:16–22). Jesus and James reject this game: all speech is spoken before God. That is what makes it a speech problem rather than a religious one, and it belongs to a letter that has said so much about the tongue. A man who must swear to be believed has admitted that his ordinary word is not reliable.

But let your yes be yes and your no be no. The remedy is not more solemn language but less. Be so consistently honest that your simple word is enough. If a man’s plain word holds, he needs no machinery to prop it up, and the machinery is itself evidence that something is wrong.

So that you may not fall under condemnation. Condemnation (krisis) is judgment. The stakes are higher than the subject seems to warrant, and that is the point. A graded oath system is a device for deceiving while appearing truthful, and God is not deceived by the gradations. Dishonesty and frivolous oaths bring God’s judgment.

Where Christians differ: are all oaths forbidden? Some groups, such as Quakers and Anabaptists, refuse to take any oath, including in court. Verdict: James and Jesus forbid casual, frivolous, evasive oaths in everyday speech, and the habit of using oaths to manipulate. They do not forbid solemn, lawful oaths when required by proper authority, as in court. God himself swore oaths (Hebrews 6:13–18); Jesus answered under oath before the high priest (Matthew 26:63–64); Paul called God as witness (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23). The Westminster Confession rightly regards lawful oaths as part of religious worship (Westminster 22.1). The heart of the command is simple, consistent truthfulness.

Does this forbid all oaths, even in court or at a wedding? Quakers and many Anabaptists have held that it does. But God himself swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), Paul calls God as witness (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23), and Jesus answered when put under oath (Matthew 26:63–64). The Reformed confessions therefore allow solemn and lawful oaths. What James forbids is casual swearing, oaths used to make some words binding and others not. A Christian’s plain word should be enough. Wedding vows and the solemn promises of church membership or ordination are lawful vows made before God, and should be kept.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may lie as long as they do not swear. It means all their words should be true.

What about phrases like I swear, honestly, or to be honest with you? They are the modern version of the same habit, and worth noticing in your own speech. If you need to say honestly, what does that imply about the rest of what you say? Most of these are thoughtless habits rather than wicked oaths, but James invites us to drop the props and let our plain words carry the weight. The same goes for exaggeration: always, never, literally, everyone. Truthful people speak plainly, and their plain speech is trusted.

The question this puts. The practical question this puts is small and searching. Do the people who know you best need you to insist? A person whose word is simply good has no use for emphasis, and the habit of over-assurance is usually a sign that somewhere the plain word has stopped being enough.

In a sentence. Above all, my brothers and sisters, do not swear, whether by heaven or by earth or by anything else. All you need to say is a simple Yes or No. Otherwise you will be condemned.

On a Tuesday. Be someone whose word can be trusted without oaths or exaggeration. Keep every promise you make this week, including the small ones: the call back, the time you said you would arrive, the thing you said you would look into. If you cannot keep one, say so honestly and early. A plain yes that is always kept is worth more than a thousand oaths.

For worship. God’s yes is yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). He swore by himself to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, so that we might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us (Hebrews 6:13–18). And Jesus, the Amen, the faithful and true witness, never once needed to swear to be believed, because every word he spoke was true. The God whose word cannot fail is shaping a people whose words can be trusted.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.

Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Three questions in quick succession, each with a one-word answer, and together they map the whole emotional range of a Christian life onto prayer and praise. Suffering (kakopathei) covers hardship generally, misfortune, the same root as the suffering of the prophets in verse 10. And the response is not resignation, not stoicism, and not a search for the reason. Pray (proseuchesthō, keep praying). The right response to trouble is not grumbling (v. 9), swearing (v. 12), or despair, but prayer. Bring it to God.

Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise. And that is the half we habitually neglect. Cheerful (euthymei) is in good spirits, happy; sing praise (psalletō) is to sing psalms, sing with music (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16). Most Christians know that trouble should send them to God; far fewer treat gladness as equally directional.

Every day goes up. The pairing is the point. There is no condition in which the answer is to do nothing Godward. Trouble goes up as prayer, joy goes up as song, and between them they cover every day anybody has. It is also a quiet correction of a besetting error, which is to treat God as an emergency service. A man who prays only when suffering has a relationship with his own need rather than with God, and the second question is there to expose it.

The gladness itself. And note that James does not require the cheerful man to become solemn before he approaches. The gladness itself is what goes up. This is the same writer who told them to count trials joy and to let laughter turn to mourning when repenting; he is not against any emotion. He is against every emotion being kept to oneself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prayer is only for the suffering and praise only for the happy. Both belong in every season: rejoice in the Lord always; in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4:4–6). But each situation has its natural response directed to God.

What if I am neither suffering nor cheerful, just flat and numb? Then bring the numbness. The Psalms include prayers from people who felt nothing but distance (Psalm 88). Read a psalm aloud and let its words carry you when your own are gone. Keep the habits of prayer and worship going even when they feel mechanical; they are like keeping a fire laid, ready to catch. Tell God plainly that you feel nothing. And if the flatness persists for a long time, talk to someone; it may be depression, which needs care, not condemnation.

I cannot sing well. Does that matter? Not at all. God is not listening for quality but for hearts. Singing in Scripture is commanded for all God’s people, not just the musical (Psalm 100:1–2), and the joyful noise counts. Sing in the car, hum while you work, read a psalm of praise aloud if singing is impossible. The point is that joy is directed to God rather than kept to yourself.

In a sentence. Is anyone among you in trouble? They should pray. Is anyone happy? They should sing songs of praise.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your mood today, take it to God: pray if you are struggling, sing if you are glad. Notice which you find more natural. If you only ever pray when things go wrong, set yourself to thank and praise God for three specific good things each evening this week. And if you only ever sing in church, try singing one verse of a hymn alone.

For worship. There is no mood God does not welcome. He bends low to hear the groaning prayer and delights in the joyful song. And the Son himself prayed with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7), and sang a hymn with his disciples on the night he was betrayed (Matthew 26:30). He has gone before us into every human condition, and now he leads the praise of his people: in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (Hebrews 2:12). Whether we weep or laugh, we never come to God alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.

Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church. Sick (asthenei) is weak, ill, probably seriously ill, since the elders come to him rather than him going to them. Note who initiates: the sick man calls (proskalesasthō, summon). And note the plural (presbyterous): not the gifted individual but the elders, the ordinary appointed leadership of the local congregation. Prayer for the sick is not left to individuals with special gifts, but is part of the ordinary pastoral care of the church’s elders.

And let them pray over him. Pray over (proseuxasthōsan ep’ auton) perhaps with the laying on of hands. The main verb is pray; prayer is the main action.

Anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. The anointing (aleipsantes, rubbing with oil) is a participle, subordinate to the praying. Oil in that world was both medicine, as when the Samaritan poured oil and wine on the wounds (Luke 10:34), and a sign of setting someone apart for God (Mark 6:13). Here it may serve both purposes: practical care, and a symbol of consecrating the sick person to God’s care and of the Spirit’s presence. Whether the gesture is chiefly medical or symbolic, it is not the operative thing. The praying is, and it is done in the name of the Lord: by Christ’s authority, depending on him.

And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick. The prayer of faith (hē euchē tēs pisteōs) is prayer offered in trust in God. The power is not in the oil or the elders, but in God, who answers prayer. Save (sōsei) means rescue, heal, restore: here primarily physical healing, though it can include spiritual restoration.

And the Lord will raise him up. Raise up (egerei): from the sickbed. The Lord does the healing.

Handled honestly. This has to be handled honestly, because read flatly it promises that every believing prayer heals, and every Christian knows it does not. Several things keep it from meaning that. The letter itself has just said that asking can be answered no when the asking is wrong (4:3). Paul prayed three times about his thorn and was refused (2 Corinthians 12:8–9), and left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). And the prayer of faith is not prayer accompanied by sufficient confidence: faith of that kind would be a work, and its absence would make the sick man’s illness his own fault, which is precisely the cruelty this verse has often been used to inflict. Better to take it as prayer offered in submission to God’s will, which is what faith always is in this letter. And the verbs support it. Save and raise up are both words with a larger reach than physical recovery, and the final raising up is guaranteed for every believer whether or not this illness ends.

And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven. The conditional is careful and merciful. If: not all sickness is caused by sin (John 9:2–3), but some is (1 Corinthians 11:30). If sin is involved, confession and prayer bring forgiveness. James allows that sin may be involved and refuses to assume it, which is exactly the balance Job’s friends failed to keep.

Where Christians differ: is this a sacrament of last rites, or a promise of guaranteed healing? Roman Catholic teaching sees this as the sacrament of the anointing of the sick (formerly extreme unction, given to the dying). Some charismatic teaching takes it as a guarantee that God always heals in response to faith. Verdict: James describes prayer for the sick aimed at recovery, not preparation for death, so it is not last rites; and Scripture names only two sacraments, or ordinances, that Christ commanded his church to keep: baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Nor is it an unconditional guarantee: God answers according to his will (1 John 5:14), and even Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20) and was not healed of his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). This passage gives a continuing pattern for church life: elders praying with faith for the sick, using oil as a sign if they choose, trusting God to heal as he wills. This is distinct from the apostolic sign gifts of healing, which have ceased; God still heals in answer to prayer.

Is this the basis for the Roman Catholic sacrament of the anointing of the sick? It was once given mainly to the dying as last rites. But James speaks of anointing the sick to pray for their recovery, the Lord will raise him up, not to prepare them for death, and the healing comes from the prayer and the Lord, not from a sacrament.

Should churches still anoint with oil? The oil was used in the ancient world both as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God; here, with prayer in the Lord’s name, it is most likely a sign. Elders may still pray over the sick and anoint them, and this does not oppose medicine; Christians should use doctors and pray. God often heals, but not always; Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean sickness is always caused by sin or lack of faith. Nor does it mean believers should refuse medical treatment; oil was itself a medicine, and Luke was a physician.

We prayed, and my loved one died. Was our faith too weak? No. Hear this clearly: the death of someone you prayed for is not proof that you lacked faith or that God did not hear. Faith is not a force that obliges God; it is trust in his wisdom and love, and sometimes his answer is to take his child home. For the believer, death is the final healing: the Lord raised them up, not from the sickbed but into his presence, where there is no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Your prayers were not wasted; they were part of carrying your loved one to the Lord. Grieve freely, as one who has hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and do not let anyone load you with guilt this verse never imposed.

How do I actually call for the elders? Simply ask. Contact your pastor or one of the elders, explain that you are seriously ill, and ask them to come and pray with you, as James says. They may come to your home or the hospital, read Scripture, ask whether there is anything you want to confess, pray for healing and for God’s will, and perhaps anoint you with a little oil on the forehead. It is not a ritual to be performed correctly but an act of the church’s care. Many believers never ask because they do not want to be a bother. James says: call them.

In a sentence. Is anyone among you ill? They should call the elders of the church to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer offered in faith will make the sick person well; the Lord will raise them up. If they have sinned, they will be forgiven.

On a Tuesday. If you are seriously ill, call your elders to pray for you. Elders, make this a regular part of your care for the flock: visit the sick, pray over them, and do not wait to be asked twice. And all of us can pray for the sick in our church by name this week, and send a message or a meal to let them know.

For worship. The Lord will raise him up. The one who says it is the Lord who healed every disease in Galilee, who took our illnesses and bore our diseases (Matthew 8:17), and who was himself raised from the dead as the firstfruits of a great resurrection. Every healing in answer to prayer is a foretaste of that day; every believer who dies is waiting for it. He was wounded for our transgressions, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). In the end, no prayer of faith for a child of God goes unanswered: every one of them will be raised up.
verseByVerse.note: Oil was used as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.

Therefore, confess your sins to one another. The therefore follows the conditional clause about sin. Since sin may sometimes lie behind trouble, deal with it, and deal with it in the open. Confess (exomologeisthe) is openly acknowledge, admit. And note the direction: to one another (allēlois). Not to a priest, and not to God only. James is describing something mutual and horizontal: ordinary Christians telling each other the truth about themselves. It requires no office and it is available in any congregation, and it is almost universally avoided.

Why it works. The reason it is avoided is the reason it works. Sin kept private grows in the dark and is fed by the fear of exposure; the man who has told somebody has already lost the thing that was protecting it. When I kept silent, my bones wasted away (Psalm 32:3–5). Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (Proverbs 28:13). Sin hidden festers; sin confessed can be healed.

And pray for one another. The pairing matters. Confession alone leaves a person exposed, so James joins it to intercession. You tell someone, and they pray for you. Believers support each other in the fight against sin.

That you may be healed. Healed (iathēte): physical healing in context, but also spiritual and relational healing (Hebrews 12:13; 1 Peter 2:24). Unconfessed sin damages body, soul and community. Healing here includes the whole person, the body in verse 15 and the soul restored through confession. And not every sickness comes from sin; James says if he has committed sins (v. 15), and Jesus denied that the man born blind suffered for anyone’s sin (John 9:3).

The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working. Has great power (poly ischyei) is is very strong, accomplishes much. The last phrase (energoumenē) is difficult and probably means in its working: prayer is not a stored potency but something powerful in operation, effective as it is being prayed. God works powerfully through the prayers of ordinary believers.

Righteous is not a rare class. And righteous (dikaios) should not be read as a rare spiritual class, or the whole verse becomes a discouragement to the very people it is written for. It means not a sinless super-saint, but a believer who lives in right relationship with God, whose sins are confessed and forgiven, as the verse has just described. The next verse settles it decisively: the righteous man James has in mind is Elijah, and the first thing he says about him is that he was made of exactly the same stuff we are.

Where Christians differ: is confession to a priest required? Roman Catholic teaching requires confession of serious sins to a priest for absolution. Verdict: James commands mutual confession to one another, among all believers, not confession to a priestly class. Forgiveness comes from God through Christ, our only mediator (1 Timothy 2:5; 1 John 1:9). Confessing sins to a trusted fellow believer or elder is a valuable means of grace, accountability and healing, but it is not a sacrament, and no human being stands between the believer and God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every sin must be confessed publicly to the whole church. Wisdom guides what to confess and to whom: a sin against a person to that person; private struggles to a trusted friend or elder.

Whom should I confess to, and how? Choose a mature, trustworthy believer of the same sex, or an elder, someone who will keep confidence, point you to Christ, pray for you and help you fight. Be specific rather than vague; I have been struggling is not confession. Say what you did. Then ask them to pray, there and then if possible, and to ask you about it again. If you have sinned against someone, confess to that person and seek to make it right. And remember that you are confessing to a fellow sinner, not to a judge: the one you tell also needs grace.

What if the person I confess to betrays my trust? That is a real risk, and it is why you should choose carefully. A believer who gossips about a confession has sinned seriously and should be lovingly confronted. But do not let the fear of that stop you entirely; most Christians, when trusted with a confession, are humbled and honoured, and keep it. Start small, with someone you have good reason to trust, and let the friendship grow. And if a confession involves a crime, particularly harm to a child or vulnerable person, it must not be kept secret; protecting the vulnerable comes before confidentiality.

In a sentence. So confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you have hidden? Confess it to a trusted believer this week, and ask them to pray for you. If you have never done this, it will feel frightening; do it anyway, and notice how much lighter you feel afterwards. And be the kind of person others can confess to: unshockable, discreet, quick to pray and quick to point to Christ.

For worship. We confess to one another, but there is one Mediator who stands between us and God, and he is not a priest who needs forgiveness himself. He is the Righteous One, whose prayer has infinite power because he is the Son. If anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:1–2). If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). The darkness where sin hid is flooded with his light, and the light does not condemn. It heals.

verseByVerse.quote: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.

Elijah was a man with a nature like ours. James puts that first, before anything about the miracle, and it is the whole reason he chose the example. With a nature like ours (homoiopathēs hēmin) means of like feelings, subject to the same weaknesses. Elijah is the most spectacular figure in the prophetic history: fire from heaven on Carmel, the ravens, the chariot. He is exactly the man a discouraged congregation would cite as proof that prayer works for other people. So James disarms the objection in the first clause: same nature, same stuff.

Not immune to despair. And the account bears him out. This is the prophet who, immediately after the greatest answered prayer in the Old Testament, ran into the desert, sat down under a broom tree and asked God to let him die (1 Kings 19:3–4). Whatever Elijah was, he was not temperamentally immune to despair. Elijah was not a superhuman. Ordinary people can pray powerfully.

And he prayed fervently that it might not rain. The Greek (proseuchē prosēuxato) is a Hebrew idiom, literally he prayed with prayer, which conveys earnestness. And notice that 1 Kings 17:1 records his announcement of the drought rather than a prayer for it; his prayer is implied. James, or the tradition he knows, understands the announcement to have rested on prayer, which says something about where a prophet’s public word comes from. The drought was God’s judgment on Ahab’s idolatry, as the law had warned (Deuteronomy 11:16–17).

And for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. The Lord gives the same figure (Luke 4:25). 1 Kings 18:1 says in the third year, likely counting from Elijah’s time at Zarephath; the total drought, including the dry season, was three and a half years.

Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit. On Mount Carmel, after the defeat of Baal’s prophets, Elijah bowed down with his face between his knees and prayed, and sent his servant to look seven times, and rain came (1 Kings 18:41–45). Both directions, the withholding and the giving, came through the same channel. God answered prayer both ways. And the closing image is agricultural, which returns to the farmer of verse 7 waiting for the early and late rains. The letter’s pictures are tying themselves together as it ends.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can command the weather by prayer whenever we wish. Elijah prayed according to God’s revealed will and word (1 Kings 17:1; 18:1). It means God hears and answers the prayers of ordinary believers powerfully, according to his will.

Can I pray for things like rain, or a job, or a parking space? Yes. Nothing that concerns you is too small to bring to your Father, who numbers the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30). Elijah prayed about the weather because it mattered to God’s purposes and to his people. Pray about everything, and hold every request with an open hand: your will be done. The difference between Elijah’s prayer and a superstitious one is not the size of the request but its submission. He prayed in line with what God had said, and he prayed for God’s name to be honoured.

What does fervent prayer look like for an ordinary person? Not necessarily long or loud, but earnest and persistent. Elijah sent his servant to look seven times. Fervent prayer means praying as though it matters, because it does: specific requests rather than vague wishes, prayer that keeps coming back day after day, prayer that grounds itself in God’s promises and asks for his glory. It might be one honest sentence prayed every morning for a wayward child for twenty years. God is not impressed by eloquence. He hears the cry of his children.

In a sentence. Elijah was a human being, just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth produced its crops.

On a Tuesday. Don’t think your prayers are too weak to matter. Elijah was just like you, discouragement and all. Choose one thing that you know is in line with God’s will, the salvation of a friend, the growth of your church, the healing of a broken relationship, and pray for it earnestly every day this week. Write down the date you started. And keep looking at the horizon, like Elijah’s servant, for the small cloud.

For worship. Elijah prayed, and the heavens were shut and opened. Jesus prayed, and the heavens were torn open and the Spirit descended (Mark 1:10). The greatest prophet’s prayers moved the rain; the Son’s prayers move the Father’s heart, because he is the beloved Son. And he prayed for us: I am praying for them (John 17:9). The God who answered a depressed prophet under a broom tree, sending an angel with bread and water and a gentle whisper, is the same God who hears us. He has not changed. The rain he gives now is his Spirit, poured out on thirsty ground.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah’s prayers are implied in 1 Kings; Jesus also gives the drought’s length as three and a half years.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.

My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth. The letter ends without a benediction, without greetings, without a signature. It simply stops, on the subject of somebody else’s soul. The verb (planēthē) is to be led astray, to go off course, to be deceived: the same root as our word planet, the wandering star. It is drift, not a decision. Nobody announces that they are leaving. From the truth means from the gospel and the way of life it requires. Someone in the church, a professing believer, drifting away.

And someone brings him back. Note how ordinary that someone is. Not the elders of verse 14, not a teacher, not an office. Someone: anyone who notices and goes after him. Brings back (epistrepsē) is turns around, restores. Every believer can be used to restore a wandering brother: you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness (Galatians 6:1; Matthew 18:15).

Let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death. That is as high a claim as could be made for a piece of personal pastoral work, and it is made about an unnamed church member. Save his soul from death: the wanderer’s soul, from spiritual and eternal death (1:15; Romans 6:23). God is the one who saves, but he uses believers as his instruments. Persisting in wandering leads to death; being turned back leads to life.

And will cover a multitude of sins. Cover (kalypsei) is hide, cover over, forgive. It echoes Proverbs 10:12, love covers all offences, also used in 1 Peter 4:8. The covering is God’s work; the human agent is the occasion of it, not the cause. The wanderer’s sins are forgiven when he returns.

Whose soul, and what death? The one who wanders is saved from eternal death by being brought back, and his many sins are covered by God’s forgiveness. Can a true believer wander so far as to be lost? Arminian Christians read the verse that way. The more likely reading is that the wanderer is either a believer whom God restores through the loving pursuit of others, or a professing member whose wandering would have shown that his faith was never real. Either way, the person who brings him back is God’s means of keeping him, which is why we must not leave wanderers alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we save people by our own power, or that the restorer earns forgiveness for his own sins. The sins covered are the wanderer’s, forgiven by God on his repentance. Nor does it mean true believers can finally be lost; God uses the restoring love of the church as one of his means of preserving his people.

A fitting last word. And that is a fitting last word. James has spent five chapters insisting that faith shows, that hearing is not doing, that religion is visited widows and unstained lives, and that the tongue reveals the heart. He ends by describing the most concrete act of love available to an ordinary Christian: noticing that someone has stopped coming, and going to find out why. The one who goes after him has been doing the very thing this whole letter has demanded, which is to be a doer. No farewell. Just a man walking out to look for somebody. The letter ends not with a farewell but with a mission: go after those who wander.

How do I approach someone who has drifted away? Go personally, not with a programme. Begin with friendship, not a lecture: a message, a coffee, an invitation to a meal. Tell them they are missed, and mean it. Listen more than you speak; there may be hurt, doubt, sin or simply busyness behind the drift, and you need to understand before you can help. Be honest, gently, about your concern for their soul when the time is right. Pray for them before and after. Do it in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself (Galatians 6:1), and do not give up after one attempt. The shepherd went after the one sheep until he found it (Luke 15:4).

What if they do not want to come back? Then you have still done what love requires, and the result belongs to God. Keep praying for them, keep the door open, keep being their friend if they will let you, without pretending that all is well. Some come back after many years, often remembering the one person who did not give up on them. If there is serious unrepentant sin, the church’s elders may need to be involved, as Jesus taught (Matthew 18:15–17), always with the aim of restoration. You cannot force anyone home. You can make sure they know the way back is open, and that someone is watching for them.

In a sentence. My brothers and sisters, if one of you wanders from the truth and someone brings that person back, remember this: whoever turns a sinner from the error of their way will save them from death and cover over a multitude of sins.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone who has drifted from church or from Christ? Think of a name: the family who stopped coming, the young person who left for university, the friend who went quiet after a hard year. Reach out to them this week with love, not condemnation. Do not wait until you know exactly what to say. James does not tell you to be eloquent. He tells you to go.

For worship. The letter ends with a man going after a wanderer, because that is what God is like. All we like sheep have gone astray (Isaiah 53:6), and the Good Shepherd left the ninety-nine and came after us, over the mountains and into the dark, until he found us and laid us on his shoulders rejoicing. He did not merely cover a multitude of sins; he bore them in his body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls (1 Peter 2:24–25). Every time one believer goes after another, it is the Shepherd’s love walking out of the door again.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you.<sup>2</sup>Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten.<sup>3</sup>Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days.<sup>4</sup>Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.<sup>5</sup>You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter.<sup>6</sup>You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.<sup>7</sup>Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains.<sup>8</sup>You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.<sup>9</sup>Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.<sup>10</sup>As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.<sup>11</sup>Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.<sup>12</sup>But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.<sup>13</sup>Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.<sup>14</sup>Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.<sup>15</sup>And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.<sup>16</sup>Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.<sup>17</sup>Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth.<sup>18</sup>Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.<sup>19</sup>My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back,<sup>20</sup>let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
